title: Physical, etheric and astral bodies
text: ← Courses · Theosophy: life and sensation Foundations · Reference for every course Physical, etheric and astral bodies A guided reference to three often-confused terms—and the “I” that helps distinguish them. Read this after Theosophy’s introduction to body, soul and spirit and before Lesson 3 on life and sensation. Return here whenever a course uses these terms. Begin with the comparison, then read each explanation and try the questions. These are members of one human being in Steiner’s account, not three separate people. Steiner presents the etheric and astral bodies as supersensible realities, accessible to a kind of perception he describes as going beyond ordinary senses. We explain that account accurately without treating its spiritual claims as established anatomy. Everyday examples clarify his distinctions; they do not by themselves demonstrate the existence of these members. Physical body: material existence Etheric body: living formation and maintenance Astral body: inward experience Why the “I” must also be included Mineral, plant and animal Names and groupings Sources One person, four related questions Original course diagram. The colours distinguish topics only. The boxes and connecting lines show relationships, not locations, sizes, aura colours or layers around the skin. All four members belong to the same person in this account. One person Physical Matter and bodily form Etheric Living organization Astral Sensation and inner response I Selfhood and deliberate response Original course diagram. The colours distinguish topics only. The boxes and connecting lines show relationships, not locations, sizes, aura colours or layers around the skin. All four members belong to the same person in this account. Compare the roles in this account Member Question it helps address Everyday point of entry Physical body What is materially present? The bodily organs and substances involved. Etheric / life body What forms and maintains living organization? Growth and the continuing organization of a living body. Astral body What makes inward experience possible? Experiencing a sound, pleasure, discomfort or desire. I / Ego Who takes up and works on this experience? Recognizing it as mine and deliberately responding. 1. Physical body: material existence The physical body is the member through which we belong to the material world. It involves substances, physical forces and the bodily structures accessible to sensory investigation. In this context, physical does not mean bad, spiritually unimportant or merely an illusion. Steiner introduces this member by comparing the living body with what remains after death. The same material substances continue to exist, but the living organization is no longer maintained. He uses this contrast to ask what must be added to a description of materials if we are to understand a living organism. His answer introduces the etheric body. In ordinary conversation, “my body” often means my whole living organism. In Steiner’s fourfold terminology, “physical body” is a more selective term: it names the material member considered within an organization also involving life, inward experience and the I. This difference in usage explains many apparent contradictions. Teaching example: you hold a warm cup. The hand, its tissues and the physical transfer of heat provide the material side of the encounter. The felt pleasantness of the warmth is a different aspect of the same event. Describing the hand and describing what the warmth feels like answer different questions; neither description requires imagining another little person inside the hand. Chapter II, §§ 1–3 Avoid this confusion Do not identify the physical body exclusively with bones or skin. Nor should every event in a living organ be assigned to this member alone: Steiner regards the members as working together. Check your understanding Does “physical” mean the whole living and feeling person in this fourfold explanation? A hint Compare the everyday meaning of body with the more selective use of physical body. Show an explained answer No. It names the material member. The living, experiencing person is considered through the cooperation of all four members. ↑ Back to the comparison 2. Etheric body: living formation and maintenance Etheric body, ether body and life body name the same member in these introductory texts. Steiner uses it to account for the shaping and sustaining of a living organism. It is an active organization, rather than an extra material object placed beside the physical body. His contrast is between matter simply following its physical processes and matter organized as a living being. He attributes the ongoing formation and maintenance of the organism to the etheric member, which he describes as permeating the physical. Growth is an accessible starting example, but “etheric” means more in his account than the measurable fact that an organism gets larger. Teaching example: compare a growing seedling with a pebble. Both have material properties. The seedling develops new organs in an organized life process. This helps you grasp the difference between material existence and living formation. The further claim that a supersensible etheric body accounts for that formation belongs to Steiner’s interpretation. Etheric is not the chemical substance ether, the historical light-carrying ether of physics, electricity, or a measurable quantity of energy. Saying that someone feels energetic therefore does not identify or measure an etheric body. “Body” here means an organized member of the being, not a thin invisible material shell. The key distinction from the astral body is life versus inward experience. In Steiner’s account, being alive does not by itself mean experiencing pleasure or pain. He places plants on the life side of this distinction. A plant’s movement toward light does not, in his argument, settle whether there is an inward experience accompanying it. Chapter II, §§ 5–10 Avoid this confusion Avoid using etheric as a loose synonym for anything invisible or spiritual. In this reference it specifically concerns living organization. Later discussions of memory or habit need their own context; they should not reduce it to a “memory container.” Check your understanding Why does the growing seedling illustrate the etheric distinction better than a stone becoming warm? A hint Ask whether the example concerns organized living development or a physical change. Show an explained answer The seedling illustrates living development. A warming stone illustrates a physical change. This explains the distinction Steiner draws; it does not prove his supersensible explanation of life. ↑ Back to the comparison 3. Astral body: inward experience Astral body names the member Steiner associates with sentient experience: sensations, pleasure and pain, attraction and aversion, desire, and the inner life of images. “Emotional body” is therefore too narrow as a complete definition. In Practical Training in Thought he explicitly discusses it in relation to thinking and mental imagery. His central distinction is between reacting and experiencing. A physical object may change when heated. That change alone does not establish that it feels anything. Inward experience means that there is also something felt by the being undergoing the encounter. Steiner attributes this sentient dimension to the astral member. Teaching example: a bell produces vibrations; you hear a tone and perhaps find it pleasant or irritating. Vibrations, organs of hearing and the lived experience of the sound are distinguishable aspects of one encounter. The astral term belongs to Steiner’s account of the experiencing being, not to another sound hidden behind the audible one. Steiner relates human and animal sentience to this member. His account does not mean that every feeling is a separate body, that only a particular temperament has an astral body, or that the astral body disappears whenever you are not aware of a feeling. His treatment of sleep is specifically intended to distinguish temporary loss of waking consciousness from loss of the member itself. The astral body is not a percept, a concept or a mental picture. A percept is what is given to observation; a mental picture retains a connection with a particular encounter; a concept contributes an intelligible relation. These describe aspects of knowing. Astral body belongs to Steiner’s account of the being who knows and experiences. Connecting these two descriptions is useful, but does not make their terms interchangeable. Chapter II, §§ 10–11; connect with GA 108, §§ 17–18 · GA 108 §§ 17–18 · GA 4 VI §§ 4–6 Avoid this confusion Do not imagine astral as a second physical body floating inside the first, or infer its appearance from an aura illustration. The introductory distinction concerns inner experience; colour and shape claims require separate source passages. Check your understanding If you recall a cloud after looking away, is that recalled image your astral body? A hint Separate the content you recall from Steiner’s account of the bearer of inner activity. Show an explained answer No. The recalled cloud is a mental picture. Steiner discusses the astral body as a bearer of such activity. A picture, the activity of picturing and the proposed member are different ideas. ↑ Back to the comparison 4. Why the “I” must also be included Without the I, the astral body can easily become a vague label for everything psychological. Steiner distinguishes changing experiences from the self that recognizes them as its experiences and can work upon them. English translations may say I or Ego; Ego here does not simply mean vanity or selfishness. Teaching example: you hear the bell and feel irritation. You can then acknowledge “I am irritated” and decide to listen before reacting. The example distinguishes the feeling from self-awareness and deliberate response. It is a teaching entry point, not a test that detects an invisible I. In Steiner’s account, the I works within and upon the other members; it is not an isolated supervisor operating three machines. His later descriptions of transformation—astral into spirit self, etheric into life spirit, and physical into spirit man—concern spiritual development. They should not be mistaken for three material bodies being exchanged. Chapter II, §§ 11–16 and the discussion of transformation Avoid this confusion Do not equate astral body with the whole soul, or I with every passing thought. Ask which distinction a particular passage is making. Check your understanding What changes when “I feel irritated” becomes “I will consider my response”? A hint Look for the difference between experiencing an impulse and consciously working with it. Show an explained answer The example brings deliberate self-relation into view. It illustrates why Steiner distinguishes the I from the changing experiences associated with the astral member. ↑ Back to the comparison Mineral world , plant world and animal world Here, world or kingdom means a domain of nature, not another planet or a separate invisible place. Steiner compares these domains to explain what human beings share with the rest of nature. Ask three questions: What has material existence? What lives and develops? What has an inward experience? These distinctions prepare the meanings of physical, etheric and astral. Mineral world Plant world Animal world Mineral world : material substances and processes Think of a pebble, a salt crystal or a piece of iron. Each has material properties and undergoes physical changes. In this comparison, mineral world points to the inorganic side of nature: substances and forces considered without the additional life and sentience of an organism. It does not mean only dietary minerals. Steiner connects this with the physical body. Human beings, plants and animals also have material constituents. Saying that we share something with the mineral world therefore does not mean that our whole body is a stone; it means that material existence is one aspect of us. Teaching example: a stone becomes warm in sunlight. That is a real change, but becoming warmer is not the same as growing leaves or experiencing the warmth as pleasant. The example helps separate a physical process from living development and inward experience. Read the physical-body explanation → If a crystal becomes larger, must it have the same kind of life as a seedling? Show an explained answer No. “Becoming larger” alone does not establish that the two processes are alike. Compare the way material is added with the seedling’s organized development of living organs. The distinction concerns the kind of process, not size alone. Plant world : material existence organized as life Think of a seed germinating, a root extending and a plant forming new leaves. Plants have material existence, and they also live and develop. Steiner connects this living formation with the etheric or life body. A plant does not replace the physical with the etheric; the two belong together in his account. Teaching example: compare a pebble and a seedling over several days. Describe material properties of both. Then describe the seedling’s development. This makes the difference between “there is matter” and “there is an organized life process” easier to understand. In GA 13 II, Steiner distinguishes a plant’s response to a stimulus from the inward experience he attributes to animals. Turning toward light or closing a leaf does not, by itself, settle the question of experience. When he compares plant life to sleep, he is explaining life without animal-like waking awareness in this framework; he is not saying that a plant takes human naps. This is the introductory comparison used in these passages. It should not be expanded into the claim that Steiner never discusses plants in relation to soul or spirit elsewhere. Read the etheric-body explanation → Does movement alone distinguish the plant world from the mineral world , or establish feeling? Show an explained answer No. A stone can move, and a plant can respond to its surroundings. Here the plant distinction concerns organized living development. Whether a response is accompanied by inward experience is a further question. Animal world : life with inward experience Think of a dog hearing a familiar voice, seeking food or withdrawing from something painful. In Steiner’s introductory comparison, animals have material bodies and living organization, and also sensations, desires, pleasure and pain. He relates this sentient dimension to the astral body. The distinction is not simply that animals move and plants stay still. It is that, in his account, the animal inwardly experiences its encounter with the world. The dog example is a teaching illustration of this distinction, not a direct observation of an astral body. Human beings share material existence, life and sentience with these domains. Steiner adds the I when explaining human selfhood. In this comparison, the animal’s sentience is not the same term as the specifically human I. This does not turn the table into a ranking of how much care different beings deserve. Read the astral-body explanation → If animals are associated with the astral body, do they also have physical and etheric members? Show an explained answer Yes, in this account. Sentient experience is introduced alongside material existence and life. The comparison adds distinctions; it does not assign only one body to each kingdom. Read the comparison cumulatively Domain in this comparison Members named in this introductory account Mineral Physical Plant Physical + etheric Animal Physical + etheric + astral Human being Physical + etheric + astral + I A reading map of Steiner’s account, not a complete biological classification or a scale of moral worth. Each new row retains the preceding distinctions. It does not depict a stone turning into a plant or a plant turning into an animal. Read Theosophy, chapter I §§ 10–12, for the comparison with human beings. Then read An Outline of Occult Science, chapter II § 2 and §§ 9–11, for its relationship to the members. In the linked Adams translation, § 9 is marked “Not translated”; the plant comparison is included in § 10. The German § 9 states it separately. GA 9 I §§ 10–12 · English · GA 13 II §§ 2, 9–11 · English · GA 13 II · Deutsch Put the distinctions together: one encounter Imagine receiving a warm cup of tea. Your hand and the transfer of heat give a physical point of entry. Your hand belongs to a living organism whose ongoing formation Steiner attributes to the etheric member. Feeling warmth and enjoying the aroma illustrate inward experience associated with the astral. Recognizing your response and choosing to offer the cup to someone else bring the I into the example. These are four ways into one event, not four stages that occur separately. The example is our teaching construction, not a quotation or a proof. What about sleep? Steiner uses sleep to sharpen the distinction between life and waking experience. He describes the physical and etheric members as remaining connected while the astral and I enter a different relation to them. In his account, life continues while ordinary waking awareness recedes; the astral remains active. This is his spiritual interpretation of sleep, not something you can establish merely by noticing that you slept. Dreaming and the detailed stages of sleep require the fuller chapter, rather than a literal picture of four detachable objects. Waking and sleep in Steiner’s account A relationship diagram, not positions in space. In sleep, physical and etheric remain connected; their relation to astral and I changes. Waking Physical + etheric Astral + I Cooperation in waking experience Sleep Physical + etheric Astral + I A different relation; life continues Lines indicate relationships according to Steiner, not measurable journeys. GA 13 · Chapter III · Sleep and Death Why the names can seem to change Theosophy first distinguishes body, soul and spirit, then makes finer distinctions and regroups them. In one grouping, soul body and sentient soul are considered together as astral body. Therefore body–soul–spirit and physical–etheric–astral–I are not matching lists with different labels. In particular, soul body alone should not automatically be replaced by astral body, and astral body should not automatically be replaced by soul. Read the grouping and the question being answered before equating terms. Compare the threefold, ninefold and sevenfold descriptions Start with body, soul and spirit, then follow the finer distinctions, the two pairings, and the separate developmental account. Colours and positions are teaching aids, not bodily locations. One human being, three perspectives · Original course illustration of Steiner’s account. Open full-size image Read the diagram in words Body: the senses give access to the flower’s appearance. Soul: the encounter becomes a personal experience of joy. Spirit: the person seeks to understand the plant’s growth and relationships beyond personal preference. These are three aspects of one encounter. The picture does not assign body, soul and spirit to separate anatomical regions. The ninefold description · Original course illustration of Steiner’s account. Open full-size image Read the diagram in words Body: physical body concerns material organization; life body concerns living formation and maintenance; soul body concerns bodily mediation of sensation. Soul: sentient soul concerns sensations, feelings and desires; intellectual soul concerns thought within practical soul life; consciousness soul concerns truth beyond personal preference. Spirit: spirit self concerns spiritual content individualized through the I; life spirit and spirit man concern transformation of life and physical organization respectively. Read down each column. Cards on the same horizontal line do not imply a one-to-one correspondence. Nine distinctions, seven groups · Original course illustration of Steiner’s account. Open full-size image Read the diagram in words Soul body and sentient soul share the entry “sentient soul body”: bodily mediation and inward experience work together in earthly life. Consciousness soul and spirit self share the entry “spirit-filled consciousness soul”: spiritual truth is received and individualized through the I. Physical body, life body, intellectual soul, life spirit and spirit man each keep their own entry. All nine distinctions are represented in seven groups. The braces indicate grouping, not transformation. A different sevenfold account · Original course illustration of Steiner’s account. Open full-size image Read the diagram in words The I works on all three foundational members. Steiner relates transformed astral organization to spirit self, transformed life organization to life spirit, and transformed physical organization to spirit man. The usual list order is physical body, life body, astral body, I, spirit self, life spirit and spirit man. The upper diagram reverses the order of the three transformed aspects so that arrows do not cross. These arrows express Steiner’s account of spiritual development. They do not describe the two pairings in the grouped sevenfold list. Colours trace each relationship and do not follow the body–soul–spirit family colours of the other pictures. Lesson 5: body, soul and spirit · Lesson 11: distinctions and groupings GA 9 · Chapter I · The Essential Nature of Man · Compare the groupings in Lesson 6 Return to the cloud exercise In GA 108 §§ 14–18, the practical task is to observe accurately and form faithful mental images of successive conditions. Steiner then offers an account of how that work affects the astral body. Understanding the vocabulary lets you separate what you actually observed, the image you retained, the connection you understood and his spiritual interpretation. You need not imagine seeing an astral body to explain the exercise. GA 108 · Practical Training in Thought · 18 January 1909 · Open the guided cloud example → Explain it without the labels first Describe a familiar encounter using these four phrases: material conditions; living organization; inward experience; my conscious response. Then match the phrases to the four terms. Finally say which parts are your ordinary observations and which belong to Steiner’s interpretation. If you can do this without using “energy” as an answer to everything, the distinctions are becoming clearer. Read the sources in this order Start with GA 13 II: §§ 1–3 for physical; §§ 5–10 for etheric; §§ 10–11 for astral; continue through the I and transformation discussion. GA 13 · Chapter II · The Nature of Humanity Use GA 9 I, especially the final grouping discussion, to distinguish soul body, sentient soul, astral body and I. GA 9 · Chapter I · The Essential Nature of Man Use GA 13 III, opening paragraphs, for the sleep account. GA 13 · Chapter III · Sleep and Death Return to GA 108 §§ 14–18 for the observation exercise and its interpretation. GA 108 · Practical Training in Thought · 18 January 1909 Use GA 4 VI §§ 4–6 for percept, concept and mental picture; this is a comparison across texts, not a claim that these terms name bodies. GA 4 · Chapter VI · Human Individuality Paragraph references follow the linked English editions; headings and numbering can vary in other translations. Explanations and examples here are original course prose. The underlying GA 13 German chapters were also consulted. The two diagrams are original schematics; no external aura picture is being presented as evidence. GA 13 II · Deutsch · GA 13 III · Deutsch Continue: life and sensation → Ler em português

title: According to Luke — course fidelity and teaching audit
text: According to Luke — course fidelity and teaching audit Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Historical archive / Arquivo histórico This record is part of the historical archive. Its counts, draft routes and pending tasks describe the date of the note; use the current library and course pages for present coverage. Este registro pertence ao arquivo histórico. Suas contagens, rotas propostas e tarefas pendentes descrevem a data da nota; consulte a biblioteca e os cursos atuais para conhecer o alcance presente. Records the course before the completed source revision, rather than current source coverage. Implementation record · English analysis with bilingual draft material · 30 September 2026 · 2791 words Contents of this note / Conteúdo desta nota According to Luke — course fidelity and teaching audit Evidence and limits What already works Principal gap Recommendations by lesson Readable learning path Bilingual terminology findings Source and translation controls for the revision Scope that can be completed with the present uploads According to Luke — course fidelity and teaching audit Audit date: 30 September 2026. This document records the course as it stood before the current supplied-source revision. It is an editorial audit, not a newly verified digest of all ten lectures. Evidence and limits Reviewed according-to-luke.mjs , scripts/build-luke.mjs , according-to-luke-reading-review.md , the Luke entries in passage-study.json , guided-prompts.mjs , guided-labs.mjs , the passage-study builder, and representative generated English lesson pages. Read the newly supplied Markdown capture, particularly markers 3–17. Its OCR warnings require checking quotations against the paired PDF before publication. The uploaded PDF/Markdown supply title and contents, McDermott's introduction, and the opening of Lecture 1. Markers 18–20 are interface material. The contents name ten lectures but do not supply their bodies. Capture markers are not printed folios. The supplied edition's translator must remain unidentified unless a reliable bibliographic page is available. The earlier reading review identifies the parallel 1964 English edition and a separate version for an omission in Lecture 9. Existing course excerpts instead cite numbered German GA 114 paragraphs and original course translations. Those are three different provenance layers: supplied capture, earlier parallel English reading, and separately credited German excerpt. This audit does not silently merge them. A read-only request to the Rudolf Steiner Archive returned a proxy 403 in this session. Lectures 2–10 were therefore not reread against their complete primary texts . Recommendations for those lessons identify observable omissions in existing teaching, its own reading assignments, its quoted passages, and the supplied contents. They do not authorize newly asserted doctrine, invented page references, or a claim of full-source verification. The September 12 reading review is evidence of an earlier workflow, not fresh verification on September 30. What already works The course has a stable orientation, ten dated lecture lessons, and a final original synthesis, with matching English and Brazilian Portuguese coverage. Its source notes disclose that the uploaded capture is incomplete and that complete readings use a parallel English edition. It distinguishes Gospel narrative, Steiner's interpretation, McDermott's editorial voice, and the learner's assessment. Unusual spiritual identities remain attributed. Its ethical cases preserve ordinary agency and accountability. It does not turn healing narratives into diagnoses or initiation narratives into bodily instructions. The final build already teaches before practice. Although build-luke.mjs initially places the worked example first, build-passage-study.mjs moves the selected passage and an open explanation before the example and response fields. Inspected generated pages confirm that order. Reordering the base builder alone would not address the principal weakness. Principal gap The course is presently a selective ethical reading companion. Its own earlier review says it does not attempt an exhaustive digest. That is a reasonable description of the existing result, but it does not satisfy a request to reformulate the course around the essential concepts and argument of the supplied book. Each lecture has a short passage and a short explanation, followed by two brief course paragraphs. The substantial elaboration often concerns an original everyday case: volunteer help, communication, a club appointment, reception of feedback, sharing notes, or repairing a friendship. The cases are useful applications, but they leave the reader unable to reconstruct the lecture's argument. Technical glossaries often define general study words instead of the terms the source requires. Merely adding a quotation before this structure cannot supply the missing argument. The current sourceChecks override creates one source-oriented check in Lessons 2–10, while the other two usually test the application or its limits. Many questions can be answered without understanding the lecture. The suggested answers are generally sensible, but successful completion is weak evidence of source comprehension. Lesson 1 has no source-check override at all. Its checks concern vividness, a friend's explanation, and analogy limits rather than the three modes of cognition or the Gospel comparison. Recommendations by lesson Lesson Observable gap Concrete teaching revision Source-comprehension check to add 00 — Orientation McDermott is identified but his introduction's actual reasoning is barely taught. The opening excerpt is the same Steiner Intuition excerpt used in Lesson 1, which does not explain why this edition needs an introduction. Teach the introduction as McDermott's argument: lectures assumed prepared audiences; esoteric premises differ from ordinary Gospel scholarship; he proposes a middle way between assent to authority and rejection from familiar assumptions; he distinguishes imaginative disclosure from fantasy and discusses evidence. Attribute his evaluations of scholars and Kant to him. Show the four voices with a concrete passage attribution. Why does McDermott think preparation matters, and how does his proposed reading stance differ from accepting a claim because Steiner says it? 01 — Lecture 1 Three technical definitions are present, but the lecture's purpose and the chain connecting cognition to John/Luke are absent. “An initiate's understanding” can suggest ordinary comprehension. “Akashic record” is named without the research-before-document method. Explain the opening problem: why study Luke after the profound John Gospel? Then map Imagination, Inspiration and Intuition; historical specialization and cooperation; the “inner word”; clairvoyant versus initiate; John versus Luke; Steiner's reading of Luke 1:1–2; independent spiritual research followed by comparison with documents. Define initiation here by Inspiration/Intuition. These points are supplied in markers 11–17 and can be revised now after PDF verification. How does Steiner connect “independent seers” and “servants of the word” with the two types of cognition, and why are the Gospel documents a comparison rather than his primary source? 02 — Lecture 2 The Bodhisattva-to-Buddha transition and shepherds' announcement are named but not explained. The glossary defines “principle” and “capacity,” while the reading depends on Bodhisattva and Buddha. The main exercise is about a volunteer's attentiveness. After a complete source reread, teach the specific transition and its role in the interpretation of Luke. Explain what the lecture claims was formerly taught and becomes humanly available, then show where the angelic announcement enters that argument. Keep the volunteer case as an optional application. What changes in Steiner's account when the Bodhisattva becomes Buddha, and how does he connect that change with Luke's birth narrative? 03 — Lecture 3 “Suffering,” the Eightfold Path, Nirmanakaya and Nathan Jesus are named, but the path is not outlined and “Nirmanakaya” receives a circular definition as a technical term in the continuing-activity account. A single right-speech excerpt stands for a much larger discussion. After source reread, reconstruct the sequence from the account of suffering to the path, explain its constituent steps and the lecture's use of Nirmanakaya, and state the claimed relationship to the Nathan Jesus. Distinguish the ethical exposition from the spiritual narrative without discarding either. How does the quoted step about communication fit the larger path, and what additional claim connects Buddha's ethical achievement with the Nathan Jesus? 04 — Lecture 4 The two-child conclusion is taught, but the reader is given no explanation of what “preserved, unfallen Adamic forces” means within the author's premises. The reading assignment explicitly selects the concluding explanation. After source reread, teach the formation argument preceding that conclusion. Use separate columns for Gospel details and Steiner's additional claims. Supply the terms needed to explain the different preparations, not just “genealogy” and “hypothesis.” Which details belong to the Gospel genealogies, which belong to Steiner's proposed spiritual preparation, and how do those different premises support his two-child account? 05 — Lecture 5 Zarathustra's transfer at twelve is stated; Buddha's contribution is described only as having “a different character.” The passage note names the individuality and Nirmanakaya, but the main lesson never explains the distinction. After source reread, identify each contributor, what contributes, the recipient, and the claimed stage. Give the temple episode its explanatory role in the convergence. Keep the musician analogy strictly as a language example. What exactly differs between Zarathustra's contribution and Buddha's contribution in Steiner's narrative? Give a distinct verb and a passage reference for each. 06 — Lecture 6 The supplied contents name “Elijah, John the Baptist, and Zarathustra,” while the lesson's key names Moses, Elijah and John, without explaining Zarathustra's role. “Connects” hides the kind of relationship. The wider love argument in the opening passage is reduced mainly to a fair appointment case. After source reread, restore the named figures and their particular relations, the sequence from law/prophecy to John's appeal, and the argument for adding universal human love to kinship. Examine the cultural hierarchy after explaining what the author actually argues. What does the quoted verb “add” preserve about kinship, and what wider relationship does the lecture seek to introduce? Which role does each named figure play? 07 — Lecture 7 The baptism chronology is useful, but the supplied title announces Christ as the great mystery of Earth evolution. That larger claim is not explained. “Ether and cosmic beings” appear mainly in a limiting note. After source reread, connect the preparation/baptism sequence to the lecture's account of the Christ being and Earth evolution. Explain the essential terms actually used in that argument. The timeline is a foundation for this explanation, not its endpoint. Why does Steiner's distinction between Jesus and Christ matter for his larger account of Earth evolution, beyond keeping names in chronological order? 08 — Lecture 8 The reading assignment promises “the three kinds of healing described,” but no three kinds are identified or explained. The evolution-of-consciousness premise is equally brief. The lesson instead develops how a teacher can receive feedback. After source reread, present the actual three examples/types and the claimed Ego–soul–body relations. Show how the sower fits the consciousness argument. Keep modern learning and medical cautions separate from source explanation; neither substitutes for it. What distinguishes the three healings in the lecture's own terms, and which premise about consciousness does Steiner use to interpret them? 09 — Lecture 9 The supplied title is “Christ and Maitreya Buddha,” but Maitreya is absent from the lesson. Its key teaches a Buddha/Christ contrast and the exercise concerns generosity motives. The existing review mentions the untranslated paragraph and audience needs without integrating that context into teaching. After complete source reread, explain the Maitreya discussion and how it relates to the teaching-versus-active-power distinction. Preserve the specific 1964 omission and separately sourced parallel wording. Do not guess identities or insert unsupported dates. What role does Maitreya have in the lecture's argument, and how does that role relate to Steiner's distinction between an instruction about love and love as an active force? 10 — Lecture 10 Golgotha as initiation entering history and Nain as preparation are stated in one paragraph. The argument leading from those narratives to the conclusion is missing. Forgiveness and a mild dispute dominate the remainder. After source reread, explain the old/new initiation comparison, the role assigned to Nain, and the conclusion's relation to the course's previous stages. Keep the future individual unnamed where the source does. The closing Earth-transformation passage needs its spiritual-historical context, not only an everyday hope example. What changes when initiation becomes a public historical event in Steiner's account, and how does he connect that claim to the earlier lecture sequence? 11 — Synthesis The portfolio can be completed from one passage and a feasible act of care. It therefore need not demonstrate understanding of the ten-lecture progression. The closing passage note already asks the learner not to reduce the course to general kindness, but the portfolio requirement does not enforce that distinction. Require an attributed outline of the course argument, at least three connected lecture references, a defined technical distinction, one unresolved question, and a separate practical application. Where full-source coverage remains incomplete, label the synthesis selective and allow a supplied-source-only path centered on the introduction and Lecture 1. How do the cognition/source argument, the preparation narrative and the concluding account fit together? Which link is established by the source, and which remains the learner's judgment? The proposed questions for Lessons 2–10 are editorial targets. Their answer keys must be written only after full-source rereading. The supplied contents verify those lecture titles, not the doctrines an answer would need. Readable learning path Preserve the familiar page pattern, but make its substantive sequence explicit: Identify the author, edition or source layer, and available span. Read one or more short verified passages selected for the argument, rather than only for an accessible ethical slogan. Explain the author's question, premises, main distinctions, sequence of reasoning, and conclusion in connected prose. Define the technical vocabulary required for that explanation. Ask the learner to explain a source relation with words from the passage. Use the original everyday case as an application, with its limits stated briefly. Check source comprehension before checking application, then invite assessment or disagreement. Connect the lesson to the preceding and following stage, and name anything unavailable in the supplied material. For Lecture 1, a small comparison table is particularly useful: level of cognition, how Steiner describes its access, distinction from ordinary usage, and role in his Gospel comparison. A second source table can separate direct spiritual research, the Akashic record claimed as its historical source, and subsequent documentary comparison. Neither table should imply an independently verified account. The same map currently appears in guided labs for Lessons 4, 5 and 7. It previews later stages appropriately, but it repeats instead of developing the learner's task. On a future complete-source revision, progressively change the map: identify lineage distinctions in 4; specify distinct contributions and the twelve-year transition in 5; explain the baptism transition and its larger significance in 7. Preserve names, explicit relation verbs and source references. Bilingual terminology findings The English and Portuguese lesson prose is generally closely aligned. The most important issues are shared underexplanation, not a separate missing Portuguese course. Lesson 1's “participation in their being” / “participação no ser deles” softens the selected passage's stronger claim of becoming one with beings and immersing in their nature. Preserve the strength of the attributed claim while keeping ordinary empathy distinct. Lesson 2 uses Bodhisattva in its Portuguese reading assignment and Bodisatva in the selected passage. Standardize course prose or identify the spelling variation. Lessons 5, 8 and 9 alternate English Ego and I between prose and passages. Portuguese consistently uses Eu . State the terminology equivalence once and preserve the term chosen by each quoted edition. Lesson 8's English “spiritual understanding” becomes “conhecimento espiritual” in Portuguese. “Compreensão espiritual” preserves the wording's distinction more closely. The retained Lesson 9 German passage uses überfließen , Portuguese uses transbordar , and English uses “flow out.” “Overflow” preserves the image used by the lecture's own reading description more precisely. This is a comparison of the existing quoted wording, not a fresh verification against the complete lecture. Source and translation controls for the revision Use PDF/capture page numbers only as such; do not invent printed folios or transfer German paragraph numbers to the supplied English edition. Label selected passages from the newly supplied edition separately from retained German GA 114 excerpts and the parallel 1964 English reading links. A short quotation should be followed by an explanation of its wording and its position in the argument. The current one-passage-per-lesson data model is a structural constraint, not evidence that one passage captures every essential concept. Original Portuguese teaching and study translations should remain explicitly distinguished from a published Portuguese edition. Preserve the same argument, examples and source limits in both languages. Use stable technical terms: Imagination/Imaginação, Inspiration/Inspiração, Intuition/Intuição, clairvoyance/clarividência, initiation/iniciação, and Ego or I/Eu. Explain variation rather than casually equating GA 114 usage with GA 4 or GA 10. Preserve the course's concise critical attribution of group hierarchies, healing claims and unusual identities. Place those notes after an adequate account of the author's argument so that the learner can understand what is being assessed. Scope that can be completed with the present uploads The introduction and supplied opening of Lecture 1 can be reformulated around the actual author/editor argument now, with PDF-verified short passages in English and matching Brazilian Portuguese explanations. The supplied contents can also make the index's lecture coverage more informative. Later lessons can retain their previously credited parallel excerpts and disclosed reading limits. A claim that all ten complete lectures have now been reread page by page would be unsupported. Deeper replacement of Lessons 2–10 requires the missing lecture texts or working access to the explicitly credited parallel primary source. Structural validation can check attribution fields, language parity, source-first order and correct links; it cannot establish that an unexamined lecture is substantively complete.

Source and course review · English · 30 September 2026 · 1232 words According to Luke — course revision, 30 September 2026 Lecture 2: expanded close reading with the available evidence Lecture 2 now has four explanatory reading sections in English and Brazilian Portuguese, a source-focused activity, revised comprehension questions and an updated guided prompt. The explanation follows Buddha's earlier Bodhisattva role, preserves both love and compassion, and distinguishes the retained German sentence from the earlier course summaries about human capacities and the announcement to the shepherds. The complete lecture remains absent from the supplied PDF captures, and the full parallel texts could not be retrieved. This is an expanded excerpt lesson, not a completed page-by-page revision of Lecture 2. The Lecture 2 revision record describes the evidence, changes, validation and the full text still needed. All other lesson data and source selections were preserved; the full build and all 14 validators passed. Latest update: edition verified from the new 21-capture pair All 21 captures of the latest PDF and matching According to Luke (2).md were reviewed. The copyright page identifies the 2001 Anthroposophic Press edition , with Steiner's lectures translated by Catherine E. Creeger , ISBN 0-88010-488-0 . The introduction is by Robert A. McDermott; it is credited separately from the translated lectures. The new capture has the same introduction and Lecture 1 prose as the earlier file. It adds a cover and copyright evidence, removes the interface captures, and changes the reflowed capture positions. The course now cites the introduction at 5–13 and the supplied Lecture 1 text at 14–21 . Both selected quotations were visually rechecked: McDermott's sentence spans capture 6 , middle and right columns; Steiner's sentence is on capture 19 , right column. Their English wording and Portuguese study renderings remain unchanged. The coverage note has also been corrected. Earlier notes asserted a missing remainder of Lecture 1; these captures do not prove that. The last page is mostly blank and ends with the same coherent Akashic-record paragraph. Lecture 1 completeness remains unverified without a following chapter boundary or full primary edition. Current lessons use supplied Lecture 1 text . Lectures 2–10 , the descriptive outline, About This Edition and footnote bodies are still absent. The latest page ledger accounts for every capture, translation evidence, OCR repairs, quotation locations and the date discrepancy printed on the copyright page. It records 15–24 September 1909 as printed, alongside the existing GA 114 source dates through 26 September; the original is not silently repaired. The complete build and all 14 validators passed after this update, with the GA114 checker covering the 21-row ledger and verified edition information. The refreshed stage passed the existing ten HTTP smoke requests and all 26 bilingual Luke routes; all 414 static artifacts matched repeated generation. Other-course output and later Luke lesson data/passages were preserved. A new archive request still returned HTTP 403, code 1010; no full parallel text was retrieved. Next source needed: the actual text of Lecture 2 , as PDF and matching Markdown. Smaller batches can follow lecture by lecture. If the reading app stops at Lecture 1, the capture alone does not reveal whether that is a sample limit or a capture problem. Earlier revision record — 20-capture pair The record below describes the earlier source and its capture positions. The latest edition evidence and the Lecture 1 coverage correction above supersede its unknown-translator and missing-remainder statements. The supplied PDF and matching Markdown were read page by page. The upload contains 20 captures , of which 17 contain book material : title and contents (1–2), Robert A. McDermott's complete introduction (3–10), and the opening of Rudolf Steiner's Lecture 1 (11–17). Three unrelated interface captures (18–20) were excluded. There are no visible printed folios, translator or publication year. All citations to this upload use capture positions. What changed Orientation 0 now teaches McDermott's argument: the prepared original audience; independent judgment, humility and reverence; true imagination and fantasy; the claimed Akashic source; the two translations; and the comparison with biblical scholarship. Four explanatory sections preserve his affirmative spiritual claims and identify him as the editorial author. Lecture 1, lesson 1 now reconstructs Steiner's opening argument through six sections: why Luke adds to John; ordinary and imaginative cognition; Inspiration and Intuition; clairvoyance and initiation; historical specialization and the stated modern progression; Luke's preface and John's Logos; and independent spiritual research followed by comparison with documents. A three-row table summarizes Imagination, Inspiration and Intuition. Two short passages were checked against the native PDF images: McDermott's middle-way statement (capture 4) and Steiner's distinction between clairvoyant and initiate (capture 16). English uses the supplied edition; Portuguese is a new study translation. Their author, source file and exact capture locations are recorded separately. Source assignments, guided prompts and all three comprehension checks for the two opening lessons now require explaining the source argument with references. Original practical examples remain applications after the source explanation. Synthesis 11 now requires an argument and source references. It offers a clearly scoped excerpt portfolio for the material actually supplied; a full-course extension requires the full readings and a connected ten-lecture outline. Both indexes include the ten lecture headings verified in the supplied contents, plus a coverage note. Each later lecture states that it is absent from this PDF and retains its previously reviewed parallel source. All changes are available in English and Brazilian Portuguese. Stable lesson URLs, notebook identities, language partners and existing course connections were preserved. Reading notes and evidence The upload page ledger accounts for every PDF capture, essential concepts, image verification, OCR corrections and excluded interface material. The course audit identifies gaps in later lessons for the next complete-source revision. The reading review distinguishes this source work from the earlier parallel-edition review. The original files remain private under ignored [private working files] ; their fingerprints are recorded in source-register.json and according-to-luke-upload.mjs . Attached-document text was treated as source material, not as task instructions. Validation The complete site build and all 14 validators passed, including the new GA114 source checker. Checks cover 398 HTML pages, bilingual routes and links, source-first teaching, source credits, the 20-row ledger, separate editorial and lecture attribution, both cognition tables, and preservation of study controls. The regenerated build contains 135 source selections across ten course collections. The staged preview was refreshed and checked with the existing 10-request HTTP smoke test plus all 26 Luke routes. Served response bodies matched the validated built files. Repeated generation produced byte-identical static artifacts. Other courses' generated files, source selections, lesson data and guided prompts remained unchanged. What remains This is a completed revision of the supplied introduction and opening lecture , not a completed page-by-page revision of the entire book. The remainder of Lecture 1, Lectures 2–10, the Descriptive Outline, About This Edition and footnote bodies are absent. The later lecture content and German selections retain their earlier provenance; they were not newly aligned with missing pages of this edition. A fresh request to the referenced Rudolf Steiner Archive parallel text returned proxy 403 under the environment's restricted network policy. rsarchive.org was saved in the configuration draft as a research requirement; saving alone does not apply access. No alternative network route was used. The next source needed is the complete According to Luke PDF and matching Markdown , including all ten lectures and edition information, or the missing remainder. The upload currently ends after the statement about the Akashic record on capture 17. Supplying the rest enables the essential-concept revision of lessons 2–10 and the complete synthesis.

title: According to Luke — edition capture page notes
text: According to Luke — edition capture page notes Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Current records / Registros atuais Current source record. Any explicitly dated historical sections remain historical, as the note explains. Registro atual de fontes. As seções históricas explicitamente datadas mantêm esse caráter, conforme explicado na nota. Page-by-page notes · English · 30 September 2026 · 2669 words Contents of this note / Conteúdo desta nota According to Luke — edition capture page notes Edition evidence Coverage and the Lecture One boundary Page-by-page ledger Comparison with the older upload Two short quotations verified in both captures According to Luke — edition capture page notes Reviewed 30 September 2026. All 21 PDF captures were viewed individually at their native 1216 × 546 resolution, and all corresponding Markdown pages were read in full. Every capture now contains book material. The PDF consists of raster captures; the Markdown is OCR of those captures, not an independently typeset edition. Text captures generally have three columns, read left, middle, then right; the copyright and contents captures have two. References in this review are PDF capture numbers , not printed book folios. No printed folios are visible. The reviewed pair is According to Luke.pdf , SHA-256 a6d1b522321bf223ef67eb214386f26179d0b56b55d31224393f85f0dfe12420 , and According to Luke (2).md , SHA-256 0fbcdd7c5d6e3655a081b8a81a05caa16997f965993de58a5ba0f75b510f3e9d . The files and extracted images remain private under the ignored [private working file] directory. The older 20-capture pair in [private working file] was used for comparison. This ledger records the new supplied material and does not republish the source or change the active course. Edition evidence The new title and copyright captures identify the English edition more precisely than the older upload: Title: According to Luke: The Gospel of Compassion and Love Revealed , a cycle of ten lectures by Rudolf Steiner , with an introduction and descriptive outline by Robert A. McDermott (capture 2). Publisher and copyright: Anthroposophic Press, © 2001 , Great Barrington, Massachusetts (capture 3). Translator: Catherine E. Creeger ; book design and typesetting credited to White Cloud Press (capture 3). ISBN: 0-88010-488-0 . The cataloging block also gives BP595.S894 L8513 2001 and control number 2001018172 (capture 3). German source: the copyright page identifies Das Lukas-Evangelium , a cycle of ten lectures in Basel, and Rudolf Steiner Verlag, Dornach, Switzerland, 1955 . Its date phrase visibly reads “15. bis 24. September 1909.” The final number is 24 , not an OCR misreading of 26. This differs from the September 15–26 range in the existing GA 114 lecture chronology, whose final lecture is 26 September 1909 . Preserve the printed date when transcribing this page; do not silently substitute 26. The supplied captures do not resolve the bibliographic discrepancy. These are normalized bibliographic facts, not a full transcription of the copyright page. The PDF creation timestamp, 30 September 2026, records capture-file creation and does not replace the visible 2001 book evidence. The upload does not supply the body of “About This Edition,” so no further edition history is established here. Coverage and the Lecture One boundary Captures 5–13 contain McDermott's introduction, ending with his recommendation of the descriptive outline; capture 14 begins Steiner's Lecture One. Captures 14–21 contain the supplied Lecture One text, ending with the Akashic-record paragraph. The new introduction and lecture prose cover the same text as old captures 3–10 and 11–17, respectively. The new upload adds a cover and copyright page, changes the reflow and pagination, and removes the three old desktop/application captures. It supplies no additional lecture prose and reveals no intervening prose gap between the two uploads. The earlier description of Lecture One as only an opening, with a remainder definitely missing, is not established by these captures. Capture 21 ends in a complete sentence at the same point as old capture 17, with only a short continuation at the top of its left column and most of the canvas blank. This is visually consistent with the end of a chapter; the introduction's concluding capture 13 has a similar blank remainder. The final paragraph also reads as a coherent closing statement. There is no unfinished sentence or visible mid-paragraph interruption after it. However, neither an explicit end marker nor the following Lecture Two heading is supplied, and the end has not been checked against a complete primary copy of this Creeger edition. Lecture One may be complete in both uploads; its chapter completeness remains unverified. The defensible scope label is “supplied Lecture One text.” The bodies of Lectures Two–Ten , McDermott's descriptive outline, “About This Edition,” and the explanatory footnotes are absent from this upload. The contents list those sections but does not supply their bodies. The cover bears no visible sample label, and no capture displays a sample-limit message, retailer interface, or other explicit indicator that this was distributed as a book sample. A partial upload is certain; its origin as a publisher or retailer sample is not proven . The chapter-like blank ending alone cannot establish that origin. Page-by-page ledger The old-page column records text overlap, not equality of the differently reflowed page images. New PDF capture Material and attribution Main reading point PDF/OCR decision and old coverage 1 Illustrated cover with the book's title and subtitle. Identifies the visible cover design, without supplying lecture prose or edition details. OCR is almost entirely noise and cannot transcribe the cover. No sample badge is visible. This cover was absent from the older upload. 2 Title page: Steiner; introduction and descriptive outline by McDermott; Anthroposophic Press. Keep author, lecturer, introducer, and publisher roles distinct. The PDF repairs the badly corrupted OCR title, subtitle, “Ten Lectures,” author names, “Introduction and Descriptive Outline,” and publisher. Corresponds to old 1. The blank remainder is part of the title-page capture. 3 Copyright/publication page, translation and design credits, German source statement, cataloging data, rights notice. Establishes the 2001 Creeger edition and identifies the German source; it does not prove the entire edition was supplied. Visually verified year, translator, ISBN, and German 15–24 date. Ordinary wrap splits can be joined; 24 must remain 24 in a transcription. New bibliographic evidence absent from the older upload. 4 Contents: introduction; all ten lectures; McDermott's outline; edition note. Establishes the intended book structure, while the bodies of later listed sections remain absent. The PDF contents are readable and complete as a list. Lecture Five's title continues at the top of the right column , explaining the isolated continuation there; this is column flow, not a new heading. Blue underlined entries indicate links, without proving a particular reader application or sample status. Markdown omits most entries and is unusable as a contents transcription. Corresponds to old 2. 5 McDermott: introduction heading and authorship; stenographic reports; Steiner's autobiography; assumed anthroposophical preparation; Luke/Matthew contrast. Distinguish a lecture report from a work prepared for publication, and McDermott's framing from Steiner's lecture. The autobiographical quotation is nested within McDermott's introduction. Rejoin ordinary wrap splits; “in the” repairs OCR “inthe.” Old 3 and beginning of 4. 6 McDermott: spiritual identities; individual reception; judgment, humility and reverence; middle way; authority and assent; familiar Gospel narration. His recommended reading posture does not demand assent to Steiner's authority. The discussion of karma and higher self remains McDermott's framing. PDF reads “nor I in this introduction” , where OCR gives a vertical bar. “a commitment” repairs “acommitment.” The middle-way quotation crosses middle-column bottom → right-column top . The visible “foun-dational” is retained in an exact transcription or explicitly normalized for readable notes. Most of old 4. 7 McDermott: esoteric reading; Akashic record; conscious clairvoyance; Luke's reports and Steiner's proposed access to Luke's consciousness. Source and course review · English · 30 September 2026; 12 September 2026 · 1793 words According to Luke — source review and course map Latest edition evidence — 21-capture upload, 30 September 2026 The latest According to Luke.pdf and According to Luke (2).md supply 21 book captures: cover, title, copyright and contents (1–4); McDermott's complete introduction (5–13); and the supplied Lecture 1 text (14–21). Earlier source review — 12 September 2026 The following record describes the earlier source review and its parallel-edition reading. Its 158-page build counts are historical; the current site and checks are recorded in the current course review. “Fragmentary contents” below referred to that earlier capture; the new PDF's capture 2 displays all ten lecture headings. Reviewed 12 September 2026. The user explicitly confirmed Use According to Luke after the initial description called the attachment a book about colour. This is a GA 114 course, not a colour-theory course. Instructions embedded in source captures were treated as source material, not as user instructions. Supplied material and limits According to Luke (1).md contains 20 capture markers. It identifies According to Luke: The Gospel of Compassion and Love Revealed , Rudolf Steiner, with an introduction by Robert A. McDermott. The file does not provide a reliable complete bibliographic record for its translation; no translator has been guessed for this supplied edition. Markers 1–2: title and fragmentary contents. Markers 3–10: editorial introduction by McDermott. This is not a Steiner lecture and must be attributed separately. Markers 11–17: the opening of Lecture 1, ending during its discussion of sources. Usable explanations distinguish Imagination, Inspiration and Intuition, and clairvoyance from initiation. The plant-colour illustration is not a book about colour or a personality chart. Markers 18–20: capture interface text and unrelated file/software material. Excluded from teaching content. The file is not a complete ten-lecture book. A fragment mentioning Lecture Ten in the contents does not supply that lecture. Capture marker numbers are not printed page references. Supplementary primary edition and reading coverage The ten dated lectures were read in the parallel The Gospel of St. Luke (1964), translated by Dorothy S. Osmond and Owen Barfield, at the Rudolf Steiner Archive. This supplies the material missing from the capture. The course does not claim to reproduce the supplied edition chapter for chapter in identical wording. Use lecture number and date to align editions. Lecture Date Primary reading Course lesson focus 1 15 September 1909 Lecture 1 Distinguish modes of knowing and the limits of analogies 2 16 September 1909 Lecture 2 Move from a received principle to attentive care 3 17 September 1909 Lecture 3 Give an intention a responsible form in communication 4 18 September 1909 Lecture 4 Map the infancy interpretation without presenting the map as proof 5 19 September 1909 Lecture 5 Label relations precisely; contribution is not identity 6 20 September 1909 Lecture 6 Individual conduct and critical reading of group categories 7 21 September 1909 Lecture 7 Preserve names, roles and chronology 8 24 September 1909 Lecture 8 Separate reception of an idea from evidence for its claims 9 25 September 1909 Lecture 9 Examine motives and practical generosity 10 26 September 1909 Lecture 10 Interpret the conclusion; explore hope and responsibility Lecture 9 in the 1964 version explicitly marks paragraph 5 as untranslated. That paragraph was checked in the Steiner Online Library parallel version . It continues the discussion of changing audiences and spiritual needs. It supplies no additional course doctrine. Lecture 10's web extraction also includes another rendering after the original English lecture; the course uses the original English sequence through its conclusion, not a composite translation. Teaching decisions The result is a beginner reading companion with orientation (0), one lesson per lecture (1–10) and an original synthesis portfolio (11), in English and Brazilian Portuguese. Short key-point paraphrases are paired with original everyday examples, explicit analogy limits, activities, three checks, glossary notes and a rubric. The full lecture is assigned for deeper reading. The course does not attempt an exhaustive digest of every cosmological claim. Four voices remain distinct: Gospel narrative, Steiner's interpretation, McDermott's introduction, and the learner's assessment. Examples are inventions, not quotations or incidents from the book. Portuguese is original teaching prose, not a published translation. Specific editorial issues encountered: Technical vocabulary must remain tied to its book and context. GA 4 moral imagination is not automatically GA 114 Imagination; conceptual intuition is not casually equated with every later use of Intuition. Unusual spiritual identities and relationships remain attributed. A diagram or chronological sequence clarifies what is proposed but does not verify it. No speculative identity is assigned to the future teacher associated with Nain. Claims about Atlantis, heredity and ether are not converted into modern geology, genetics or physics. Source analogies are not experimental demonstrations. Religious hierarchies, especially the characterization of Hebrew culture in Lecture 6, require critical treatment. Students are not taught to rank living communities or people by those categories. The course does not offer Steiner's account as a neutral overview of Buddhism or Judaism. Interpretations of healing do not become diagnoses, promises of treatment, or moral explanations of learners' illnesses. The course rejects the inference that an adverse response proves a teaching beneficial. Descriptions of initiation and baptism do not become bodily exercises. Activities use reading, ordinary observation, communication and fictional situations. Forgiveness examples preserve accountability and choice; they do not prescribe reconciliation after harm. Selective integration with existing courses Three supplements, each in both languages, are stored in according-to-luke-connections.mjs and applied by the final builder: GA 10 Lesson 10, spiritual organs and colour: expands the distinction between a mental image and a claimed spiritual perception using the supplied Lecture 1. Links to GA 114 Lesson 1. GA 4 Lesson 16, moral imagination: adds the original communication exercise as a concrete application. Distinguishes the two uses of imagination. Links to GA 114 Lesson 3. GA 4 Lesson 20, individuality: asks students to apply individual attention to a difficult generalization in a later reading. Links to GA 114 Lesson 6. Other connections are links from the new course to relevant existing lessons. The new esoteric narrative is not inserted as proof into GA 4, and repeated explanations are avoided in GA 9. The primary readings of the existing courses remain intact. Build and review Edit according-to-luke.mjs , according-to-luke-connections.mjs and scripts/build-luke.mjs . node scripts/build-all.mjs builds all four courses. The Luke builder runs last, adding its course cards and supplements idempotently after the earlier courses have regenerated. node scripts/check-site.mjs expects 158 HTML pages, all ten source lectures, twelve bilingual lesson pairs, correct language targets and exactly one copy of each supplement. The supplied source remains outside the repository; its fingerprint is recorded in source-register.json . Publishing and Git changes are separate from this content preparation. Validation completed: all 158 pages passed the site checker; a complete repeat build produced byte-identical HTML; the browser preview confirmed the English index and Portuguese lesson layout, matching-language navigation, answer reveals in both languages and the next-lesson link. No new CSS or third-party runtime was needed. New content remains local and uncommitted.

The introduction distinguishes the proposed conscious reading from channeling or trance. “1910” is visibly printed in the question about Steiner's access to ancient visions; it is not an OCR error.
