Capture 96 lists the Steiner reference as the 1944 The Four Temperaments , page 6. That citation inside Childs must remain distinct from the newly supplied 2012 English Steiner capture used by the course. Combined-course coverage and targeted additions The combined course already teaches the four portraits, education, mixtures and practical observation. Its original examples, continuing case, exercises, answers and transfer questions should remain intact. The complete Childs source supports seven short additions, each 138–157 English words with a Portuguese counterpart. The additions provide named source concepts; fuller chapter-by-chapter teaching remains in the thirteen-lesson Childs companion. Main lesson Existing Childs link Source-based addition or sufficient existing coverage 00, Meet the person before the type Companion 00 Add Chapter 1’s cards metaphor and working meanings of personality, individuality and character. Add companion 01 as a reading link. 01, The four tendencies and their background Companion 02 Explain Childs’s introversion/extroversion and convergent/divergent coordinates, his claim of no appreciable intelligence difference, and his particular meaning of stability. 02, Choleric: purpose and correction Companion 03 Existing teaching is sufficient. The Childs connection can cite Chapter 7 explicitly for receiving advice and correction. 03, Sanguine: interest and follow-through Companion 04 Existing teaching is sufficient. The Childs connection can distinguish Chapter 4’s uncompleted plans from Chapter 7’s schedules and deadlines. 04, Phlegmatic: steadiness and participation Companion 05 Existing teaching and connection already distinguish preparation time and invitation from a fixed role. Preserve them. 05, Melancholic: sensitivity and care Companion 06 Existing teaching distinguishes sensitivity and practical care from the author’s broad caricature. Preserve it. 06, Mixtures, context and change Companion 10 Add the age overlays in Chapter 2 and the book’s tension about changing temperament. Add companion 02 while retaining 10. 07, Supporting a learner Companion 06 Existing Steiner teaching is sufficient. Companion 02 is a useful optional further link for Childs’s full child-support discussion, captures 21–24. 08, Working together Primary companion 07 Add mutual dependence, aptitude, guided hands-on trials, invitations to share unspoken improvements, and explicit work schedules. Add a source-concept check. 09, Relationships and communication Primary companion 08 Add the exact qualifications of ten pairings, shared outlook, exchanging responsibilities, and conditional similarity/complementarity. Add a source-concept check. 10, Self-education through a small experiment No Childs link Add deliberate exercise of compensating qualities from Appendix I and link companion 10. Compare the emphasis with the existing Steiner source without changing its teaching. 11, A more attentive encounter Companion 12 Add Chapter 9’s body/soul/spirit premise, birthlessness/deathlessness argument and practical love. Add companion 09 while retaining synthesis 12. The primary book objects are spread into main lessons 08 and 09. Revised Childs key, context, goal, terms and reading fields can therefore propagate through the existing design. The main course’s own scenes, activities, explanations, questions, transfer fields and special relationship goal are separate authored material. Those fields should retain their current values. Secondary source titles and comparison takeaways also derive from the companions. Only Childs’s source descriptions should change through this revision; Steiner and The Mystery of Temperaments retain their own editions, claims and reading assignments. What the new source clarifies Childs’s Chapter 1 uses character for what imparts characteristics and helps identify habitual responses. He explicitly says moral respectability or criminality is not the issue in this definition (capture 10, column 2). The course also uses the term in discussing moral qualities. Attribution must make the difference legible instead of making one definition stand for both. Chapter 2’s stable groups phlegmatic and sanguine patterns together. For Childs, changing interests can themselves form a consistent pattern (17, column 3; 18, column 1). This is not a claim that the sanguine portrait is always dependable. Introversion/extroversion and convergent/divergent thinking are his proposed psychological classifications, distinct from Steiner’s four-member explanation. The complete book has a real tension about change. Chapter 2 rejects changing a child’s basic temperament (21, column 3); Chapter 7 says its use can mature while the temperament is given (48). Appendix I explicitly permits modifying and even changing temperament if the ego is sufficiently strong (78, column 3), then describes consciously exercising dormant compensating qualities (81–82). A main-course supplement should preserve that tension rather than silently choosing one assertion. Chapter 7 gives more than occupational matching. It opens with mutual interdependence, acknowledges manual and intellectual aptitude (47), recommends guided practical trials (49–50), discusses advice and correction (50), asks for unspoken suggestions (50, column 3), and recommends a work schedule with a stated deadline (51, column 2). Childs also endorses graphology and offers type-based occupational generalizations. The companion should describe these as his claims. The main course’s demonstrated-skill, preference and review plan remains an original adaptation. Chapter 8 first calls its sketches skewed and approximate, includes secondary temperaments, personality, health, upbringing and education, and allows unexpected responses (54, column 1). Its choleric/choleric example identifies a shared outlook as a bond irrespective of temperament and suggests exchanging responsibilities or assigning leadership by suitability (54, columns 2–3). Its choleric/phlegmatic example makes complementarity conditional on situation and secondary tendencies (56–57). The source still proposes predictability of typical reactions and contains gendered, hostile and aggressive caricatures. Preserve that authorial context; retain the course’s existing questions and revisable agreements. Chapter 9’s ethical conclusion depends on an explicit spiritual account. Body, soul and spirit, soul mediation, existence before birth and after death, reincarnation and the four members occupy 69–75. Care, consideration and non-possessive love expressed in deeds conclude 76–77. This sequence should be visible in the combined synthesis rather than treating the conclusion as an isolated modern communication recommendation. Appendix II remains important companion reading. It develops a historical body-type and embryological argument (83–95); it does not require another practical test in the main course. The existing distinction between a visible behaviour and an additional claim about bodily constitution remains appropriate. Selected source passages and connections Main lesson 08 can select the complete sentence beginning “Of course, whoever is chosen to do what must depend…” at capture 47, column 2. It grounds the discussion of individual aptitude and occupies one column. The new Portuguese quotation is a course translation. The native source has an en dash before “or both”; the OCR Markdown uses a hyphen. Main lesson 09 can retain its current exact English sentence beginning “Various aspects of reality are of course present…” and ending “are deliberately skewed.” It is verified at capture 54, column 1. The same column supplies the additional qualifications used in the new concept check. Previous locators 112 and 131 belong to the superseded capture of this same Childs book. If earlier selected text or notes are retained as evidence, label them as a previous selection or previous capture. A different reference edition must not be invented. All Steiner-primary selected passages in main lessons 00–07 and 10–11 remain unchanged. The existing Childs connections to the Steiner companion need only two attribution refinements. The choleric connection’s appreciation/flattery distinction is Chapter 3, capture 28; advice and correction are explicitly Chapter 7, capture 50. Its shared defect check remains original course practice. The sanguine connection’s plan/completion distinction is Chapter 4, capture 34; schedules and deadlines are Chapter 7, capture 51. The phlegmatic preparation/invitation connection and the compatibility/caricature connection already fit the complete source. The private draft at [private working file] provides the bilingual sections, additive checks, two verified passage records, source-link recommendations and precise connection wording. This review does not propose changes to the course’s original cases, exercises, transfer questions or Steiner-primary quotations.

Spirit/body/soul: 69–70; birthlessness and reincarnation: 71–72; Steiner intermediary quotation: 72; fourfold charts and exposition: 73–75; practical love and full ending: 75–77. 10 Appendix I: spirit, appearance and conscious practice Appendix I, PDF captures 78–82, especially 78 column 3 and 81–82. Compare Chapter 7, captures 47 column 3–48 column 1. Capture numbers are not printed folios. 11 Appendix II: reconstructing the four-body-type hypothesis Appendix II, PDF captures 83–95; Figures 3–7 in 87–92, Composite Table in 89 column 1, final table in 94 column 2. References in capture 96. Printed folios are not visible. 12 Synthesis: from the book's model to a considerate action Revisit Chapters 1–9, PDF captures 9–77, and Appendices I–II, captures 78–95. For the social aim read 75 column 3–77 column 1; references are in capture 96. Publisher catalogue capture 97 is excluded. The revised course teaches Childs's precise working meanings of temperament, individuality, personality and character; his prediction and outward-recognition claims; historical humours; attention and perseverance; the three psychological classifications; all four portraits; original child-education proposals; developmental overlays; workplace interdependence and aptitude; all ten partnership sketches; and the explicit soul, spirit, reincarnation, fourfold-constitution and practical-love argument. Both appendices receive full explanations of their reasoning, qualifications and proposed models. The practical course adaptations remain distinct from the author's stronger prescriptions. His advice to withhold choleric advice until requested, prolong tragic stories for melancholic children, narrate real or fictitious woes, use graphology, match occupations by temperament and infer temperament from appearance is explained with attribution. The course's feedback agreements, honest voluntary care and demonstrated-skill exercises are identified as later applications rather than presented as his own instructions. Important source tensions are retained: formal sanguine stability means consistent changeability even though later rhetoric calls it instability; capture 16 contains an apparent refuge-sentence slip; Chapter 7 rejects changing temperament while Appendix I explicitly allows modification and even change. Appendix II's earlier mesomorphic mapping differs from its final rejection of a separate mesomorphic type. The revision records these differences rather than silently harmonizing them. Figures and tables Four accessible source-based teaching tables explain attention/perseverance (lesson 1), orientation/thinking/stability (2), the fourfold spiritual mapping (9), and the final two-family, four-variant body-type proposal (11). Their source captions distinguish Childs's model from measurements or causal proof. The full composite table's additional dimensions are explained in the appendix guide. The existing ten-pair discussion table, the appendix argument map and separate contemporary genetics context are preserved. The figure review records every numbered figure, relevant table, axis direction and early/final correspondence distinction. English and Portuguese tables have semantic headers and labelled focusable regions. Related temperament teaching The twelve-lesson Understanding Temperaments course keeps all original cases, examples, activities, explanations, questions, transfer tasks and notebook controls. Seven compact additions explain Childs's vocabulary, psychological distinctions, age overlays and change tension, guided workplace experience, qualified pairings, compensating qualities and spiritual/social conclusion. Lessons 8 and 9 now have an additional source-comprehension check and correctly located passages from this supplied book. Five further reading links connect the precise companion sections. Two existing Childs supplements in the Steiner companion now attribute receiving correction to Chapter 7 and distinguish Chapter 4's unfinished plans from Chapter 7's schedules and deadlines. The other two supplements are preserved. All ten active Steiner-primary passage records in the combined course remain unchanged. Older Childs page numbers 112 and 131 are kept only as labelled superseded capture evidence from the same book; no different edition is invented. See the combined-course review . Validation and preservation The full site build and all 17 validators pass. The checks cover all 97 page records, nine chapters and both appendices, author and edition credits, thirteen bilingual source guides, four source tables, every passage assignment, teaching before practice, bilingual routes, local links, study controls and the existing courses' requirements. The site still contains 398 HTML pages and 414 static artifacts . There are now 160 passage-selection records across twelve collections, assigned to 170 lesson pairs / 340 bilingual lesson pages. Changed output is limited to 28 Childs companion pages, 24 combined-course lesson pages and four Steiner companion pages containing the refined Childs connections. Every other generated course page and asset matches the pre-revision baseline. The existing companion examples and explanations, all primary-course practice fields, previous teaching sections and source checks, all non-Childs passage records and unrelated guided prompts are preserved. The staged preview build also passed all seventeen validators. All 78 temperament HTML routes and the stylesheet passed HTTP checks, alongside ten general preview checks; all 414 staged artifacts match the workspace build. Publication has not been performed.

title: Understand Your Temperament!: figures and teaching tables
text: Understand Your Temperament!: figures and teaching tables Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Current records / Registros atuais Current source record. Any explicitly dated historical sections remain historical, as the note explains. Registro atual de fontes. As seções históricas explicitamente datadas mantêm esse caráter, conforme explicado na nota. Illustration provenance · English · 30 September 2026 · 849 words Understand Your Temperament!: figures and teaching tables Reviewed 30 September 2026 against the newly supplied 97-capture PDF. All positions below are PDF capture indices and columns; printed folios are not visible. The new copy supplies readable original figures and tables, superseding the previous damaged-figure notices. Original illustrations remain in the private book; the course uses accessible tables and explanations. Original item Verified location Meaning and teaching treatment Elements and humours table 11, left Choleric/fire/yellow bile; sanguine/air/blood; phlegmatic/water/body fluids; melancholic/earth/black bile. Historical humoral associations, not modern bodily measurements. Explained in Chapter 1. Arousal and perseverance chart 13, left Melancholic: attention not easily aroused, strong perseverance; phlegmatic: least easily aroused, strong perseverance; choleric: most easily aroused, strongest perseverance; sanguine: easily aroused, little perseverance. New lesson 1 table keeps these two dimensions distinct. Introvert/extrovert and difficulties tables 16, left; 18, middle Phlegmatic/melancholic are reflective introverts; choleric/sanguine active extroverts. The difficulties table divides inward personality difficulties from outward behavioural difficulties. These are Childs's categories. Figure 1 19, middle Stable at top, unstable at bottom; introvert/convergent left and extrovert/divergent right. Phlegmatic and sanguine occupy the stable half; melancholic and choleric the unstable half. Elements and qualitative traits surround the quadrants. Expanded lesson 2 table preserves the mappings, with a caption explaining the author's specific use of stability. Unnumbered quadrant 20, right Reverses the vertical display: unstable at top, stable below. It keeps melancholic/choleric above and phlegmatic/sanguine below, with the same introvert/extrovert allocation. Do not infer changed associations from the changed placement. Figure 2 21, left Four stereotyped bodily silhouettes, ordered melancholic, sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric. Described as the author's outward-recognition proposal; not reproduced as a tool for assigning a person a temperament. Chapter portrait motto/theme tables 26, 31, 36 and 42 Short humorous framing for each portrait. The source guides explain their role without substituting slogans for the chapter's argument. Fourfold constitution table 73 Fire/ego/choleric, air/ astral /sanguine, water/ etheric /phlegmatic, earth/physical/melancholic. New lesson 9 table presents Childs's spiritual interpretation, separately from the retained contemporary genetics context. Historical body-type tables 86, left and middle Compare Martigny's mesoblastique/chordoblastique/entoblastique/ectoblastique terms and the proposed Sheldon/temperament correspondences. The early mapping gives choleric a mesomorphic association; the prose and final proposal later change or reject this terminology. It is not flattened into one unchanging table. Figure 3 87, middle; caption at right top Martigny's four bodily sketches within the discussion of three main types. Childs describes where the attempted correspondences fail. This is a stage of the argument, rather than the final scheme. Figure 4 87, right; caption at 88, left top Childs's adaptation adds temperament labels and eurymorphic/leptomorphic groupings to Martigny's arrangement. Kept distinct from the later interface proposal. Figure 5 88, middle Ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm layers with mesoderm interfaces; severe and moderate leptomorphic and eurymorphic variants. The text introduces its links as a proposed explanation. Lesson 11 explains the model before judging its evidential support. Composite Table of Attributes 89, left Columns phlegmatic/choleric/sanguine/melancholic combine origin, physique, somatotype, orientation, thinking, balance, time, direction, difficulties and social attitude. Moderate choleric/sanguine rows name mesoderm, while Figure 5 also discusses interfaces with the neighbouring layers. Their different presentations remain explicit. Germ-layer and organ-system table 89, right → 90, left Childs connects ectoderm with head/sensory organization, mesoderm with chest, and endoderm with digestion. The surrounding discussion acknowledges interdependence and loose destinations. The course attributes the temperament inference instead of teaching it as established causal anatomy. Figure 6 91, right Proposed head/melancholic, lung/sanguine, heart/choleric and digestive/phlegmatic organization, with severe/moderate form labels. New lesson 11 table includes the functional regions. Figure 7 92, left Four form variants with orientation, cognitive pattern, stability and difficulty labels. The final lesson 11 table retains the author's two families and two variants, without copying the silhouettes. Final body-type table 94, middle Melancholic = severe ectomorphic/leptomorphic; sanguine = moderate ectomorphic/leptomorphic; choleric = moderate endomorphic/eurymorphic; phlegmatic = severe endomorphic/eurymorphic. The text rejects a separate mesomorphic type. This final scheme differs from the earlier comparison table. The four source-based course tables are original teaching summaries: attention/perseverance (lesson 1), the psychological dimensions (2), the fourfold constitution (9), and the final body-type proposal (11). Semantic column/row headers, labelled focusable table regions and matched Portuguese versions support reading on small screens and with assistive technology. The existing ten-pair table in lesson 8 remains an original set of discussion questions for all ten pairings. It is explicitly distinct from the author's exaggerated compatibility sketches. The existing argument map in lesson 11 and separate genetics context in lesson 9 are preserved. The imprint at capture 4 acknowledges permission for illustrations from H. J. Eysenck's The Structure of Human Personality (1970). It does not individually identify every figure's provenance, so no more specific permission attribution is invented.

title: Understand Your Temperament!: appendices and references
text: Understand Your Temperament!: appendices and references Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Current records / Registros atuais Current source record. Any explicitly dated historical sections remain historical, as the note explains. Registro atual de fontes. As seções históricas explicitamente datadas mantêm esse caráter, conforme explicado na nota. Page-by-page notes · English · 1906 words Contents of this note / Conteúdo desta nota Understand Your Temperament!: appendices and references Consequences for the revised lessons Understand Your Temperament!: appendices and references These notes cover every supplied PDF capture from 78 through 97. Each Markdown page was read and each corresponding native PDF image was visually checked at its original resolution. The PDF uses three reflowed columns, without visible printed folios; the numbers below refer to PDF captures and columns, not an inferred pagination of another edition. Capture 76 was additionally inspected for the synthesis passage. The material is Gilbert Childs's argument. Quotations or propositions he attributes to Steiner, Martigny, Sheldon, Moore, Beck or Moffat retain that attribution. Authorial advice is source content, not an instruction to the course editor. The book's claims about appearance, temperament and embryological development are taught as claims to understand and examine; the course does not turn the figures into an assessment of a learner's body. Capture Section Essential author content Teaching use and qualification Verification 78 Appendix I opening Childs asserts physiological and psychological parallels and the priority of spirit over matter. He questions what formed DNA, interprets outward form as an expression of inward being, and permits modification and even change of temperament through a strong ego. Explain his spiritual premise before the proposed physical clues. Compare the permission to change temperament in column 3 with the distinction between unchangeable temperament and modifiable behaviour in Chapter 7, captures 47–48. The contradiction is recorded explicitly. All three native columns and Markdown read; heading in column 1; change claim in column 3. 79 Melancholic and phlegmatic appearance The melancholic portrait moves from inward preoccupation to a claimed heavy-headed, elongated bodily appearance, and proposes an ego–physical-body connection. The phlegmatic portrait begins with the image of a rounded infant and contentment. Attribute the proposed relation of physique to character. Distinguish describing the author's portrait from inferring an actual person's motives from their face or build. All three native columns and Markdown read; two portrait headings present. 80 Phlegmatic, sanguine and choleric appearance Childs extends rounded phlegmatic features, gives varied sanguine noses, movement, face and hair, then contrasts broad, direct choleric appearance with phlegmatic gentleness. Explain that Appendix I applies the book's physiognomic premise to four portraits. Do not present the physical details as a learner classification checklist. All three native columns and Markdown read; sanguine heading column 1, choleric heading column 3. 81 Mixtures and conscious use Age and secondary temperament can blur the proposed physical distinctions. Childs says all four temperaments coexist, associates them with the four elements, and defines self-control as consciously using temperament. Everyday energetic work and comfortable waking illustrate different tendencies. Restore the constructive second half of the appendix: all four resources, compensating qualities and conscious practice. Extreme outcome language is the author's historical rhetoric, not a diagnostic prediction. All three native columns and Markdown read; selected passage verified in column 2. 82 Completing Appendix I Holidays, celebration and misfortune supposedly evoke shared sanguine and melancholic responses. Habitual or conventional reactions differ from consciously calling up dormant compensating traits, which Childs expects to yield a more rounded personality and reduced strain. Separate Childs's everyday examples from a new course exercise. A response chosen deliberately is the transferable idea; the promised health effects are claims, not demonstrated outcomes. All native text in columns 1–2 and blank column 3 checked against Markdown; appendix ends here. 83 Appendix II opening The apparent mismatch is four temperaments versus three somatotypes. Childs introduces the embryonic disc, ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, and outlines ectomorphic, mesomorphic and endomorphic builds. Start an argument map with the question and the proposed requirement of one-to-one correspondence. Distinguish the biological vocabulary from the asserted temperament connection. All three native columns and Markdown read; appendix heading and three definitions visible. 84 Germ layers and historical twofold build Quotations cited to Moore and to Beck and Moffat emphasize differentiation and the limited rigidity of germ-layer descriptions. Childs lists proposed organ systems and mesenchyme, then traces two basic builds to Hippocrates and recommends Eysenck. Explain how Childs uses flexibility in development to challenge a rigid three-type theory. The embryology quotations do not independently establish his later personality mapping. All three native columns and Markdown read; superscript reference markers 2 and 3 visible. 85 Three-type table and Martigny A table pairs endoderm–endomorphic, mesoderm–mesomorphic and ectoderm–ectomorphic. Childs criticizes fitting facts to three types, then introduces Martigny's fourth, chordoblastic type as a possible solution. Keep the historical three-type scheme separate from the later authorial scheme. A numerical mismatch between classifications does not itself prove an error or a biological cause. All three native columns and Markdown read; table continues from column 1 to column 2. 86 Comparing rival terminology Martigny's mesoblastic, chordoblastic, entoblastic and ectoblastic terms are paired with four builds. The comparison table associates mesoblastic/mesomorphic with choleric and chordoblastic with sanguine. The later prose shifts the mesomorphic correspondence toward sanguine and says choleric is combined with phlegmatic as endomorphic. Teach the table and subsequent reinterpretation as distinct stages. This is an internal inconsistency in terminology, not a reason to invent one seamless historical mapping. All three native columns and Markdown read; both tables inspected, including the column break. 87 Figure 3 Childs credits Martigny with identifying four somatotypes while criticizing his arrangement. The figure and repeated diagram show muscular, balanced, abdominal and lean forms with author-added temperament labels. Use the available figure to explain what Childs accepts and revises. The caption calls it a representation of three main body types although four illustrated categories appear; preserve that tension. All three native columns and Markdown read; diagrams visible in columns 2 and 3, caption in column 3. 88 Figures 4–5 and interfaces Figure 4 is captioned as Childs's adaptation. He links chordoblastic to neural development, then proposes two ectoderm-related leptomorphs and two endoderm-related eurymorphs. Figure 5 assigns moderate forms to interfaces with mesoderm. Explain the speculative step signalled by “I venture to suggest” and “I suggest.” Melancholic and phlegmatic are extreme forms; sanguine and choleric are moderate forms. Do not convert a proposed interface into established causation. All three native columns and Markdown read; Figure 4 caption column 1 and Figure 5 with labels column 2 visible. 89 Composite Table of Attributes The table combines four origins, physiques, somatotypes, orientations, thinking styles, stability, time attitudes, directions, difficulties and social attitudes. The prose extends threefolding to head/senses, chest/rhythm and digestion while insisting that systems interdepend. Restore the readable table's actual content. Its Origin row assigns mesoderm to both moderate types, whereas the preceding prose also invokes their ectodermal or endodermal interfaces; explain those roles separately. All three native columns and Markdown read; complete table visually read in column 1. 90 Organ-system table and further extension The table lists germ-layer contributions to organ systems. Childs acknowledges a sketch and latitude, then compares interdependent bodily functions with cognition, feeling and willing rather than rigid compartments. Teach his transition from embryological categories to an integrated physical–psychological model. Interdependence is an organizing analogy, not proof of a temperament-specific organ. All three native columns and Markdown read; full table continued in column 1. 91 Figure 6 and polar opposition Melancholic is proposed as cerebral/head and phlegmatic as digestive/metabolic. Childs contrasts their location, function and consciousness. Figure 6 places melancholic at the head, sanguine at lungs, choleric at heart and phlegmatic at digestion. Explain the named four organ correspondences and the shared introversion of the opposing extreme types. The author's assertion about conscious digestion is not adopted as a medical rule. All three native columns and Markdown read; full Figure 6 labels visible in column 3. 92 Figure 7 and chest organs Figure 7 combines extreme/moderate build, stable/unstable, convergence/divergence and introversion/extroversion. Childs argues that the two remaining temperaments must connect with chest organs, then describes complementary heart and lung functions. Follow the argument's elimination step: assigning head and digestion first does not by itself establish that remaining types belong to heart and lungs. Include the full four-row model in study notes. All three native columns and Markdown read; complete Figure 7 in column 1. 93 Lungs, blood and interfaces Childs explicitly connects sanguine with lungs and choleric with blood. He adds proximity and interface arguments, proposes extroversion and divergence for both, and translates embryonic strata into a vertical adult-body scheme. Attribute these as his deductions and correspondences. A coherent arrangement can suggest a hypothesis while still requiring evidence independent of the chosen categories. All three native columns and Markdown read; explicit lungs/blood statement column 1. 94 Final two-by-two model The final table gives severe ectomorphic melancholic, moderate ectomorphic sanguine, moderate endomorphic choleric and severe endomorphic phlegmatic. Childs denies a distinct mesomorphic type and concludes that two broad physiques, each severe or moderate, yield four somatotypes. State the final model accurately and distinguish it from earlier tables that still used mesomorphic terminology. Reconstructing the model and evaluating its evidence are separate tasks. All three native columns and Markdown read; final table column 2 and selected two-by-two passage column 3 verified. 95 Appendix II conclusion One continuing sentence claims that the argument vindicates some nineteenth-century suspicions about mesenchyme or layer interfaces. The rest of the capture is blank. This is the genuine end of the appendix, not an extraction gap or missing diagram. Include the concluding claim when identifying the scope of the supplied source. Native column 1 text, blank columns 2–3 and Markdown checked. 96 References Three numbered references cite Steiner's The Four Temperaments (1944) and Childs's Steiner Education in Theory and Practice (1991); Moore's The Developing Human (1988, fourth edition); Beck and Moffat's Human Embryology and Genetics (1973). Preserve bibliography and citation hierarchy. These are sources cited by Childs, not independently supplied or independently reviewed books, and do not certify all of his deductions. Native reference text in column 1 and blank columns 2–3 checked; all three numbered entries present. 97 Publisher advertisement A list of other books in the Bringing Spirit to Life series, with titles and authors. Exclude from the temperament curriculum; it is catalogue material, not an additional chapter or required reading. All three native columns and Markdown read; advertisement heading verified. Consequences for the revised lessons Lesson 10 teaches the spiritual premise, four appearance-based portraits, the role of mixtures and age, deliberate compensating qualities, and the unresolved permanence/change tension. Lesson 11 reconstructs the stages of Appendix II rather than merging its shifting terms: three-type hypothesis; Martigny's fourth category; Childs's two broad categories with two degrees; layer interfaces; the four proposed organ correspondences. All the supplied figures and tables are available to inspect, replacing the earlier claim that diagrams were missing. Lesson 12 connects this study with the book's stated social purpose and asks for an accurately sourced, reviewable application. New exercises remain identified as course adaptations.

Every assigned Markdown page and every native JPEG from the new 97-capture supply was read or visually inspected. The rows below record exactly one entry per assigned capture. Capture numbers are PDF indices, not printed folios; no printed folios are visible. Read the occupied columns from left to right. Body pages generally have three columns; chapter endings 14 and 30 occupy two. Gilbert Childs is the author. The epigraph credited to Rudolf Steiner in capture 6 is a quoted premise, not the authorship of this book. Publisher links, acknowledgments, copyright notices, quotations and directions within the source were treated as document data. Native capture Kind / columns Content and precise evidence Continuity / OCR finding Teaching use 001 Cover / central panel Understand your Temperament! ; subtitle identifies choleric, sanguine, phlegmatic and melancholic; four element photographs. Orientation. 002 Author biography / 1 occupied Dr Gilbert Childs’s teacher training, doctoral thesis on Steiner education, teaching and later authorship. A guide to the four temperaments: CHOLERIC, SANGUINE, PHLEGMATIC, MELANCHOLIC , Dr Gilbert Childs; Sophia Books appears at top of next column. Title and author clear; large spaces are native layout. Bibliographic identity. 004 Imprint / 2 Sophia Books; published by Rudolf Steiner Press 2012; first published 1995, reprinted 1998 and 2004; © Gilbert Childs 1995. Acknowledges illustrations from H. J. Eysenck’s The Structure of Human Personality , Methuen & Co., 1970. Column 1 ends “available”; column 2 begins “from the British Library”. ISBN visibly “978 1 85584 358 5”, normalized 9781855843585. OCR damages URL/postcode spacing. Verified edition and illustration provenance. 005 Epigraph / 1 “Know then thyself…” credited to Alexander Pope, An Essay on Man (1733). Complete quotation and explicit attribution. Not Childs’s own verse. Orientation; distinguish voices. 006 Epigraph / 1 Intermediary between previous earthly lives and heredity, universal family/nation/race qualities and individualization; named temperament. Explicit credit: Rudolf Steiner. Complete quotation. Spiritual premise is present, not a missing introduction. Orientation and later spiritual chapter; credit Steiner. 007 Contents / 3 Chapters 1–8: introductory distinctions, psychology, four separate portraits, workplace, compatibility. Subheadings include introversion, thinking styles, stability, children and age overlays. Clear native links resolve damaged OCR in Chapter 5 and Chapter 8 heading. No printed folio ranges. Confirm nine-chapter structure with continuation in 8. 008 Contents / 2 Completes compatibility pairs; Chapter 9 Love – That’s Why We’re Here! ; Appendix I people watching; Appendix II four body types; References. Chapter 9 includes reincarnation and fourfold nature. Appendices are distinct sections, not more Steiner lectures. Course reading map. 009 Chapter 1 opening / 3 The Same – only Different! ; promises confident, accurate classification; predictable familiar behaviour and doubt when character judgments fail; personality/character heading. Column 1→2 “and / also”; 2→3 “sep- / arated”. Ends “certain general”, continued by 10. Orientation excerpt: column 1; attribute prediction promise. 010 Chapter 1 / 3 Personality expressed through deeds; temperament cards dealt at birth and individuality’s way of playing them. Character concerns habitual responses, not moral respectability. Infers bodily constitution and outward appearance from consistency. Starts “categories”; column 1→2 “may be / said”; 2→3 “nature / of habit”. Ends “with the”, continued by 11. Lesson 1 distinctions; do not convert claimed bodily inference into fact. 011 Chapter 1 / 3 Historical table: choleric/fire/yellow bile; sanguine/air/blood; phlegmatic/water/body fluids; melancholic/earth/black bile. Sketchy dictionary definitions, objections, Shakespeare and composers; three somatotypes versus four temperaments. Table is visually intact, though OCR extracts columns separately. Preserve “body fluids” rather than replacing it with another humoral label. Ends “fascinating,” continued by 12. Lesson 1 historical model. 012 Chapter 1 / 3 Endomorphic, ectomorphic, mesomorphic definitions; Childs rejects three-category adequacy, proposes two kinds of tall/thin and two short/fat. Polarities melancholic/sanguine and phlegmatic/choleric; longer observation and predictive “acid test”. Column 2→3 “clearly / mainly extrovert”. Ends “and”, continued by 13. Author claims temperament built into constitution and visible, not mere analogy. Lesson 1 classification argument and limits. 013 Chapter 1 / 3 Attention diagram: melancholic not easily aroused/strongly persevering; phlegmatic least easily aroused/strongly persevering; choleric most easily aroused/most strongly persevering; sanguine easily aroused/little perseverance. No best type; all four in unequal proportions, normally two main, third trace, fourth overpowered. Column 1→2 “and / this”. Ends “to what”, continued by 14. Source juxtaposes long observation with reliable clues after minutes of conversation. Lesson 1 excerpt column 1; exact attention chart. 014 Chapter 1 end / 2 occupied Promise of greater tolerance; limits of self-knowledge; others may see us more clearly; Burns’s “To a Louse”; telling a friend the truth can risk friendship. Column 1→2 “better / than”. Ends complete friendship sentence. Empty third area is layout, not gap. Orientation/lesson 1 reflective close. 015 Chapter 2 opening / 3 The Psychology of the Temperaments ; defends long tradition and common-sense observation against scientific objections. Public outer world/private inner world; reflective introverts and active extroverts. Column 1→2 “Development in / Appendix II”; 2→3 “but / this trait”. Ends “impulsively,” continued by 16. Lesson 2: author’s rationale and first axis. 016 Chapter 2 / 3 Table: introvert/reflective=phlegmatic, melancholic; extrovert/active=choleric, sanguine. Convergent concentration/memory/logical and object-focused stereotype; divergent imagination, intuition and sociability. Native column 3 genuinely says divergents “take refuge in things from people”, then convergents “from people in things”. This repeats the same direction despite preceding contrast; do not silently repair or blame OCR. Ends “knowledge”, continued by 17. Lesson 2 precise terms and textual tension. 017 Chapter 2 / 3 No appreciable intelligence-range difference claimed; exam-style distinctions. Divergent=choleric/sanguine; convergent=phlegmatic/melancholic. Stable=phlegmatic/sanguine; unstable=choleric/melancholic. Thinking-style table splits across columns 1 and 2. Column 2→3 “be- / haviour”. Ends “consist-”, continued by 18. Lesson 2: retain three distinct classifications. 018 Chapter 2 / 3 Sanguine stable because consistently inconsistent; map of personality difficulties: melancholic/unstable introvert, phlegmatic/stable introvert; behavioural difficulties: choleric/unstable extrovert, sanguine/stable extrovert. Source stereotypes and pathological language follow. Exact table in column 2. Column 2→3 “with / their bodily comforts”. Ends “very”, continued by 19. “Stable” is used inconsistently with ordinary predictability; explain author’s patterned-consistency sense. Lesson 2 exact map, not mental-health classification. 019 Chapter 2 / 3 Strength can become weakness in excess. Figure 1 circular quadrant, column 2: TOP stable, BOTTOM unstable; LEFT introvert/convergent, RIGHT extrovert/divergent. Phlegmatic upper-left, sanguine upper-right, melancholic lower-left, choleric lower-right. Element imagery; gravity and water. Native diagram readable; OCR largely destroys axes and descriptors. Column 1→2 “arrange themselves / as two”; 2→3 “temperaments / with”. Ends “can”, continued by 20. Lesson 2 visual mapping. 020 Chapter 2 / 3 Water tolerance/possible storm; fiery compulsive choleric activity; air-like shifting sanguine activity and alleged nervous breakdowns. Unnumbered quadrant in column 3: TOP unstable, BOTTOM stable; LEFT introvert/reflective, RIGHT extrovert/active; melancholic/choleric above phlegmatic/sanguine. This quadrant reverses Figure 1’s vertical orientation while preserving pairings. Column 1→2 “over- / whelming”. Do not call it the body caricature Figure 2 shown next. Lesson 2 polarities and attributed extreme claims. 021 Chapter 2 / 3 Figure 2 body caricatures in order melancholic, sanguine, phlegmatic, choleric. Says temperaments determined at birth; family differences exceed heredity; all children up to ten/eleven have sanguine overlay. Warns against changing temperament as built into constitution. Caricatures intact. Column 1→2 “and / personality”; 2→3 “quar- / relsome”. Ends “only by”, continued by 22. Lesson 2 source’s bodily and developmental claims. 022 Chapter 2 / 3 Choleric child: challenges just beyond capability, ready help if difficulty misjudged, no breaking will, distraction/joining, praise and demonstrated skill. Sanguine child: monitor varied interests, seek durable attention, flower visits as example. Column 1→2 “are / appropriate”; third column begins sanguine passage. Ends “life-long interest”, continued by 23. Teach actual source routes before course adaptation. 023 Chapter 2 / 3 Sanguine attachment to sympathetic person; phlegmatic peer interests with patient skilled companions; melancholic sensitivity, no forced cheerfulness, respect inwardness. Column 1→2 “them- / selves”; 2→3 “bois- / terous”. Ends “to sit”, continued by 24. Four routes and particular author rhetoric. 024 Chapter 2 / 3 Melancholic proposal: prolonged tragic story, preferably true, hoping vicarious misery becomes future charitable action. Aging appearance claims; childhood sanguine, adolescence choleric overlays. Complete tragic-story paragraph in column 1. Column 2→3 “it / were”. Ends “voluntary”, continued by 25. Source proposal is stronger than an ordinary manageable act of care. Lesson 2 development; distinguish applications. 025 Chapter 2 end / 3 Completes youthful idealism; middle-age melancholy/resignation and late-life phlegmatic comforts; humorous retirement voice and offered life wisdom. Column 1→2 “of / physical attractiveness”; 2→3 “No / more commuting”. Ends complete rhetorical close. Lesson 2 four age overlays, not universal timetable. 026 Chapter 3 opening / 3 The Choleric Temperament ; motto “When the going gets tough, the tough get going”, theme My Way . Fire/blood analogy; stocky build, facial traits, gait; gendered attractiveness/chivalry claims. Column 1→2 “is / linked”; 2→3 “oppos- / ite”. Ends “deliberately and”, continued by 27. No illness or temperament diagnosis from the portrait. Lesson 3 actual author portrait and rhetoric. 027 Chapter 3 / 3 Purposeful activity; unstable/extrovert/divergent labels and high-blood-pressure claim. Natural leadership, will, courage, perseverance and duty alongside stubbornness, impatience and sensitivity to criticism. Column 1→2 “matter / of course”; 2→3 “invariably / looking”. Ends “throw”, continued by 28. Lesson 3 strengths and one-sidedness. 028 Chapter 3 / 3 Choleric “collapse” after wounded pride and belittlement; possible rage or dejection. Recommends letting them work, offering labour, advice only when requested, appreciating real efforts while rejecting flattery. Also rationalizes deserved mistreatment. Column 1→2 “of / ruthless brutality”. Ends “original”, continued by 29. Author’s handling rule differs from course’s proposed feedback agreement. Lesson 3 source proposal; short passage column 3. 029 Chapter 3 / 3 Entrepreneurial initiative, risk and optimism; intolerance of others’ inefficiency and personal criticism; business success then blame/rage/failure caricature, ignored executive warning. Column 1→2 “eye / for detail”; 2→3 “Care- / less”. Final ellipsis intentionally trails the anecdote, not a missing page. Lesson 3 cooperation and correction application. 030 Chapter 3 end / 2 occupied Individuality and self-will; claims self-control is a lesson of earthly life. Choleric/melancholic mixture allegedly characterizes “manic-depressive” person; alternating failure/dejection and renewed optimism. Column 1 ends “degree”; column 2 starts “When failure”. Complete final sentence; empty third area is layout. Psychiatric association is source claim, not a diagnosis. Lesson 3 spiritual and medical attribution. Assigned chapter boundaries are now established from the new supply: Chapter 1, captures 9–14; Chapter 2, 15–25; Chapter 3, 26–30. Their text is continuous and each ends complete. There are no blank-page or missing-prose gaps in this assigned range. The earlier course’s 239-page capture ranges and statements about surviving fragments must not be reused. Full-book continuity outside 1–30 belongs to the other assigned reviews. The historical humoral table is taught as a historical association. Childs’s appearance-based recognition, prediction, hereditary inference, developmental overlays, psychiatric associations and medical generalizations are explicitly attributed. Course examples concerning roles, feedback, option generation and revisable observations remain later practical applications rather than silent replacements for his positions.

title: Childs: sanguine, phlegmatic and melancholic portraits
text: Childs: sanguine, phlegmatic and melancholic portraits Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Current records / Registros atuais Current source record. Any explicitly dated historical sections remain historical, as the note explains. Registro atual de fontes. As seções históricas explicitamente datadas mantêm esse caráter, conforme explicado na nota. Page-by-page notes · English · 1789 words Childs: sanguine, phlegmatic and melancholic portraits Every Markdown capture 031–046 was read in full and compared with its matching native JPEG. These sixteen captures contain complete chapters 4–6 of Gilbert Childs’s Understand Your Temperament! , not lectures by Rudolf Steiner. The PDF uses reflowed three-column views; capture numbers are not printed folios, which are not visible. The new 97-capture source supersedes the earlier 239-page extraction and its reported gaps. No assigned capture is blank, and no text gap is indicated in these chapters. Short chapter endings leave columns empty normally. The author/title were also visually checked at capture 003. Capture 004 explicitly records “Published by Rudolf Steiner Press 2012,” “First published in 1995 and reprinted in 1998 and 2004,” and “© Gilbert Childs 1995.” Publication year and copyright year are distinct here. The study guides attribute recognition, conduct, illness and handling claims to Childs; the existing course examples remain original fictional adaptations, not evidence for those claims. Capture Essential ideas and authorial reasoning Native evidence and actual extraction differences Teaching implication 031 Chapter 4, sanguine: Air and levity organize quick, birdlike movement and interests. Blood is invoked for constant movement and running hot/cold. Childs claims recognition from slender physique, springy gait, complexion, eyes, facial shape and nose, contrasting melancholic slowness. Native opening has an aligned two-row Motto / Theme tune table: “Promises, promises!” / Blue Skies . OCR flattens its reading order and renders a small expansion-control icon as “ra.” Prose is intact after line-wrap normalization; no portrait illustration appears. Explain the Air analogy and recognition claim as the author’s model. Body, sex and beauty generalizations are not observational proof of a person’s temperament. 032 Charm, good taste, imagination and sociability are paired with changeable mood, poor concentration, weak memory and low endurance. Childs calls sanguines poor scholars but credits intuition, discrimination, criticism and experiential learning. Resilience and forgetfulness help them recover. Three-column prose agrees with OCR; joined “to a” and artificial word splits are minor extraction artifacts. The final “increas-” continues on 033. No diagram or missing paragraph. Preserve the reasoning that novelty aids perception while impeding sustained study. Do not quietly replace the author’s strong scholarship claim with a neutral learning preference. 033 Novelty produces intense but short enthusiasm, rearranged homes and extravagant spending. Witty conversation and acting charm can mask superficial knowledge. Rapid interest shifts yield unfinished or rushed work, and others inherit the cleanup. Exact selected quote for lesson 4 is in column 1: “Changeable, and themselves loving change, sanguines invariably find it difficult to stick to a task and get it finished.” Native heading “Just look at that!” is in column 2; italics emphasize completion. OCR retains prose but loses some emphasis. No illustration. Distinguish interest from completion, while attributing Childs’s sweeping judgments about unreliability, gossip and domestic mistakes. The course’s small task agreement is a modest fictional adaptation. 034 Plans are imagined as already accomplished. Optimism/flexibility support changing direction. Companions and admired heroes affect the impressionable person. Childs links this to a sanguine overlay in youth and mocks older people’s attempts to look young. Sociability also becomes concern for others. Native emphasis on “in their minds” and “fix anything in concrete” is lost in plain OCR. Prose agrees. “Stran-” continues as “ger” on 035; that split is not missing text. Explain how imitation, social influence and optimism are both resources and liabilities. Keep age, dress and gender caricatures visibly Childs’s judgments. 035 Charitable sympathy and empathy complete the portrait. Childs recommends kindness, firm anchoring, composure, thoughtfulness and small gifts; rejects intimidation, blackmail and physical violence. He contrasts quick recovery from small slights with extreme resentment over serious injury. Native chapter ending occupies columns 1–2, with column 3 empty. Prose is complete after line-wrap normalization; no chapter text is lost. Give the specific firm-and-kind handling advice, including the author’s warning against domination; do not reduce the chapter to an admonition to finish tasks. 036 Chapter 5, phlegmatic: Water’s even surface conceals depths. Childs extends the symbol to bodily fluids, digestion, appetite and comfort, with stocky/rounded versus choleric square/muscular bodies. Includes a gendered appeal to feeding a man. Native Motto / Theme Tune table reads “Procrastinate tomorrow!” / Home, Sweet Home . OCR flattens it and adds “ra” from the same control icon. Text is intact; “phleg-” continues on 037. No body image. Explain the distinction between outward evenness and inward depth. Eating, body size and the gendered stomach proverb remain attributed caricatures rather than recognition tools. 037 Quiet, patience and tolerance protect an intense inner life; observers may mistake reserve for stupidity. Childs gives facial/voice criteria, comfortable clothes and dislike of fashion or change. Native heading “I just can’t be bothered” is column 3. Descriptive prose agrees; italics and the heading’s relative prominence are reduced by OCR. No diagram. Keep the internal contrast: the portrait criticizes inertia but explicitly rejects equating quietness with absence of inward life. 038 Privacy and security explain reluctance to disclose and rejection of intrusion. Hurt prompts withdrawal and a wish to think in peace. Demanded opinions cause confusion; advance notice permits preparation. Childs then escalates to an “Andy Capp” couch-potato caricature of inactivity. Selected quote for lesson 5 is exact in column 2: “They merely want to think things over quietly and thoroughly, and ask for the peace in which to do so.” OCR joins “be a”; otherwise prose intact. The armchair/snack scene is described in words, not pictured. Teach the author’s connection between preparation, privacy and a considered reply. Separate that argument from his laziness and weight caricatures; do not pretend the caricatures are missing from the source. 039 Low confidence and self-effacement inhibit initiative; a choleric secondary temperament can enable leadership. Slow learning but durable memory and practice lead to careful work. Childs infers lawfulness from lack of imagination, recommends routine/private work, yet credits calm emergency performance. Full three-column text agrees after dehyphenation; native ends “Do not underestimate their capabilities.” No diagram or gap. Present both valued reliability and the author’s restrictive employment/creativity claims. Task suitability should remain a question tested by actual skill, rather than a hiring rule from the portrait. 040 Under suitable conditions phlegmatics can be charming, witty, sympathetic listeners and advisers. Reflection often stays unspoken. Indecision and suspicion resist persuasion; careful financial comparison and preference for proven quality oppose hurried purchases. OCR “Witha” is native “With a”; “witha” is “with a.” No substantive prose omission. Native italics on “antiques” are not retained. The sentence on tolerance continues at 041. Explain why unspoken reflection, caution and a deliberate pace can be resources. Avoid equating difficulty deciding with lack of competence or assumed motives. 041 Persistent pressure can provoke anger and even extreme violence, according to Childs. Patience coexists with stubbornness; benefit may permit concession. Apathy and few complaints may allow exploitation. The quiet exterior conceals complex character. Native short ending occupies columns 1–2; column 3 empty. Prose agrees after line-wrap normalization. No missing chapter ending. Describe the handling argument against coercion and badgering. Do not justify violence by a temperament label; preserve the author’s own tension between predictability and hidden complexity. 042 Chapter 6, melancholic: Earth/gravity and mineral bones/teeth are used to explain heavy bearing and tall, thin appearance. Childs proposes many bodily recognition criteria. He distinguishes inward mental preoccupation and unstable moods from phlegmatic bodily comfort and stability. Native opening table: Motto “Life is real, life is earnest.” / Theme Tune Yesterday . OCR flattens the table and merges “in a.” Chapter title and recognition heading complete. No illustration. Attribute the body-to-character inference and the stability/introversion categories. They are model claims, not a physical examination or mental-health diagnosis. 043 Childs says worry is no greater in quantity than others’ but sensitivity is keener. He characterizes self-pity and attention-seeking as an inner counterpart to choleric domination, links oversized ego to inferiority, and says cheering or “snap out of it” attempts fail. Native “misunderstood” is italic, while OCR treats it as ordinary prose. Prose is complete. Final “cannot” continues on 044. Give the actual argument about inward domination without adopting its presumption that a person enjoys depression or feigns feeling. Explain why the source seeks a different response from simple reassurance. 044 Proposed tactic: narrate real or fictitious woes with exaggerated pathos, even feigned tears, to call forth sympathy. Requests for help and caring professions should redirect self-concern into compassion. Childs praises maturity through another’s suffering but returns to pessimism and resistance to reason. Three-column prose fully visible; no tears, caregiving or medical illustration. OCR agrees after dehyphenation. The fiction/feigned-tears recommendation is actual source content, not extraction noise. Name the manipulative tactic expressly as Childs’s proposal. The course adapts concern for another into honest, optional assistance rather than fabricated distress or demands. 045 The wish for understanding, sensitivity to insincerity, financial caution and secure fixed beliefs are connected. Attention can make persuasion more acceptable, yet contradiction threatens security. A gendered story begins about a woman claiming illness to avoid an outing. Native heading “Nobody understands me!” in column 1; emphasis on understanding is lost in OCR. Native “on a” is merged as “ona.” No chapter break: the illness sentence continues on 046. Relate rigidity to the author’s proposed need for security. State that the gendered illness interpretation is a historical caricature, not evidence that a real person’s report is false. 046 Childs continues the accusation of rehearsed symptoms and mutual self-sacrifice, asserts suffering benefits everyone, then derives philanthropy from familiarity with distress. Practical mercy can overcome egotism and produce goodwill. Selected quote for lesson 6 is exact in column 2: “They enjoy putting themselves out for others, and will go to endless trouble to give help and support to those in need.” The last sentence continues into column 3, leaving a large empty region below; no text is missing. Preserve the movement from self-absorption to practical compassion and its ascetic premise. Understanding that movement does not authorize dismissing symptoms, inventing woes or making temperament a medical category. All three chosen quotations are short, visually verified statements by Gilbert Childs , at 033/1, 038/2 and 046/2. The body, health, gender, learning and employment generalizations are included as authorial claims for study; the companion’s existing fictional examples are smaller adaptations whose usefulness depends on the specific situation.

title: Understand Your Temperament! — workplace, compatibility and love capture notes
text: Understand Your Temperament! — workplace, compatibility and love capture notes Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Current records / Registros atuais Current source record. Any explicitly dated historical sections remain historical, as the note explains. Registro atual de fontes. As seções históricas explicitamente datadas mantêm esse caráter, conforme explicado na nota. Page-by-page notes · English · 30 September 2026 · 2678 words Contents of this note / Conteúdo desta nota Understand Your Temperament! — workplace, compatibility and love capture notes Understand Your Temperament! — workplace, compatibility and love capture notes Reviewed 30 September 2026. All 31 assigned captures, 47–77 , were viewed individually at their native 1216 × 546 resolution, and all corresponding Markdown pages were read in full. References are PDF capture numbers, not printed book folios. Three-column prose normally reads left → middle → right. The supplied PDF has 97 captures , SHA-256 9a07e6670bc0de850de829493fd97a2999ec7c8cabb0758a7efc9ecd1a0a7ac9 ; its Markdown has SHA-256 c30a70d8d2a005a3c868b8a0e77a2ebc32293a2b66a1fc866587356bb2cbaf3c . The source and images remain private under [private working file] . These captures supply Childs’s complete Chapter 7 (47–52), Chapter 8 (53–68), and Chapter 9 (69–77) . The short final captures 52 and 77 and the two-column ending at 68 are readable chapter endings, followed by new chapter headings in 53 and 69 and Appendix I, Hints for Dedicated People-Watchers , at 78. The Appendix I boundary was additionally viewed. These are not missing-body gaps. The old 239-capture references should be replaced for these chapters. The ten compatibility sketches are Childs’s prose, with his explicit deliberately skewed verbal caricature qualification at 53–54. The existing bilingual ten-pair visual questions are original course teaching and should be retained as such. Childs’s job matching, graphology, spiritual physiology, reincarnation argument, caricatured relationship predictions and responses involving violence remain attributed source proposals, rather than assessment rules or advice adopted by this review. PDF capture Material and attribution Main reading point Native-image / Markdown decision and boundary 47 Childs, Chapter 7 heading; mutual dependence; aptitude; temperament and occupational fit; “The leopard and its spots.” He opposes workplace status games, presents temperamental prediction as a measure of understanding, and says aptitude and its application matter in matching work. Three columns. Chapter heading is readable. “I have” repairs OCR “Ihave.” The final paragraph continues into 48 after “counter-”; join the capture-spanning word “counter-productive.” The chosen aptitude excerpt is in column 2 near the bottom. 48 Childs: permanence of temperament, maturation of behaviour, integration of secondary and remaining tendencies; younger/older choleric employer. He distinguishes changing a temperament from modifying and refining its behaviour. Self-discipline and practice can call up secondary, and eventually other, qualities for the situation. All three columns readable. Join ordinary wraps only; the source’s blood-pressure claim remains attributed. The last word “resource-” continues as “fulness” in 49. No prose gap at this boundary. 49 Childs: maturity and age; “Jobs for the – right – boys (and girls)?”; introvert/extrovert occupational sorting; graphology; “Getting down to cases.” He recommends temperament-sensitive selection, endorses useful handwriting indications, but acknowledges changing personal circumstances and growth in a role. Three columns. The image visibly says “variations in temperamental suitability are there are,” so the awkward “are” is printed, not an OCR repair to make silently. The hands-on-experience sentence continues into 50. Health and aging claims are source rhetoric, not verified forecasts. 50 Childs: guided hands-on experience; choleric leadership and correction; phlegmatic reliability, regularity, direct invitations and unspoken suggestions. The chapter supplies practical experience alongside typological role recommendations; it also asks supervisors to inquire rather than expect suggestions to be volunteered. Three columns, normal continuation. The quoted reply reads “Well, nobody asked me.” Choleric overreach and phlegmatic occupational descriptions are Childs’s assertions. The final list of relatively independent professions continues into 51. 51 Childs: phlegmatic professions; sanguine sociability and pace, weak routine/completion, schedules; melancholic caring work, empathy, continuity and security. He pairs characteristic aptitudes with limitations and supervisory supports, then assigns the melancholic a preference for established work and secure employment. Three columns. The phlegmatic list continues directly from 50. OCR “ina” is “in a.” The last sentence ends mid-thought after “appeals to” and continues in 52. No missing material is indicated. 52 Childs: Chapter 7’s final pension/life-insurance joke. Completes the melancholic security portrait and ends the workplace chapter. A short paragraph occupies the upper left; the rest is blank. The final sentence ends “approach to life!” Chapter 8 begins on 53. A clipped parenthesis at the far left is a capture artifact, not another source section. 53 Childs, Chapter 8 heading; “Mixed in due proportion”; all four temperaments; hypothetical pure-type extremes; association and complementary qualities; caricature introduction. He gives relationship predictions a mixed-constitution background and explicitly begins to qualify the coming descriptions as verbal caricatures. Three columns. The hypothetical illness/extreme language belongs to Childs. The final word “carica-” continues as “tures” in 54. This cross-capture continuation is essential to the author’s qualification. 54 Childs: deliberately skewed sketches, unexpected responses, secondary tendencies and individual factors; choleric/choleric — an explosive mixture . Personality, health, upbringing and education qualify approximation. The first pair combines rivalry and forceful will with common outlook, cooperation and exchange of leadership responsibilities. Three columns. The exact approximate-combinations excerpt is in column 1. “themslves” is visibly printed near the right-column bottom; do not silently claim it is only OCR. The first-pair argument continues in 55. 55 Childs: choleric/choleric cooperation, collapse and sympathetic response, aggression and exclusion; choleric/sanguine — hot air . He proposes cooling rather than intensifying an eruption, recalling one’s own distress, and contrasts choleric planning with sanguine impatience and lost interest. Three columns. The first pair ends in the upper right before the second heading. Distinguish the source’s treatment of aggressive or violent situations from the course’s ordinary agreement questions. Second-pair prose continues into 56. 56 Childs: choleric/sanguine creativity plus execution, shared pace, consolidation and later-life limits; choleric/phlegmatic — fire and water . He moves from shared outward initiative to opposites that can either generate energy together or cool excessive heat through method and caution. Three columns. The third heading is in column 3. The final “com-” continues as “plement” in 57. The author’s retirement and inner-resource predictions remain attributed, not relationship success scores. 57 Childs: choleric/phlegmatic tolerances, goodwill and divided tasks; choleric/melancholic — irresistible force meets immovable object . He contrasts active enterprise with patient routine, then caricatures forceful assertion versus strategic manipulation and mutual ego claims. Three columns. The fourth heading’s first word is partly clipped at the left edge of column 3; its pair is established by the Markdown and continuous prose. The paragraph explicitly calls the coming scenario “somewhat exaggerated.” It continues into 58. 58 Childs: extended gendered choleric/melancholic domestic caricature; sanguine/sanguine — What’s new, Pussycat? heading. Competing narratives of devotion and sacrifice escalate effort and grievance; the partner imagines greater professional success resolving the other’s difficulties. Three columns. Retain that this is an exaggerated author scenario, including the migraine/depression assertions; it is not a clinical explanation. The next heading sits at the right-column bottom, with its body beginning in 59. 59 Childs: sanguine/sanguine butterflies, competing timing and ideas, volatility, secondary tendencies, maturation of social gifts. Similar lively temperaments may magnify changeability and rivalry, yet Childs expects maturity to add composure and consideration. Three columns. The first paragraph is the body for the heading in 58. The sentence ending “near and” continues normally with “dear” in 60. Join wraps without smoothing away his strong predictive wording. 60 Childs: sanguine/sanguine inward-resource problem and secondary support; sanguine/phlegmatic — bubbles . He describes sanguine instability as the stable feature, then contrasts outward fantasy with steady material grounding in the next pair. Three columns. The image confirms the paradoxical wording that both are stable “in their basic structure” because sanguine instability is constant; do not silently recast his stability terminology. Sixth-pair prose continues in 61. 61 Childs: sanguine/phlegmatic selectivity, forbearance, finances, shopping, reversed gender scenario and friction. The caricature credits balance but warns about phlegmatic stubbornness and sanguine excess; patience may involve choosing what to notice. Three columns. OCR “anew” is “a new” and “toa” is “to a.” Gendered household and finance roles are the author’s chosen scenario. The final conditional continues into 62. 62 Childs: sixth pair’s secondary-temperament warning; sanguine/melancholic — chalk and cheese ; concert/book, locked-bedroom and reconciliation scenario. Opposite flexibility and reserve can balance, but conflicting attention and security demands become prolonged negotiation or rupture in his sketch. Three columns. The seventh heading is in column 1. The source’s printed “nuptual” is not normalized to “nuptial” in an exact transcription. The second partner’s reaction continues into 63. 63 Childs: sanguine/melancholic nerves, change versus security, time and secondary tendencies; phlegmatic/phlegmatic — Tweedledum and Tweedledee: a rare pair . He contrasts escape into events with preservation of home security, then presents doubled phlegmatic steadiness as both stability and inertia. Three columns. The image repairs the OCR-damaged humorous formula to inertia / inertia = inertia . This is caricatured analogy, not a valid physical/mathematical inference. The formula’s explanation continues to column 3. Eighth-pair prose continues in 64. 64 Childs: phlegmatic/phlegmatic minimal communication, reinforcement of passivity, secondary rhythm, stubbornness, comfort and visitors. Their supplementary temperament supplies movement; quiet endurance does not mean either partner is a pushover. Three columns. Source spelling “moreso” is visible. The telepathy remark is Childs’s speculative joke, not an established mechanism. The final visitor/chocolate-biscuit sentence continues into 65. 65 Childs: eighth pair’s routine boundary; phlegmatic/melancholic — “There’s a hole in my bucket” . He caricatures passivity against demanding pessimism, hidden self-interest and attempts at control; secondary temperaments are acknowledged but primary tendencies remain forceful. Three columns. OCR’s vertical bar in “so I intend” is a printed capital I. The author calls this the “starkest sort of scenario” yet also characteristic. Its resentment narrative continues into 66. 66 Childs: phlegmatic/melancholic resentment, cornering, possible violence and melancholic self-torment; melancholic/melancholic — blue moons heading. The ninth sketch reaches melodramatic violence while claiming feasibility; the other partner’s insecurity deepens without recognizing his own provocation. Three columns. The source explicitly labels the scenario “somewhat melodramatic.” Do not adopt its causal generalizations about crimes, depression or temperament. The tenth heading appears at column 3 bottom; its body starts in 67. 67 Childs: melancholic/melancholic sensitivity, expected reciprocity, selective care, pride and demands for solicitude; extremes and secondary mitigation. Compassion for outsiders can coexist with neglect of intimates in his caricature, and disappointed claims for recognition intensify the pair’s inward difficulties. Three columns. “compatibilty” and “fragmentedly” are source wording visible in the image. He expressly calls the possibilities extremes and acknowledges mitigation by secondary temperaments. The final “remem-” continues in 68. 68 Childs: tenth pair’s security, self-torment and suffering with/for/by each other; later wisdom and betterment. Ends the compatibility chapter by predicting that tribulations may produce nobler character and benefit others. Two occupied columns; the right is blank. The sentence is complete at the end of column 2, ending “world.” Chapter 9 begins on 69. This ending is supplied, not a missing remainder. 69 Childs, Chapter 9 heading; dealt cards, heredity and individuality; critique of scientific/material/mechanical reduction; soul/spirit heading. He asks how the temperamental cards were acquired, treats heredity as partial, and argues for considering soul and spirit. His sibling argument is not itself a scientific refutation of genetic contributions. Three columns. “In a” repairs OCR “In acertain.” The soul/spirit subsection begins near the right-column bottom and continues into 70. Claims about science and medicine are Childs’s characterization, not neutral contemporary findings. 70 Childs: inner/outer worlds, historical spirit/matter account, immortal spirit versus mortal body, soul as interaction, genetic/social account and prenatal temperament. His model makes soul the relation of spirit “from above” and matter “from below,” while acknowledging that readers may reject it. Three columns. The text visibly says “an certain lack” near the final column’s bottom, so that grammar is printed. The lack-of-choice problem continues into 71. Historical generalizations remain attributed to Childs. 71 Childs: chance/choice; “Is the notion of reincarnation so very weird?” ; eternal spirit, deathlessness, birthlessness and unbornness. He argues that an eternal spiritual entity must have existed before birth as well as after death, and describes the logic as compelling. This depends on his stated premises, not on survival alone. Three columns. Italics emphasize the pre/post-existence vocabulary. The final consequence continues in 72 as “the concept of re-incarnation.” No interruption or gap is visible. 72 Childs: repeated embodiments, karma, choosing parents; quotation attributed to Steiner’s The Four Temperaments ; Our fourfold nature ; spirit/body/soul interaction. Temperament mediates earlier individuality and heredity in the cited account. Childs differentiates the threefold body/soul/spirit discussion from the fourfold constitution. Three columns. The image supplies superscript note 1 after “temperament” in the Steiner quotation; the MD drops it. The quotation spans column 2 only and is embedded in Childs’s argument. Its credit must remain distinct from Childs’s own sentences. 73 Childs: bodily/spiritual temperament grouping; element/principle/temperament chart; physical and etheric descriptions. Chart 1 groups phlegmatic/melancholic as introverted/passive and sanguine/choleric as extroverted/active. Chart 2 maps Fire–Ego–Choleric; Air– Astral –Sanguine; Water– Etheric –Phlegmatic; Earth–Physical–Melancholic. Two real source charts occupy columns 1 and 2; visually reconstruct their rows because OCR scrambles order. Small black expansion glyphs below the charts are capture-interface artifacts. Physical weight and etheric regeneration descriptions are attributed spiritual physiology. Etheric prose continues in 74. 74 Childs: etheric life, growth, reproduction and death; plant illustration; gland/fluid account; astral feeling, nervous system and animal consciousness; sanguine intensity. He distinguishes physical substances, formative life and sentient experience, attaching predominance claims to phlegmatic and sanguine tendencies. Three columns. Read the astral paragraph across middle → right. These claims about organismal life, plant consciousness and glands are Childs’s exposition of spiritual physiology, not diagnostic observations. The final “Variable as” continues in 75. 75 Childs: I/self-consciousness, memory and development; fire/blood/choleric; Of course you love your neighbour ; understanding, forgiveness, restraint and timed response. Self-knowledge is connected with self-control and tolerating habits, but he says this does not mean accepting manipulation or injury. Three columns. The I paragraph spans column 1; the practical subsection begins at column 2 bottom. His example of imparting “life-wisdom” ends “a punch on the nose” and continues in 76; preserve that source wording in discussion without making it course guidance. 76 Childs: shoulder-to-cry-on continuation; all four temperaments and auction example; common constitution, self-knowledge, world family and non-possessive Christian love; actions and needs. The conclusion derives appropriate regard from a shared human constitution and learning to step into another’s situation. Deeds reveal motives more than words, feelings or thoughts. Three columns. The repeated “physical” in the common-stuff list is visibly printed. The exact deeds excerpt is in column 3 at the bottom. The final argument continues in 77; source face-line interpretation remains Childs’s claim rather than a course assessment. 77 Childs: final Chapter 9 paragraph on action as expression of the inner self and love across race, colour, creed and temperament. Completes the chapter’s ethical conclusion rather than adding a new spiritual demonstration. A short upper-left paragraph ends “or temperament.”; the rest is blank, apart from a clipped far-left parenthesis artifact. Appendix I, Hints for Dedicated People-Watchers, begins at 78. No final love paragraph is missing. The private companion draft for IDs 7–9 supplies bilingual source explanations, exactly three source-comprehension checks per lesson, four-section guides, and three short native-image-verified passages. Integration should preserve the existing original examples/explanations and ten original compatibility questions, while replacing their obsolete missing-capture statements. A concrete course action can be assessed separately from the validity of Childs’s spiritual, genetic, vocational or predictive claims. The additionally viewed Appendix I opening at 78 permits modifying and even changing temperaments if the ego is strong enough, whereas 48 rejects changing a temperament while allowing refinement of behaviour. Read these two formulations as an internal tension; the Chapter 7 guide preserves a concise cross-reference rather than silently harmonizing them.

title: Colour — audit before the PDF revision
