Return to the text: use the currently assigned Chapter 3 passage and the existing Basis markers 20–23; distinguish retrospective inquiry from an assertion that one was unconscious while reasoning. Transfer / Aplicação: “A meeting starts at 9:00. The journey takes 30 minutes and you want to arrive 10 minutes early. Explain your departure time. What changes if the journey takes 40 minutes?” / “Uma reunião começa às 9h. O trajeto leva 30 minutos e você quer chegar 10 minutos antes. Explique o horário de saída. O que muda se o trajeto levar 40 minutos?” Check: 8:20 changes to 8:10 because the travel-time premise changes. Ask the learner to explain the dependency. The task does not establish a claim about the brain or certify ethical freedom. Pilot B: Colour 02 — notice before being told EN opening: “Compare two yellow studies: one has a dense centre and pale edge; the other a pale centre and dense edge. Where does your attention go? Describe a difference, or say that none is clear.” PT-BR opening: “Compare dois estudos amarelos: um tem centro intenso e borda clara; o outro, centro claro e borda intensa. Para onde vai sua atenção? Descreva uma diferença ou diga que nenhuma ficou clara.” Show the arrangements without emotional labels. Offer a text description and a paint, pencil or imagined-composition alternative. A simple reversal control changes the distribution while keeping hue, size and ground constant. Hint / Dica: “What stayed the same? What changed?” / “O que permaneceu igual? O que mudou?” After the response, reveal Steiner's proposed yellow tendency from Lecture 2 and return to its assigned reading. Ask how the learner's description relates to it. Then compare the blue arrangement. Screen appearance is not pigment mixing, and a different reported impression remains a valid observation. Feedback: “Both are yellow” correctly names hue but does not yet compare distribution. “The first draws my attention to the middle” identifies a specific relationship. “I notice no difference in movement” is acceptable; invite a description of density and position, not an invented feeling. EN closing: “Keep the first version and a revision. Explain one artistic decision and one thing this comparison cannot establish.” PT-BR closing: “Guarde a primeira versão e uma revisão. Explique uma decisão artística e algo que esta comparação não permite estabelecer.” Pilot C: Encountering the Self 03 — let another voice change the answer EN opening: “A child used someone else's materials without asking. What would you say first?” PT-BR opening: “Uma criança usou materiais de outra pessoa sem pedir. O que você diria primeiro?” Offer three authored responses and an open alternative: a global accusation, a neutral description followed by a question, or immediate repair without hearing the account. Explain the tradeoffs; do not assign virtue scores to the learner. Reveal a possible next line: “I thought the box was for everyone.” / “Achei que a caixa fosse para todos.” This is one invented continuation, not a prediction of a child's response. Prompt / Pergunta: “What does that change? What still needs repair?” / “O que isso muda? O que ainda precisa ser reparado?” Model response: “I understand why the box looked shared. These materials belong to someone else. Let's ask what needs replacing, and then make the labels clearer.” / “Entendo por que a caixa pareceu ser de todos. Estes materiais pertencem a outra pessoa. Vamos perguntar o que precisa ser reposto e depois deixar as etiquetas mais claras.” Feedback: The new information changes the explanation of intention; it does not erase the effect. A good response makes room for an adult's contribution to the confusion and an appropriate repair. Return to the assigned Dear Parents section: identify the relationship between adult self-examination, listening and guidance. Transfer to a different case where the boundary was clear and ask which part of the response must change. How to judge whether the revision helps Begin with the three pilots above. Compare the existing and revised versions with a small formative learner review; this can find confusing wording but cannot establish general effectiveness. Look at the first response, the revision and a later transfer response rather than enjoyment or completion alone. Use four observable criteria: accurate meaning, a stated connection or reason, relevant source support, and an appropriate response to changed information. Keep the existing acceptance of reasoned disagreement. For art, assess the explanation of a decision rather than emotional conformity; for personal reflection, assess the structure of inquiry rather than private beliefs. Before wider rollout, verify keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels and feedback announcements, mobile layout, optional storage and export, English/Portuguese equivalence, correct source attribution, and a usable complete lesson when JavaScript is unavailable. Each new interactive element must support a stated learning objective. Decorative animation is not evidence of a better teaching method. Implementation sequence Prototype the three different activity forms in GA 4 Lesson 04, Colour Lesson 02 and Koepke Lesson 03. Revise Theosophy 01 and its quick-start introduction so new learners immediately encounter the method. Introduce source maps for Luke and misconception feedback in the philosophy lessons. Extend case-based interactions through Higher Worlds and the two temperament courses. Roll out the per-lesson changes in the appendix, preserving a distinct teaching form for each course. Build cumulative portfolios from existing opening cases instead of creating unrelated homework. The proposed result is a course that asks the learner to look, think, make and revise, with enough guidance to continue independently. The measure is the explanation the learner can now produce, not the number of features on the page.

title: The Four Temperaments: source review and teaching map
text: The Four Temperaments: source review and teaching map Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Current records / Registros atuais Current source record. Any explicitly dated historical sections remain historical, as the note explains. Registro atual de fontes. As seções históricas explicitamente datadas mantêm esse caráter, conforme explicado na nota. Use the latest revision banner and section headings; do not promote old source gaps, draft lesson numbers or past implementation counts as current. Source and course review · English · 30 September 2026; 12 September 2026 · 1084 words The Four Temperaments: source review and teaching map Update: complete supplied edition, 30 September 2026 The newly supplied 23-capture PDF and Markdown contain the complete lecture (captures 6–13), Notes (14), Further Reading (15) and Publisher's Note (16). All pages have been reviewed. The earlier 31-capture ranges and gap statements below are retained as historical records and are superseded for current teaching. All eleven bilingual book lessons and the relevant combined-course lessons now use the complete supplied edition. See the completed revision, corrected reading map and validation . Reviewed 12 September 2026. Request: repeat the preceding bilingual course-development workflow with the supplied book and make relevant existing-course improvements. Source and capture limits The supplied The Four Temperaments.md has 31 numbered capture pages. Its imprint identifies Rudolf Steiner Press 2012, B. Kelly’s translation first published in 1987, revised by Matthew Barton with translation copyright 2008. It contains one lecture , not a chapter collection: Berlin, 4 March 1909, GA 57. Course sections are explicitly identified as original teaching divisions. The supplied lecture text was read throughout, including education and self-education. Capture pages 15 and 18 are blank within continuing text; page 13 loses part of the sanguine mapping, page 14 has damaged wording, and page 21 loses the end of a historical extreme-outcome description. Page 28 is blank after the surviving closing text. The publisher’s note on page 29 is interrupted by a blank page 30. The contents list Notes and Further Reading without usable corresponding captured sections. Page 31 is advertising and was excluded. Source instructions, advertising and publisher text were treated as document contents, not as user commands. Two primary parallel resources were checked: The Four Temperaments, Brian Kelly, 1987 : complete parallel English lecture, including the inward-contentment passage, bodily descriptions, and final social aim of responsive human love. This is the public reading link. It is not presented as the identical Barton revision. GA 57 German/English comparison, 4 March 1909 : confirms the date, the four-member mapping (§7), descriptive sequence (§§9–14), and qualification about mixtures (§16). Its wording is distinct from the supplied revision. Only brief paraphrases of missing material are used. The original source is not copied into the public site; its fingerprint is recorded in the source register. Assignments use capture page numbers plus an explicit parallel-edition note where gaps matter. No missing wording is silently invented or attributed to the supplied capture. Course structure Lesson Topic Capture reading Teaching purpose 0 Meet the person before the type 6–7; 19–20 Explain one-lecture structure, individuality and limits of labels. 1 Two streams and their meeting 7–12 Temperament as intermediary between heredity and proposed reincarnating individuality; analogy is not proof. 2 Four members, four tendencies 12–14 + parallel Correct mapping; all four members belong to the person; predominance is relational. 3 Choleric 14; 16–17; 22–23 Purpose, resistance and competence; original construction example. 4 Sanguine 14–15; 21–22 + parallel Readily awakened, changing interest; original bounded attention activity. 5 Phlegmatic 15; 24–25 + parallel Inward contentment and engagement through companions’ interests. 6 Melancholic 15–16; 23–24 + parallel Burden, sensitivity and compassion; acknowledge personal feeling. 7 Mixtures and appearance 16–21 + parallel Pure types do not occur; examine generalizations and counterexamples. 8 Education 21–25 Compare four proposed routes; start with a capacity already present. 9 Self-education 25–27 Reason arranges situations indirectly; small reviewable practice. 10 Synthesis 6–27 + parallel closing Fictional case, source concept, counterexample and revisable response. Each language has eleven lessons with examples, source explanations, glossary, activity, three explained checks, rubric and relevant cross-course link. Lessons 2 and 8 have a semantic comparison table; orientation and synthesis use a three-step observation-to-response sequence. No personality scoring, physical-feature portraits or diagnostic quiz is added. Editorial judgments Retain Steiner’s spiritual explanation and distinguish it from the practical example. Do not quietly redefine etheric , astral or I-bearing members as modern psychological measurements. Teach the four correspondences accurately: I-bearer/choleric, astral /sanguine, etheric /phlegmatic, physical/melancholic. No pairing signifies greater human worth or sole possession of a member. Explain the source’s biological comparisons as parts of its argument, without treating differences between relatives as proof of a previous life. Do not re-teach its embryological recapitulation or historical-science anecdotes as established contemporary biology/history. Acknowledge physiological and physiognomic claims explicitly. Body size, eye colour and gait do not become classification tools in this course. Historical psychiatric language is not reproduced as an illness prediction, intelligence ranking or contemporary diagnostic framework. The source’s child-guidance claims are proposals, not demonstrated universal outcomes. Affection, companionship, understanding and capable guidance are not restricted to assigned types. Label adaptations clearly: achievable challenges instead of engineered conflict; predictable activities instead of withdrawal of affection; voluntary ordinary acts of care instead of manufactured distress; manageable practice instead of anger provocation or prolonged boredom. The distinction between source and adaptation is visible in student text. The final case remains fictional and revisable. Students may understand the book without claiming to diagnose someone or accepting every spiritual proposition. Existing-course improvements Theosophy Lesson 6: compare the purpose of this fourfold map with the several classifications in GA 9. Explain predominance rather than separate human kinds. Higher Worlds Lesson 7: add a concrete application of patient attention through an existing capacity and a response that can be revised. Philosophy of Freedom Lesson 20: compare mixed temperaments with individuality beyond generic descriptions. The later lecture does not supply a necessary spiritual-physiological premise for GA 4’s argument. All three supplements are bilingual. Existing Luke and Colour supplements remain intact. Other courses are linked where relevant without adding repetitive source blocks throughout the site. Files and checks Edit content/temperaments.mjs for lessons and connections, content/temperaments-visuals.mjs for the reading maps, and scripts/build-temperaments.mjs for rendering. Scoped table styles are in docs/temperaments.css . The builder runs after Colour and adds one card per homepage and one block per target lesson. The site now comprises six bilingual courses and 212 HTML pages. Validation covers links, anchors, headings, language partners, reading assignments, lesson sections, eleven ordered lessons, comparison tables and nonduplicated supplements. A repeat build is checked for identical generated output. Current additions remain local, following the established prepare-then-publish workflow.

title: Theosophy: chapter-by-chapter teaching plan (1971 edition)
text: Theosophy: chapter-by-chapter teaching plan (1971 edition) Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Historical archive / Arquivo histórico This record is part of the historical archive. Its counts, draft routes and pending tasks describe the date of the note; use the current library and course pages for present coverage. Este registro pertence ao arquivo histórico. Suas contagens, rotas propostas e tarefas pendentes descrevem a data da nota; consulte a biblioteca e os cursos atuais para conhecer o alcance presente. Historical 1971 Monges/Church edition record. Its 23-lesson mapping and printed-page references describe the September revision. The published course now has 28 readings based on the supplied Shields translation (1910). Editorial plan · English · 11 September 2026; 30 September 2026; 2 October 2026 · 6950 words Contents of this note / Conteúdo desta nota Theosophy: chapter-by-chapter teaching plan 1. Source and scope 2. Course design decision 3. Prefaces and introduction: how to approach the book Key takeaways 4. Chapter I — The Essential Nature of Man A. Opening: the threefold relationship to the world — pp. 1–6 B. Corporeal, soul, and spiritual nature — pp. 6–11 C. Body, Soul and Spirit — pp. 11–39 Chapter I lesson plan and checks 5. Chapter II — Re-embodiment of the Spirit and Destiny Key takeaways Teaching method Lessons and checks 6. Chapter III — The Three Worlds III.1 — The Soul World, pp. 70–86 III.2 — The Soul in the Soul World after Death, pp. 87–101 III.3 — The Spiritland, pp. 101–110 III.4 — The Spirit in Spiritland after Death, pp. 110–127 III.5 — The Physical World and Its Connection with the Soul and Spiritland, pp. 127–140 III.6 — Thought Forms and the Human Aura, pp. 140–153 Chapter III lesson divisions 7. Chapter IV — The Path of Knowledge Key takeaways Lessons and checks 8. Integrate every addendum into the reading 9. Make understanding visible Repeatable lesson pattern Assessment rubric Useful misconception questions and feedback Lesson 22 — Final synthesis / Síntese final 10. First lesson: a concrete starting draft plan 11. English–Portuguese terminology decisions 12. Decisions before publishing lessons Theosophy: chapter-by-chapter teaching plan Historical teaching plan — 1971 Monges/Church edition. Prepared 11 September 2026; revised 30 September 2026 from the supplied 228-page PDF and its page-marked Markdown. This plan records the earlier 23-lesson course. The published course is available here: Theosophy in English · Teosofia em português . It now has 28 readings based on the supplied Elizabeth Douglas Shields translation (1910). See the current course review for its chapter sequence. This historical plan's printed-page references and thirteen addenda belong to the 1971 edition; they do not identify the primary source assignments in the current lessons. The new course revision review records the implemented changes. Page-level source notes cover frontmatter and all addenda , Chapter I , Chapter II , Chapter III , and Chapter IV . Together they account for every PDF page, including covers and blank versos. 1. Source and scope Book: Rudolf Steiner, Theosophy: An Introduction to the Supersensible Knowledge of the World and the Destination of Man , Anthroposophic Press, New York, 1971; GA 9. The copyright page identifies Henry B. Monges as translator and Gilbert Church as reviser . The isolated name on the scanned title page is not the translation credit. Source read: the user's 1971 PDF and matching Markdown, page by page, including the prefaces, introduction, all four chapters, all thirteen addenda, and nonsubstantive front/backmatter. Extracted PDF text and the matching Markdown were compared. Selected quotations, damaged passages, bibliographic details and uncertain blank pages were additionally checked against rendered PDF images. This does not claim that the complete OCR transcription has been corrected. The full source is retained outside the public course and identified by filename and SHA-256 in source-register.json . The file contains 228 scan-page markers. It is OCR text, not a visually verified transcription. Page references below are to the printed book , not the Markdown line numbers. In the main text, scan page = printed page + 28. For example, printed pp. 1–5 are scan pages 29–33. Sections sometimes start midway through a page, so lesson ranges intentionally overlap at boundaries. Book section Printed pages Scan pages Prefaces to early editions vii–xi 9–13 Preface to revised English edition xiii–xv 15–17 Introduction xvii–xxiii 19–25 I. The Essential Nature of Man 1–39 29–67 II. Re-embodiment of the Spirit and Destiny 40–69 68–97 III. The Three Worlds 70–153 98–181 IV. The Path of Knowledge 154–178 182–206 Addenda 1–13 181–195 209–223 Text-quality limitations and recovery: OCR still contains damaged headings, page numbers and bleed-through noise. The new PDF images settle the earlier gaps on printed pp. 36–37 (PDF 64–65) and the opening of Chapter IV on p. 154 (PDF 182). These passages are now taught from this 1971 edition rather than through a different translation. The edition comparison retains the historical recovery record and explains the current verification status. English lesson quotations use the supplied edition, with whitespace and line-end hyphenation normalized; Portuguese quotations are new, labelled study translations. 2. Course design decision Keep the agreed starting point: Theosophy itself supplies the sequence . Use the book's own prefaces and introduction for Lesson 0, then begin Chapter I with the opening encounter with flowers. The general site guide and later-book connections remain supplementary. Expand outward only as the book introduces its concepts. Recommended structure: 21 book lessons, plus Lesson 0 and a final synthesis (Lesson 22) . These are implemented teaching units, not a compulsory timetable. Aim for 30–45 minutes per session; split the longer readings into two sessions if beginners cannot explain the central distinction after the first. Each page range is a unit envelope, not a demand to read the whole range aloud at once. The course must preserve three things together: Fidelity: explain what Steiner actually claims, including that he regards spiritual worlds as real. Do not quietly convert the entire book into metaphor or generic mindfulness. Clarity: distinguish descriptions of ordinary experience, philosophical arguments, analogies, and reports of supersensible perception. Understanding the text is not independent confirmation of its claims. Learner independence: reward accurate explanation, careful questions, and reasoned disagreement. Neither belief nor reports of spiritual experiences are learning requirements. Teach terminology progressively. Do not present all the threefold, fourfold, sevenfold, and ninefold classifications in Lesson 1. Do not equate body/soul/spirit with thinking/feeling/willing as a simple one-to-one correspondence. 3. Prefaces and introduction: how to approach the book Role in the argument: Steiner explains what kind of knowledge he claims, why he thinks it matters for practical life, and how he expects the reader to participate. This is the reading contract behind the entire work. Key takeaways Slow, active reading matters: the prefaces ask readers to work through ideas rather than merely accumulate statements. Steiner distinguishes discovering supersensible realities from understanding another person's account of them. In his view, the latter can precede direct perception. Ordinary language is stretched to describe experiences he says are unlike physical objects. The revised-edition preface stresses mobile rather than rigid conceptions. He regards spiritual knowledge as a contribution to practical life, not an escape from it. His claims about the adequacy of his method are part of the book's position. A learner can reconstruct them without having to accept his criticisms of skeptics. Teaching use: add a brief source-reading segment to Lesson 0. Ask students to mark a claim, an analogy, and a question in a short assigned paragraph. Revisit the longer methodological material with Chapter IV rather than making it a long preliminary hurdle. Check: How does Steiner distinguish understanding a report from having the reported experience? Expected answer: he says readers can thoughtfully understand a spiritual investigator's account before acquiring the capacities for firsthand perception. Understanding the account and independently verifying it are different achievements. Likely misunderstanding: “If I question the text, I am unfit to study it.” Correct this explicitly. The course permits questioning and does not use the text's rhetoric about disbelief to dismiss students. 4. Chapter I — The Essential Nature of Man Central question: What distinctions does Steiner think are needed to understand a human being? Chapter outcome: the learner can explain the progression from ordinary experience to Steiner's more elaborate account of human constitution, and identify where new spiritual premises enter it. A. Opening: the threefold relationship to the world — pp. 1–6 Key takeaways The flower example separates the encountered object, the individual's pleasure and memory, and the knowledge sought about the object's enduring relations. Body initially names our bodily relationship to the environment; soul names individual inward experience; spirit names the relationship to truth and intelligible order beyond private liking. These are introductory definitions. Later descriptions extend them, and should not be imported prematurely into this opening. The same encounter can involve all three aspects. They are not three separate people or three sealed containers. Teach with: a flower, leaf, or familiar object; three columns for perception, personal response, and an explanation that could be examined by another person. A question about growth is a starting point for inquiry, not already knowledge of a growth law. Misunderstanding to prevent: “Anything I think is spirit, therefore whatever I think is true.” Steiner distinguishes a claim to truth from personal preference; the learner still needs reasons. B. Corporeal, soul, and spiritual nature — pp. 6–11 Key takeaways Steiner considers human embodiment alongside mineral, plant, and animal existence, then emphasizes the specifically human relation to thought. Sensory organs and the inward experience of a sensation are distinguished. Soul includes sensation, feeling, and willing; it does not mean emotion alone. Thinking can examine perceptions and guide actions. In this account it is not merely an instrument for satisfying desire. Teach with: a fictional encounter with a bell: vibration and hearing, the listener's response, and inquiry into the sound or a decision about how to respond. State which distinctions come from the text. Misunderstanding to prevent: “A description of private experience proves that the brain has no role.” The chapter itself discusses the brain as an instrument. The further philosophical conclusion requires its own examination. Editorial issue: the Carus quotation on p. 7 uses demeaning disability terminology, and pp. 7 and 11 make claims about brain organization. Explain their historical place in the argument; do not turn them into judgments about human worth or present them as a current biology lesson. Any contemporary scientific comparison requires separate sourcing. C. Body, Soul and Spirit — pp. 11–39 This subsection is much longer than the first three and needs four lessons. 1. Life and sensation, pp. 11–20 Physical constitution, formative life, and inward sensation are differentiated. Etheric / life body is Steiner's term for a proposed supersensible formative organization. It is not the physicist's ether, a chemical substance, or simply a synonym for metabolism. Read the long note on pp. 14–15 with Addendum 1: Steiner distinguishes his formative organization from an older vital-force explanation that changes inorganic laws. Soul body / sentient body and sentient soul are related but introduced as distinct. They should not be collapsed before their relationship is explained. 2. Differentiations of soul, pp. 20–26 Sentient soul concerns sensation, desire, and impulse. Intellectual or mind soul brings thinking into the soul's life, including thinking in the service of desires. Consciousness soul concerns the soul's relation to truth and goodness beyond personal preference. It does not mean ordinary wakefulness or consciousness in every everyday sense. The distinctions describe interacting aspects, not labels for sorting classmates into superior and inferior kinds of people. 3. The I and spiritual development, pp. 26–35 The I unifies experience and is described as acting through body and soul while receiving spiritual content. Self-reference, self-awareness, and selfishness are different concepts. The I is not simply egotism. Consciousness soul and spirit self are distinguished: openness to truth versus its individual appropriation in the I, in the chapter's account. Intuition has a technical meaning tied to spiritual content, not a casual hunch. Addendum 6 qualifies its use here. Spirit self, life spirit, and spirit man introduce a further spiritual differentiation. Explain their role before asking learners to recall names. 4. Bringing the classifications together, pp. 35–39 Steiner gives different groupings of the same human constitution, combining closely related members for particular purposes. The ninefold account distinguishes physical body , life body , soul body, sentient soul, intellectual soul, consciousness soul, spirit self, life spirit, and spirit man. Its order and A–I labels are corroborated by the comparison edition; this is not a verified quotation of the 1971 scan. The text then combines soul body with sentient soul and consciousness soul with spirit self. The complete intermediate list checked against the 1971 PDF is: physical body ; ether or life body ; sentient-soul-body; intellectual soul; spirit-filled consciousness soul; life spirit; spirit man. Use the 1971 source reference and distinguish this regrouping from the subsequent sevenfold transformation list. The simplified account uses physical body , life body , astral body , and I; pp. 38–39 relate spiritual transformation to astral , life, and physical constitution. These are intended by Steiner as real distinctions perceived spiritually, not merely a convenient arbitrary taxonomy. Our diagram is a teaching model of his account, not evidence for it. Teach with: a progressive concept map whose nodes are added across lessons. Use connecting arrows, not an anatomical cross-section pretending to locate invisible organs. Chapter I lesson plan and checks Lesson Reading Task Check and expected response 1. Encountering the world / Nosso encontro com o mundo pp. 1–5; stop before subsection 1 on p. 6 Sort perception, response, and reasoned explanation using the flower example Can two people respond differently to the same flower? Yes: personal responses differ; claims about its characteristics need reasons beyond either person's liking. 2. Embodiment and inner experience / Corpo e experiência interior pp. 6–11, ending before subsection 4 Annotate a bell or music example Is soul just emotion? No: the section includes sensation and willing as well as feeling. 3. Life, sensation, and formative organization / Vida, sensação e organização formativa pp. 11–20; Addenda 1–2 Separate observed growth from Steiner's proposed explanation Does observing growth alone demonstrate the etheric body ? No: growth is the observation; the supersensible formative organization is the further claim. 4. Three aspects of soul / Três aspectos da alma pp. 20–26; Addendum 4 Compare wanting, planning to obtain, and examining a principle Why is consciousness soul not just being awake? Steiner uses it for a particular relation to truth and goodness, not all awareness. 5. The I and spiritual individuality / O Eu e a individualidade espiritual pp. 26–35; Addenda 5–6 Explain I, consciousness soul, and spirit self without using them as synonyms Does saying the word I establish the moment self-awareness begins? No: Addendum 5 distinguishes word use from the associated idea. 6. One human being, several classifications / Um ser humano, diferentes classificações pp. 35–39; Addendum 3; PDF images 64–67 Build and explain a grouping diagram, identifying which members are combined Why do the counts change? Related aspects are grouped differently; the text describes an interpenetrating whole, not unrelated competing sets. Chapter checkpoint: explain a new everyday encounter through the introductory threefold distinction, then identify which later claims cannot be established by that encounter alone. Revisit Lessons 1–3 if the learner treats sensory examples as proof of all later members. 5. Chapter II — Re-embodiment of the Spirit and Destiny Central question: What persists through experience, and why does Steiner extend his account beyond a single lifetime? Chapter outcome: the learner can reconstruct the argument for repeated lives and karma, distinguish them, and explain the limits identified in Addendum 7. Key takeaways Memory and action connect different times. Memory brings a past experience into present life; an action changes the world and creates continuing consequences (pp. 40–44). Remembering is not described as retrieving an unchanged picture. Steiner describes a new present visualization arising through the effects of an earlier encounter (pp. 44–46). Remembered episodes and acquired capacities differ. We can retain an ability without recalling each episode through which it developed. The reading-and-writing example anchors this distinction (pp. 46–47). The argument then changes scope. Steiner extends from learning during one life to claims about dispositions carried from earlier lives. His appeal to individuality, biography, and heredity supplies the bridge (pp. 47–60). Make the added premises visible rather than treating this as a direct observation. Re-embodiment and karma do different work. Re-embodiment concerns the recurring spiritual individuality; karma concerns the connections of deeds and destiny. His closing arrangement relates body to heredity, soul to destiny, and spirit to repeated lives (pp. 60–69). Read the qualification alongside the argument. Addendum 7, especially p. 188, calls the reasoning a preparatory exercise giving a silhouette rather than a proof. The assertive language of the chapter and this qualification should both be taught, not smoothed into one another. Teaching method Draw a two-part map. First: an ordinary experience, later recollection, acquired skill, and an action's continuing effect. Second: the additional claims required to extend this pattern across death and rebirth. Use a fictional biography so no learner has to expose private history. Important distinction: an analogy may help a reader imagine the claim without establishing that the two processes share the same cause. The sleep/death analogy illustrates continuity; sleep is not an experiment demonstrating reincarnation. Lessons and checks Lesson Reading Task Check and expected response 7. Memory, learning, and lasting effects / Memória, aprendizagem e efeitos duradouros pp. 40–47 Compare remembering one practice session with retaining a skill Can the skill remain when the episode is forgotten? Yes; the book distinguishes the fruits of experience from its remembered images. 8. Individuality and repeated lives / Individualidade e vidas sucessivas pp. 47–60; Addendum 7 Map premises, analogies, and conclusion Does unique biography by itself demonstrate a previous life? No; explain Steiner's additional argument and the addendum's qualification. 9. Action and destiny / Ação e destino pp. 60–69; revisit Addendum 7 Trace consequences in a fictional story, then mark the cross-life extension How do karma and re-embodiment differ? One concerns the connection of deeds and destiny; the other the spiritual individuality's repeated earthly lives. Likely misunderstandings: karma as a simple reward scoreboard; reincarnation as unchanged personality returning; ability as proof of a particular past life; destiny as a reason to do nothing now. Teaching boundary: the book makes strong claims about self-created destiny. Accurately explain those claims without attributing a real person's illness, abuse, poverty, or other suffering to supposed past deeds. No task asks students to infer anyone's past lives or deserved fate. Historical remarks about heredity and animals must not be passed off as a current genetics or animal-cognition curriculum. Chapter checkpoint: a learner should be able to say both “Here is why Steiner argues this” and “Here is what the assigned argument does and does not establish.” 6. Chapter III — The Three Worlds Central question: How does Steiner describe the physical, soul, and spiritual worlds and their relationship to human life? Chapter outcome: the learner can explain the role of each world, trace the proposed after-death sequence, and interpret descriptive imagery without confusing it with physical geography. This is the largest chapter. Its six subsections deserve separate attention. Students need a conceptual map before any detailed list of regions. III.1 — The Soul World, pp. 70–86 Key takeaways The worlds interpenetrate: they are not planets or locations outside the physical universe (especially p. 74). Spiritual organs, substances, space, and motion are described with words borrowed from physical experience. The text expressly qualifies that borrowing. Sympathy and antipathy are technical relational forces: attraction/union and repulsion/separation, not simply kindness and cruelty. The seven regions differentiate patterns of these forces. Grasp the changing relationships before memorizing their names. Reference map: regions 1–3 concern differing proportions of attraction and separation; region 4 concerns the soul's inward liking/disliking; regions 5–7 describe more outward, enlivening activity. In the terminology of this edition: Region Name Main reading distinction 1 Burning Desire Attraction is constrained by predominant repulsion and self-seeking. 2 Mobile Sensitivity The two forces balance; impressions are received with relative neutrality. 3 Wishes Attraction predominates but still draws things into its own sphere. 4 Liking and Disliking Sympathy acts within the formation; inner feeling comes to the foreground. 5 Soul Light Receptivity to other beings becomes more outward and less self-enclosed. 6 Active Soul Force The account develops the outward enlivening activity further. 7 Soul Life Completes the description of the higher regions' enlivening participation. Do not invent detailed independent mechanisms for regions 6 and 7: their initial treatment is brief. The next subsection shows their role in the purification narrative. Activity: compare attraction that wants to possess with interest in something for its own sake. Label the comparison as an analogy to the text, not a spiritual observation. Check: Are these seven regions stacked above one another? No; pp. 85–86 explicitly describe interpenetration. III.2 — The Soul in the Soul World after Death, pp. 87–101 Key takeaways The soul is the intermediary between body and spirit. Its attachments can remain, in this account, when bodily means of gratification are no longer available. Purification describes the release of attachments to the completed bodily life so that the spirit can enter its own sphere. The narrative follows affinities with the regions; it is not a uniform timetable assigning everyone the same experience or duration. Read the distinction on p. 91: attachments tied to the just-completed incarnation are treated differently from connections addressed by karma through a later incarnation. Distinguish dissolution of bodily attachments from loss of the fruits that the spirit takes onward. Activity: annotate a diagram of the proposed sequence: embodied life → release from body → release of bodily attachments → spiritual assimilation → renewed embodiment. Every stage beyond physical death is labelled as Steiner's account. Check: What is supposed to disappear, and what is supposed to continue? Bodily-life attachments are relinquished; assimilable fruits of experience can remain with the spirit. This is more precise than saying “the whole person disappears” or “nothing changes.” Sensitive source passage: p. 97 makes a specific claim about the postmortem suffering of people who die by suicide. Do not repeat it as a verified outcome, a threat, or a judgment on a deceased person. If included, discuss it explicitly as a claim in the historical text; do not build a quiz or role-play asking students to assign such suffering to anyone. The course is textual study, not bereavement advice. III.3 — The Spiritland, pp. 101–110 Key takeaways Archetypes are described as living creative beings, not merely abstract categories or static blueprints invented by humans. The book distinguishes ordinary thought from the fuller spiritual reality it says thought reflects. Continents, flowing life, atmosphere, colours, and music describe claimed spiritual experiences through comparisons. The claims are intended as real, even though the descriptions are not literal physical geography or acoustics. Regions 1–3 concern archetypes of physical forms, life, and soul formations; region 4 their broader coordination; regions 5–7 the sources of creative impulses and purposes. Addendum 9 distinguishes creative mobility from restless agitation. Addendum 10 warns against importing narrowly human meanings into spiritual purposes. Activity: mark in a paragraph what is being compared and what the comparison helps explain. Then state what would go wrong if taken physically. Check: Is the archetype simply a mental sketch in a human artist's head? No. The artist is an analogy; Steiner proposes a creative reality not produced by that human mind. III.4 — The Spirit in Spiritland after Death, pp. 110–127 Key takeaways Earthly life supplies experience and a field of action; the interval between lives is described as transforming its fruits into capacities and intentions. The architect illustration connects doing, learning, and preparing future activity. It is an explanatory analogy. The lower regions' descriptions connect family and friendship, reverence and wider belonging, and service to others with future capacities. The fourth region brings human cultural creativity into focus; the higher regions concern the enduring self and purposes. The book explicitly allows a subsequent life to be less perfect than an earlier one (pp. 113–114). Avoid promising a simple upward staircase from life to life. Ordinary acts can matter; spiritual significance is not equated with fame (p. 123). Addendum 12 clarifies the claimed difference between earthly wishes and a pre-birth will-like orientation toward difficult experience. This is a substantial metaphysical claim, not permission to explain another person's suffering. Activity: build a two-column map, “earthly experiences” and “capacities the text says may be developed from them.” Use impersonal examples of friendship, learning, and service. Check: Does the book say that each successive life must be visibly more successful? No; it qualifies the general developmental picture and does not identify spiritual value with public success. III.5 — The Physical World and Its Connection with the Soul and Spiritland, pp. 127–140 Key takeaways This section reconnects the previous descriptions with ordinary earthly existence: in Steiner's view, humans participate in the three worlds simultaneously. The ice/water comparison describes sensible things as a manifestation of soul-spiritual reality. Do not turn it into a physical phase-change claim about spirits. Mineral form, living formation, sentience, and human thought organize his account of the kingdoms. The three elementary kingdoms refer to proposed formative activity; they are not three additional ordinary biological categories. The later discussion extends the account to national/folk spirits, the spirit of an age, and elemental beings. These are spiritual beings in his account, not just poetic nicknames for observable social trends. The same passage insists that descriptions of elemental beings should not be treated as bodily creatures visible to ordinary senses. Activity: follow one example—plant growth—through the observation, Steiner's proposed formative account, and the analogy used to express it. For the social passage, distinguish an observed shared custom from a claim about its spiritual agency. Check: Does a shared custom establish a national spirit? No. The observable pattern and Steiner's proposed explanation are different levels of claim. Do not use this section to assign a fixed character or spiritual rank to individuals by nationality or ethnicity. III.6 — Thought Forms and the Human Aura, pp. 140–153 Key takeaways Steiner describes thoughts and feelings as having spiritually perceptible manifestations or effects. Read pp. 143–144 before discussing the colour descriptions: these are not ordinary colours appearing to physical sight. The three interpenetrating auras express bodily influence, soul life, and spiritual activity. They are not three separate coloured shells. Their meaning depends on context; the text does not support reducing the chapter to a simple personality colour chart. The closing paragraph rejects a questionable practice of reading character from hallucinatory auras. Addendum 13 explains why Steiner does not accept ordinary experimental demands as governing such perception. Teach this as a methodological position, not as experimental corroboration or a way to dismiss all questions. Activity: analyse the language of two descriptions. Students may draw a labelled conceptual illustration, but must not diagnose, classify, or claim to read a classmate's aura. Check: Would seeing an outline of colour around a person establish the experience described here? No; the text expressly distinguishes its account from ordinary visual colour and hallucinatory character reading. Chapter III lesson divisions Lesson Title, English / Portuguese Reading and focus 10 The soul world / O mundo anímico pp. 70–86; first teach interpenetration and relational forces, then the region map. Split into two sessions if needed. 11 Attachment and release / Apego e desprendimento pp. 87–101, stopping before subsection 3; the proposed postmortem purification and its difference from karma. 12 Archetypes and spiritland / Arquétipos e mundo espiritual pp. 101–110, stopping before subsection 4; Addenda 9–11 as relevant. Addendum 8 is primarily read with Lesson 18. 13 Experience becoming capacity / Da experiência à capacidade pp. 110–121; the architect, relationships, and service. 14 Individuality, purpose, and return / Individualidade, propósito e retorno pp. 121–127, stopping before subsection 5; Addendum 12 and limits of a simple progress narrative. 15 Nature and the three worlds / A natureza e os três mundos pp. 127–137; physical manifestation, kingdoms, and formative activity. 16 Collective and elemental beings / Seres coletivos e elementais pp. 137–140, stopping before subsection 6; distinguish observed phenomena, proposed beings, and descriptive imagery. 17 Thought forms and the aura / Formas-pensamento e aura pp. 140–153; Addendum 13. Focus on meaning and method rather than memorizing colours. Chapter checkpoint: reconstruct the proposed sequence across death and rebirth, distinguishing the function of soul-world purification from spiritland assimilation. Correct a diagram that incorrectly places the three worlds on separate planets. Explain why analogy does not mean either literal physical description or arbitrary fiction. 7. Chapter IV — The Path of Knowledge Central question: What changes in thinking, feeling, and conduct does Steiner say make spiritual knowledge possible? Chapter outcome: the learner can explain the proposed path and distinguish attentive study from credulity, emotional numbness, fantasy, or withdrawal from everyday responsibility. Key takeaways Thinking is the starting point (pp. 154–159). The account does not present sensation-seeking or vague images as a substitute for disciplined thought. Receptivity is not the abandonment of judgment (pp. 159–161 and footnotes). Hear or observe before applying a habitual verdict; then examine carefully. Feelings are to be transformed in their role, not erased (pp. 162–165). The aim described is finer responsiveness, less automatic personal reaction. Thought should have continuity and reasons (pp. 165–168). Mathematics is offered as a possible discipline, not a requirement for every learner. Conduct and motive matter (pp. 168–171). The proposed path includes ethical action rather than intellectual accumulation alone. Ordinary life remains important (pp. 172–178). The end of the chapter rejects making a temporary research disposition into permanent withdrawal from living. Freedom is distinguished from arbitrary self-will (pp. 174–175), and spiritual union is distinguished from erasure of individuality (p. 177). The promises of spiritual perception and beneficial effects remain the author's claims. Course completion does not certify spiritual attainment or guarantee experiences. Lessons and checks Lesson Reading Task Check and expected response 18. Thoughtful receptivity / Receptividade e pensamento pp. 154–161 Explain a short passage fairly before evaluating it Is open-mindedness blind belief? No; the footnotes distinguish receiving an impression from substituting premature judgment, without requiring blind faith. 19. Feeling without automatic reaction / Sentir sem reagir automaticamente pp. 161–165 Examine a fictional mild disagreement: feeling, interpretation, possible response Does equanimity mean feeling nothing? No; Steiner describes transformed and finer feeling rather than numbness. 20. Coherent thinking and responsible action / Pensamento coerente e ação responsável pp. 165–171 Write a short chain of reasons and identify where a preference interrupts it; consider one ordinary act of responsibility Is mathematics mandatory? No; the text allows other routes to disciplined thinking. 21. Freedom, individuality, and everyday life / Liberdade, individualidade e vida cotidiana pp. 171–178 Compare self-will, action from principle, and loss of individuality Does the conclusion demand withdrawal from ordinary life? No; the final qualification says the special research attitude is not a general demand over all life. Practical adaptation: use brief, optional observation, attentive listening, and reflective writing. Label these as classroom adaptations; they are not a complete initiation method. A student may choose a fictional example instead of personal disclosure. Do not score spiritual experiences, prescribe strenuous practices, or interpret distress as evidence of advancement. Chapter checkpoint: write a realistic study routine and explain its relation to the assigned chapter. Include how questions will be examined and how ordinary responsibilities will remain intact. Assessment concerns the explanation, not private religious practice. 8. Integrate every addendum into the reading Do not leave all the qualifications until students have already learned oversimplified versions. Addendum Printed pages Attach to Teaching use 1 181–182 Lesson 3 Formative life and the limitations Steiner places on the language of vital force; read with pp. 14–15. 2 182 Lesson 3 General responsiveness versus differentiated senses; qualify the main-text wording. 3 183–184 Lesson 6 His rationale for differentiating an integrated being; analogy does not itself verify the classification. 4 184–185 Lessons 4 and 15 His animal group-ego account; avoid the inaccurate simplification that animals contain no thought at all. 5 185 Lesson 5 The idea of I versus merely learning the word. 6 185–186 Lesson 5 Technical intuition and its introductory use here. 7 186–188 Lessons 8–9 The explicit limit of the reincarnation/destiny argument as preparation rather than proof. 8 188 Lesson 18; optional reference in Lesson 12 More detailed practices are referred to other books; this course is not an exhaustive training manual. 9 188–189 Lesson 12 Spiritual mobility can include rest; avoid imagining endless agitation. 10 189 Lessons 12 and 14 Purpose language is qualified, not a simple projection of ordinary human planning. 11 189 Lesson 12 A reference to further treatment of the Spiritual Word, not extra detail supplied in this book. 12 189–190 Lesson 14 Distinguish the text's proposed pre-birth perspective from present-life wishes; no diagnosis of other people's destiny. 13 190–195 Lesson 17 Aura language, claimed conditions of perception, and experimental testability; distinguish the spiritual aura from Benedikt's physical observations discussed in the note. 9. Make understanding visible No course can guarantee understanding by presenting material alone. Build opportunities to explain, receive feedback, correct, and return to earlier concepts. Repeatable lesson pattern Retrieve: ask one question about the previous lesson before showing the answer. Read: assign a short passage within the unit's page range, with no more than a few new technical terms at a time. Explain: read the open close-reading explanation and chapter teaching, then ask for a two-sentence paraphrase grounded in the passage. Distinguish: use one example and one misleading example. Examine the argument: identify an observation, inference, analogy, or supersensible claim. Apply: transfer the distinction to a fresh example. Exit check: one explained answer and one unresolved question; provide a precise passage to reread if needed. This is our proposed teaching method, not a verbatim instruction from Steiner. Assessment rubric Score each dimension 0–2 for feedback, not for measuring spiritual development. Dimension 0 1 2 Accurate meaning Major confusion Partly accurate Accurate explanation in the student's own words Distinctions Collapses key terms Distinguishes with prompts Distinguishes independently and identifies an exception or boundary Source use No support or wrong passage Relevant but vague support Correct passage and clear explanation of its relevance Claim awareness and transfer Treats every statement as the same kind of evidence Notices a distinction Identifies the kind of claim and applies it to a new example Suggested readiness rule: at least 6/8, with no zero for accurate meaning or key distinctions. This threshold is a course-design proposal, not a validated test. Offer rereading and another example rather than locking a learner out. Multiple-choice recognition alone is insufficient; include one short explanation at every checkpoint. Useful misconception questions and feedback “The soul means feelings and nothing else.” Return to pp. 8–9: sensation and willing are also part of the discussion. “If I forget the lesson, I cannot retain anything from it.” Return to p. 47: distinguish episodic recall from an acquired capacity. “A convincing analogy proves reincarnation.” Return to Addendum 7: identify its preparatory rather than demonstrative role. “Seven regions means seven physical places.” Return to p. 86 and p. 119: interpenetration and changes of capacity matter. “Aura colour is a visible personality test.” Return to pp. 143–144 and 153, and Addendum 13. “To study correctly I must stop questioning.” Return to the footnotes on pp. 160–161 and distinguish attentive reception from blind faith. “Spiritual development erases individuality.” Return to p. 177: the conclusion explicitly distinguishes union from annihilation. Lesson 22 — Final synthesis / Síntese final Ask students for a concept map and a short written or spoken explanation answering four questions: What does Chapter I distinguish within the human being? How does Chapter II connect experience, individuality, and destiny? What different roles do the worlds and postmortem processes play in Chapter III? Why does Chapter IV return to thought, feeling, conduct, and ordinary life? Require one example of an analogy with its limits, one addendum that changes or qualifies a first reading, and one question the learner still considers unresolved. A well-supported disagreement can receive full marks. 10. First lesson: a concrete starting draft plan Reading: printed pp. 1–5 (scan pages 29–33). The opening closes just before subsection 1 on printed p. 6. The short transition at the top of p. 6 can be included when preparing the final reading extract. English working title: Encountering the world: body, soul, and spirit. Portuguese working title: Nosso encontro com o mundo: corpo, alma e espírito. By the end, a learner should be able to: distinguish an observed feature, a personal response, and a reasoned claim about the object; explain the three introductory terms through Steiner's flower example; say why the observation does not establish all later claims in the book. 30-minute session: 0–3: recall Lesson 0 and introduce the source and the question of how we encounter the world. 3–7: observe a flower or leaf, or use a described object if visual observation is not accessible. Record features separately from feelings and interpretations. 7–15: guided reading of selected parts of pp. 1–5, including the returning-to-the-meadow example and the definitions on p. 4. Allow rereading rather than covering every sentence at speed. 15–22: compare two people's responses and introduce the three terms with a simple relationship map. 22–27: apply the distinction to a different object or sound. Ask for a reason that another person could examine, not just a personal judgment. 27–30: exit questions and feedback. Exit questions with answer guidance: Is “this flower makes me happy” the same kind of statement as “this flower has five petals”? No: one reports personal response; the other an observed feature, subject to checking. Is asking why the plant grows already knowledge of its growth? No: it is a question; developing and examining an explanation is the next step. In this passage, why is spirit not just another word for emotion? Steiner uses it for the relation to truth or intelligible order beyond private feeling. Does noticing these distinctions demonstrate a separate spiritual world? No. The activity helps interpret the starting distinction; later claims need their own study. Take-home task: bring three notes about a new encounter and one question about the reading. No spiritual experience is expected. 11. English–Portuguese terminology decisions These are provisional teaching equivalents, not quotations from an identified Portuguese translation. Check them against the Portuguese edition chosen for the course and preserve edition-specific alternatives in the glossary. English in this edition Proposed Portuguese Teaching caution Body / soul / spirit Corpo / alma / espírito Introductory meanings expand as the book proceeds. Physical body Corpo físico Do not confuse with all meanings of body in the text. Ether or life body Corpo etérico ou vital Not physical ether or a measurable fluid. Soul body / sentient body Corpo anímico / corpo de sensações Verify the chosen translation; distinguish from sentient soul. Sentient soul Alma da sensação Not just a bodily receptor. Intellectual / mind soul Alma do intelecto / alma do entendimento Confirm the edition's preferred term. Consciousness soul Alma da consciência Not a synonym for being awake. I / ego Eu Not automatically egoísmo. Spirit self Si-mesmo espiritual Keep distinct from Eu; verify translation. Life spirit Espírito vital Do not confuse with corpo vital . Spirit man Homem-espírito Explain the historical terminology as referring to the human being. Re-embodiment Reencarnação / novas encarnações Spiritual continuity, not an unchanged everyday personality. Destiny / karma Destino / carma Explain the author's usage, not only the everyday sense of fate. Soul world / spiritland Mundo anímico / mundo espiritual Not physically separated territories. Sympathy / antipathy Simpatia / antipatia Relational forces in the technical account, not just friendliness/dislike. Intuition Intuição Technical use; not any spontaneous guess. Archetype Arquétipo A proposed creative being here, not just an abstract template. Supersensible Suprassensível Beyond ordinary sensory perception, not unusually sensitive eyesight. Keep concept IDs and source ranges the same across both languages. Translate questions for equivalent meaning, not merely matching words. Never grade English proficiency as evidence of conceptual understanding. 12. Decisions before publishing lessons Use the now-verified 1971 PDF for the classification content. All 23 selected English lesson excerpts have been checked against PDF images; retain printed and PDF locators and label Portuguese study translations. Choose the Portuguese source edition or clearly identify our Portuguese text as original explanation of this English edition. Start by fully drafting and reviewing Lesson 1, then test it with beginner explanations before fixing a release timetable for all 21 units. Keep the full supplied book outside docs/ . This plan uses summaries and reading references; it does not authorize republishing the 1971 translation. Preserve challenging passages in the editorial reading record while making context and attribution explicit in lessons. Do not silently sanitize the author's claims or adopt them as judgments about students. Current status: source read and chapter teaching plan prepared. The website still contains the original orientation; no new lesson has been published by this task.

title: Theosophy: historical course revision against the supplied 1971 book
text: Theosophy: historical course revision against the supplied 1971 book Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Historical archive / Arquivo histórico This record is part of the historical archive. Its counts, draft routes and pending tasks describe the date of the note; use the current library and course pages for present coverage. Este registro pertence ao arquivo histórico. Suas contagens, rotas propostas e tarefas pendentes descrevem a data da nota; consulte a biblioteca e os cursos atuais para conhecer o alcance presente. Historical 1971 Monges/Church edition record. Its 23-lesson mapping and printed-page references describe the September revision. The published course now has 28 readings based on the supplied Shields translation (1910). Source and course review · English · 30 September 2026; 2 October 2026 · 1035 words Theosophy: course revision against the supplied 1971 book Historical course revision — 1971 Monges/Church edition. This record describes the revision completed 30 September 2026, when the course had 23 lessons: orientation, 21 book lessons, and final synthesis, with matching English and Brazilian Portuguese pages. The published English course and Portuguese course now contain 28 readings based on the supplied Elizabeth Douglas Shields translation (1910). The current course review explains that sequence and its source references. The 1971 source analysis below remains available for comparison; its page numbers and lesson mapping describe the earlier revision. Source and reading record Rudolf Steiner, Theosophy: An Introduction to the Supersensible Knowledge of the World and the Destination of Man , GA 9, Anthroposophic Press, 1971. The copyright page credits Henry B. Monges as translator and Gilbert Church as reviser. The name George E. Maycock on the title page is an ownership stamp. All 228 PDF pages are accounted for in five reading ledgers. Each substantive page has original notes identifying the essential concept, its place in the argument and the lesson that teaches it. Covers, blank pages and backmatter are recorded separately from teaching content. PDF extraction and the corresponding Markdown blocks were read and compared; selected quotations, damaged passages, bibliographic details and uncertain blank pages were additionally checked in rendered PDF images. This is not a claim that the complete OCR was corrected. Source section Printed pages PDF pages Teaching route and notes Prefaces and Introduction, with frontmatter vii–xv, xvii–xxiii 1–28 Lesson 0; frontmatter notes I. The Essential Nature of Man 1–39 29–67 Lessons 1–6; Chapter I notes II. Re-embodiment of the Spirit and Destiny 40–69 68–97 Lessons 7–9; Chapter II notes III. The Three Worlds 70–153 98–181 Lessons 10–17; Chapter III notes IV. The Path of Knowledge 154–178 182–206 Lessons 18–21; Chapter IV notes Thirteen addenda, with endmatter 181–195 207–228 Revisited in the relevant lessons; addendum notes and mapping The PDF and Markdown are identified by filename, size and SHA-256 in source-register.json . Full books and extracted page text remain private under the ignored [private working files] directory. Only selected attributed excerpts and original teaching material are published in docs/ . What changed Orientation: Lesson 0 now teaches this book's own purpose and reading method: active work with individual passages, flowing rather than rigid conceptions, and the distinction between discovering spiritual facts, understanding an account and independently verifying it. Its opening excerpt comes from the preface on printed p. viii / PDF p. 10. The later lecture connections remain labelled supplements. Chapter I: The flower example now develops perception, personal response, memory and knowledge in sequence. The lessons explain physical, life and soul bodies; three aspects of soul; the I and its relation to spiritual content; and spirit self, life spirit and spirit man. The ninefold, regrouped sevenfold, fourfold and transformation-based classifications are distinguished. PDF images resolve the previous OCR gaps on pp. 36–37; another translation is no longer needed to supply that teaching. Chapter II: The course explains memory as a new present representation, the difference between remembered episodes and acquired capacities, the author's spiritual-biography argument, inherited tendencies versus individuality, and the inner and outer effects of deeds. Re-embodiment and karma have separate roles. The strong conclusions are read with the qualifications on pp. 60 and 65 and Addendum 7, rather than treating an ordinary learning example as proof of a previous life. Chapter III: The lessons follow the forces and seven regions of the soul world, the soul's purification, the creative regions of Spiritland, assimilation between lives, return to embodiment, and the relationship of these worlds to earthly nature and collective beings. They explain thought forms and aura language in the author's intended mode of perception. Region names follow the supplied translation; the explanatory analogies are distinguished from physical geography and from evidence. Chapter IV and synthesis: The course teaches living thought, the role of a researcher and the learner's judgment, receptivity, education of feeling, coherent thought and will, patience, spiritual perception and practical participation in life. The final lesson connects the four chapters through cited passages, an addendum, an analogy and a remaining question. Supplementary material no longer replaces the book-based exercises in Lessons 18 and 21. Passage and lesson design Every lesson has its own passage assignment, printed and PDF page locator, edition credit, English source wording, Portuguese study translation, and original close-reading explanation. Concise existing excerpts were retained where their wording and location were verified; their explanations now connect the actual words to the expanded chapter teaching. Lesson 0 has a separate preface passage instead of reusing Lesson 1's excerpt. The learner reads the passage and open explanation before answering or applying it. Activities and suggested answers now check the author's distinctions and argument, alongside source use and thoughtful questions. The course accurately attributes spiritual claims to Steiner; understanding them is assessed without requiring belief or reports of spiritual experience. Existing lesson URLs, bilingual partners, notes, export controls and supplementary course links are retained. Build corrections preserve that teaching when the site is regenerated: course-count substitutions now affect course labels rather than altering “ninefold” in a lesson objective, and repeated builds retain one passage stylesheet link per page. Validation Rebuild with node scripts/build-all.mjs , then run node scripts/check-theosophy.mjs and all existing scripts/check-*.mjs validators. The Theosophy check covers all 228 reading records, the four-chapter route, all thirteen addenda, 23 individual source passages, 46 bilingual lesson pages and preservation of the main book's exercises. The site-wide checks cover links, anchors, guided study, passage order and the other courses. Verified on 30 September 2026: the complete build and all ten validators passed, including the 398-page site check. A second build from the generated tree produced byte-identical site files. The refreshed preview passed ten smoke requests, and all 46 Theosophy lesson responses matched the revised files with their source teaching and notebook controls intact. Browser interaction with note saving and export was not manually tested. This revision changes the repository and generated course locally. It does not record a website deployment.

title: Theosophy: recovery of damaged passages
text: Theosophy: recovery of damaged passages Original authored English; any bilingual material is retained as written. Inglês original do autor; os trechos bilíngues permanecem como foram escritos. Current records / Registros atuais Current source record. Any explicitly dated historical sections remain historical, as the note explains. Registro atual de fontes. As seções históricas explicitamente datadas mantêm esse caráter, conforme explicado na nota. Parallel-source record for the 1971 Monges/Church edition. The published course uses the supplied Shields translation (1910); keep these editions and their page references distinct. Edition comparison · English · 11 September 2026; 30 September 2026 · 1052 words Theosophy: recovery of damaged passages Historical comparison checked 11 September 2026; verification update 30 September 2026. Current source decision: the newly supplied 1971 PDF has now been read with its matching Markdown. Images of printed pp. 36–37 (PDF 64–65) and p. 154 (PDF 182) resolve the old OCR gaps. Lesson 6 now teaches the lists directly from the 1971 edition, and Chapter IV begins from its own verified text. The ownership stamp GEORGE E. MAYCOCK on the title page is not a translation credit; the copyright-page image confirms Henry B. Monges and Gilbert Church. See the new course review and per-page notes for current evidence. The following targeted comparison is retained as historical recovery work, not the current source for 1971 quotations. Statements below about unverified images describe the earlier review. It was not a complete collation of the two translations. Sources Main course reference: the user's 1971 Anthroposophic Press Markdown transcription, translated by Henry B. Monges and revised by Gilbert Church. Printed pp. 36–37 correspond to scan pages 64–65. Comparison: a supplied Markdown transcription labelled as a 2023 Passerino edition. Its metadata identifies an EPUB source; its translator's foreword is signed Elizabeth Douglas Shields . The supplied publication details have not been independently verified. The full source is retained separately from the public repository. The comparison text is a different English translation, not a clean transcription of the same 1971 edition. Its late publication label does not establish that it contains later revisions: its foreword describes an early English appearance, and its closing notes are dated Munich, 28 August 1910. Use it to recover parallel meaning, not to silently replace missing 1971 wording. 1. Nine-member list: recovered clearly 1971 printed p. 36 has damaged list markers. The comparison file, chapter-9 (book Chapter 1), lines 276–292, supplies the labels A–I clearly: Label Member, with hyphenation normalized A Physical body B Ether body C Soul body D Sentient soul E Intellectual soul F Consciousness soul G Spirit self H Life spirit I Spirit man This corroborates the order inferred in our plan. The two texts explicitly combine C with D and F with G for the next classification. 2. Seven-member list: missing continuation recovered The 1971 OCR retains items 1–3 on printed p. 36 but loses items 4–7 around the start of p. 37. The parallel list is complete in the comparison file, chapter-9, lines 296–308: Physical body . Ether or life body . Sentient-soul-body. Intellectual soul. Spirit-filled consciousness soul. Life spirit. Spirit man. Names above normalize hyphenation and omit the comparison edition's parenthetical Sanskrit equivalents. Those equivalents are present in this comparison text; they are not assumed to be present in the missing 1971 lines. Teaching consequence: the nine-to-seven change is explained by two combinations , not by discarding two aspects. C + D becomes item 3; F + G becomes item 5; E remains item 4; H and I remain items 6 and 7. This account must also be distinguished from the later sevenfold list that explicitly includes the I and transformed bodies. 3. Damaged explanatory paragraphs on p. 37: meaning recovered The comparison file, chapter-9, lines 310–312, clearly explains the following: The I becomes the bearer of the spiritual human being through receiving spiritual content. The human being participates in physical, soul, and spiritual worlds; the soul mediates between bodily rootedness and spiritual development. The I manifests in the consciousness soul but permeates the whole soul. Soul aspects interpenetrate rather than having the boundaries of bodily limbs. The intellectual and consciousness souls are brought together as the bearer of the I, which is their kernel. A simplified classification therefore names physical body , life body , astral body , and I. In this context, astral body joins soul body and sentient soul. The subsequent paragraph describes transformation through the spirit self. These points clarify the garbled 1971 passage. They are paraphrases of the comparison text, not a claimed restoration of every word on printed p. 37. The surviving 1971 wording also contains explanatory phrasing not identically reproduced in the comparison. 4. Chapter IV opening: meaning recovered The damaged opening at 1971 printed p. 154 / scan page 182 has a readable parallel at chapter-12, line 651 of the comparison file. Its meaning is that the knowledge described in the book can be sought personally, and that thinking and thoughtful engagement with accounts of the higher worlds form a starting point. The comparison uses “Theosophy” where the surviving 1971 sentence uses “spiritual science.” Use a paraphrase unless the precise 1971 sentence is checked against its scan. 5. What this comparison does not settle It does not verify the exact typography, punctuation, or wording of the 1971 scan. It does not restore the 1971 printed contents-page pagination; its own chapter links and embedded note page numbers belong to another edition. Its nine notes do not substitute for the thirteen 1971 addenda. By topic, the comparison notes 1–9 correspond to 1971 Addenda 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, and 11, with wording and length differences. In particular, its closing notes have no separately corresponding entries for 1971 Addenda 3, 7, 12, or 13. Preserve those 1971 discussions of classification, the limits of the reincarnation argument, destiny, and aura methodology in our plan. This is a finding about the closing notes, not a claim that no related material occurs anywhere else in the comparison book. The comparison itself contains a suspicious sentence in its spiritual-nature subsection (line 220) that repeats a soul/body distinction where the parallel 1971 passage distinguishes spirit from soul. It should not be adopted as an error-free replacement merely because it is easier to read. Course decision Keep the 1971 edition as the main reference for page assignments and addenda. Use the comparison as an explicitly identified supporting source. The classification content is now sufficiently corroborated for drafting a paraphrased teaching diagram; direct quotations attributed to the 1971 edition still require checking its page images or a matching reliable transcription. No original source files were modified.
