Source PDF position 100 · English Read the searchable source transcription The Six Essential Exercises Following Steiner, who called them Nebentibungen (“side exercises”), these six exercises are called “subsidiary,” or supplementary, because they should supplement or accompany whatever meditation path or practice we follow. They are essential and should be part of the life of every practitioner because they ensure that the “main,” or central, practice (that they accompany) will be healthy. Steiner refers to them repeatedly, recommending them at all levels of inner work. One version, entitled “General Requirements for Anyone Wishing to Undertake Esoteric Schooling,” was circulated as early as 1906. In other words, Steiner considered them foundational. Though sometimes spoken of in an offhand manner, they are really the keys to inner development. As such, they may also be thought of as “chakra” exercises. ## A series of qualities We must develop a series of qualities. To begin with, we must master our thoughts, particularly our train of thought. This is called control of thoughts. Just consider the way thoughts whirl about in our souls, how they flit like will-o’-the-wisps; one impression arises here, another there, and each changes our thinking. It is not true that we govern our thoughts; our thoughts govern us completely. We must reach the point where, at a given time in the day, we can become so absorbed in a thought that no other thought can enter and disturb our soul. In this way, we hold the reins of thought life for a while. The second quality is to find a similar relationship to our actions, that is, to exercise control over our actions. Here it is necessary, occasionally at least, to act in ways that are not precipitated by anything external. Whatever is initiated by our place in life, our pro- fession, or our situation does not lead more deeply into higher life. Higher life depends on such intimate matters as one’s resolve to do something that springs completely from one’s own initiative—even if it is something absolutely insignificant. No other actions contribute anything to the higher life. Source PDF position 101 · English Read the searchable source transcription The third quality to strive for is equanimity. People fluctuate back and forth between joy and sorrow. One moment they are beside themselves with joy, the next they are unbearably sad. Thus we allow ourselves to be rocked on the waves of life, on joy or sorrow. We must reach equanimity and steadiness. Neither the greatest sorrow nor the greatest joy must disturb one’s composure. One must become steadfast and even-tempered. The fourth soul quality is to understand every being. Nothing expresses more beautifully what it means to understand every being than the legend passed down to us, not by the Gospel, but by a Persian story. Jesus was crossing a field with his disciples, and as they went along, they encountered the decaying corpse of a dog. It looked horrible. Jesus stopped and looked at it with admiration, saying, “What beautiful teeth this animal has!” Within the ugly, Jesus found an element of beauty. Try always to approach what is wonderful in every phenomenon of outer reality. You will see that everything contains an aspect that can be affirmed. Do as Christ did when he admired the beautiful teeth of the dead dog. Practicing this will lead you to a great ability to tolerate anything, and you will gain an understanding of everything and of every being. The fifth quality is complete openness toward everything new that meets us. Most people judge new things according the old things they already know. If someone comes and tells them something new, they immediately respond with an opposite opinion. But we must not confront a new communication immediately with our own opinion. We must instead always remain alert for the possibility of learning something new. We can learn, even from a small child. Even if you were the wisest person, you should be willing to hold back your own judgment and listen to others. We must develop this ability to listen, because it enables us to encounter matters with the greatest possible openness. In esotericism, this is called “faith.” It is the power not to oppose, which weakens the impression made by the new. The sixth quality is something we all receive after we have developed the first five. This is inner harmony. Those who have the other qualities are also inwardly harmonious. Furthermore, it is necessary for those seeking spiritual development to strengthen their feeling for freedom to the greatest degree. A feeling for freedom enables us to look within ourselves for the center of our being and to stand on Source PDF position 102 · English Read the searchable source transcription our own two feet, so that we do not have to ask everyone what we should do. Thus, we can stand upright and act freely. This also is a quality that one needs to acquire. Once we develop these inner qualities, we stand above all the dangers that can arise from the division in human nature. The qualities of our lower nature can no longer affect us. We can no longer stray from the path. These qualities, therefore, must be formed with the greatest precision. Then we enter the esoteric life. —Berlin, December 7, 1905 ## The six exercises from the point of view of rhythm There is a universal cosmic rule we must never forget: rhythm restores power. This is a fundamental esoteric principle. Most people today live their lives completely devoid of any regular rhythm, especially in their thinking and behavior. Those who allow the distractions of the outer world to take hold cannot avoid the dangers to the physical body during esoteric development, because the forces of renewal are withdrawn. Consequently, we must work to introduce a rhythmic element into life. Naturally, we cannot arrange our days so that each day is exactly the same. But we can at least pursue some activities regularly. Indeed, this is necessary for anyone who wants to develop on the esoteric path. For example, we should do certain meditation and concentration exercises at a deliberate time every morning. We can also bring rhythm into our lives if every evening we review the events of the day in reverse order. The more regular- ities we can introduce, so much the better. In this way, life exists in harmony with the laws of the world. Everything in the system of nature is rhythmic—the sun’s course, the seasons, day and night, and so on. Plants, too, grow rhythmically. True, the higher we go in the kingdoms of nature, the less rhythm we find, but even in animals we can observe a certain degree of rhythm—for example, they mate according to regular cycles. Only human beings lead a chaotic life with no rhythm; nature has deserted it. Our task, therefore, is to deliberately infuse some rhythm into this chaotic life. And we have certain means available to us through which we can bring harmony and rhythm into our physical and etheric bodies. Both bodies then gradually develop rhythms that will Source PDF position 103 · English Read the searchable source transcription self-regulate when the astral body withdraws. When they are forced out of their proper rhythm during the day, they will, on their own, regain the right kind of movement while at rest. The means to do this involve the following exercises. These practices must be done in addition to meditation: 1. Thought control. This means that, at least for a short time each day, you stop all sorts of thoughts from drifting through your mind. For a space of time, you allow peace and tranquillity to enter your thinking. You think a definite idea, place it in the center of your thinking, and logically arrange your thoughts so that they are all closely related to the original idea. If you do this even for only a minute, it can be very important for the rhythm of the physical and etheric bodies. 2. Initiative in action. You must perform some action, however trivial, that originates with your own initiative. This is some task you have assigned yourself. Most actions are a response to family circumstances, education, vocation, and so on. Consider how little arises as the result of your own initiative. Consequently, you must spend a little time performing acts derived only from you. They need not be important; very insignificant actions accomplish the same purpose. 3. Detachment, imperturbability. You must learn to regulate your emotions so that you are not up in the sky one moment and down in the dumps the next. Those who refuse to do this for fear of losing their unconventional nature or artistic sensibility can never develop esoterically. Detachment, or imperturbability, means that you master yourself throughout the greatest joys and the deepest grief. Indeed, we become truly receptive to the world’s joys and sorrows only when we do not enter them egotistically. The greatest artists owe their great achievements precisely to this detachment, because, through it, they opened their eyes to the subtle, inwardly significant impressions. 4. Impartiality or freedom from prejudice. This quality sees goodness in everything and looks for the positive element everywhere.... Source PDF position 104 · English Read the searchable source transcription 5. Faith. In the esoteric sense, faith implies something rather different than what it usually means. During esoteric development, you must never allow your assessment of the future to be influenced by the past. In esoteric development you must exclude all that you have experienced thus far, so that you can meet each new experience with new faith. The esotericist must do this quite consciously. For instance, if someone comes to you and says that the church steeple is leaning at a forty-five degree angle, most people would say that this is not possible. Esotericists must always allow for the possibility of belief. They must go so far as to have faith in everything that happens in the world; otherwise, they block their way to new experiences. You must always remain open to new experiences. In this way, your physical and etheric bodies will assume a condition that may be likened to the contented mood of a setting hen. 6. Inner Balance. Inner balance is a natural result of the other five qualities; it is formed gradually from the other five qualities. You must keep these six qualities in mind, grasp life, and progress gradually—like drops of water wearing away a stone in the proverb. —Stuttgart, September 2-5, 1906 ## Qualities needed for attaining higher knowledge There are certain qualities that should acquired through practice by those who want to find the way into the higher world. Before all else, these emphasize the soul’s mastery over its train of thought, its will, and its feelings. The method for bringing about such mastery through practice has two goals. First, the practice is meant to imbue the soul with stability, certainty, and equilibrium to the extent that it retains these qualities even when a second “I” is born out of it. Second, it is meant to give this second “I” strength and support for its journey. What our thinking needs most of all for spiritual training is objectivity. In this regard, life is the great teacher of the “I” in the physical world. If the soul chose to allow its thoughts to wander aimlessly, life would immediately correct. It would not allow our thinking to come into conflict with life. The soul's thinking must correspond to the actual course of life’s realities. When we turn our attention away Source PDF position 105 · English Read the searchable source transcription from the physical world of the senses, we are no longer subject to its automatic correction. Our thinking will go astray if it is not able to self-correct. This is why students of the spirit must train their thinking so that it can set its own direction and goals. Their thinking must teach itself inner stability and the ability to stick strictly to one subject. For this reason, the appropriate “thought exercises” we undertake should not deal with unfamiliar and complicated objects, but with ones that are simple and familiar. Over a matter of months, if we can overcome ourselves to the point of being able to focus our thoughts for at least five minutes a day on some ordinary object (for example, a pin, a pencil, or the like), and if, during this time, we exclude all thoughts unrelated to this object, we will have made a big step in the right direction. (We can consider a new object each day or stay with the same one for several days.) Even those who consider themselves thinkers because of their scientific education should not scorn this means of preparing themselves for spiritual training, because if we fix our thoughts on something very familiar for a certain period of time, we can be certain that we are thinking objectively. If we ask, What is a pencil made of? How are these materials prepared? How are they put together to make pencils? When were pencils invented? and so on, our thoughts correspond to reality much more closely than they do if we think about the origin of human beings or the nature of life. Simple thought exercises are better for developing objective thinking about the Saturn, Sun, and Moon phases of evolution than any complicated scholarly ideas, because what we think about is not the point, at least initially. The point is to think objectively, using our own inner strength. Once we have taught ourselves objectivity by practicing on sense-perceptible physical processes that are easily surveyed, our thinking becomes accustomed to striving for objectivity even when it does not feel constrained by the physical world of the senses and its laws. We break ourselves of the habit of allowing our thoughts to wander without regard for the facts. The soul must become a ruler in the domain of the will just as it is in the world of thoughts. Here again, life itself appears as the controlling element in the physical world of the senses. It makes us need certain things, and our will feels roused to satisfy these needs. For the sake of higher training, we must get used to strictly obeying our own commands. If we do this, we will become less and less inclined to desire nonessentials. Dissatisfaction and instability in our life of will, however, are based on desiring things without having Source PDF position 106 · English Read the searchable source transcription any clear concept of realizing these desires. This dissatisfaction can disrupt our entire mental life when a higher “I” is trying to emerge from the soul. A good exercise is to tell ourselves to do something daily at a specific time, over a number of months: Today, at this particular time, I will do this. We then gradually become able to determine what to do and when to do it in a way that makes it possible to carry out the action in question with great precision. In this way, we rise above damaging thoughts, such as: “I’d like this, I want to do that,” which disregard totally the feasibility of what we want. In Faust, Goethe put these words into the mouth of his seeress, Manto: “I love whomever longs for the impossible.” Goethe himself said, “Living in ideas means treating the impossible as if it were possible.” These statements, however, should not be used as objections to what has been presented here, because what Goethe and his seeress Manto ask can be accomplished only by those who have trained themselves in desiring what is possible in order to then be able to apply their strong will to “impossibilities” in a way that transforms them into possibilities. For the sake of spiritual training, the soul should also acquire a certain degree of composure with regard to the domain of feeling. For this to happen, the soul must master its expressions of joy and sorrow, pleasure and pain. Many prejudices become evident with regard to acquiring this particular quality. We might imagine that we would become dull and unreceptive to the world around us if we could not empathize with rejoicing or pain. However, that is not the point. The soul should rejoice when there is reason to rejoice, and should feel pain when something sad happens. It is only meant to master its expressions of joy and sorrow, of pleasure and displeasure. With this as our goal, we will soon notice that rather than becoming dulled to pleasurable and painful events in our surroundings, the opposite is true. We are becoming more receptive to these things than we were previously. Admittedly, acquiring this character trait requires strict self-observation over a long period of time. We must make sure that we are able to empathize fully with joy and sorrow without losing ourselves and expressing our feelings involuntarily. What we are meant to suppress is not our justified pain, but involuntary weeping; not our abhorrence of a misdeed, but blind rage; not alertness to danger, but fruitless fear; and so on. Exercises like this are the only way for students of the spirit to acquire the mental tranquillity that is needed to prevent the soul from leading a second, unhealthy life, like a shadowy double, alongside the higher “I” when this “I” is born and especially when it begins to Source PDF position 107 · English Read the searchable source transcription be active. Especially with regard to these things, it is important not to succumb to self-deception. It can easily seem to people that they already possess a certain equilibrium in ordinary life and that they therefore do not need this exercise, but in fact it is doubly necessary for people like this. It’s quite possible to be calm and composed in confronting things in ordinary life and yet have our suppressed lack of equilibrium assert itself all the more when we ascend into a higher world. It is essential to realize that for purposes of spiritual training, what we seem to possess already is much less important than systematically practicing what we need to acquire. This sentence is quite correct, regardless of how contradictory it may seem. No matter what life may have taught us, what we teach ourselves is what serves the purposes of spiritual training. If life has taught us excitability we need to break that habit, but if it has taught us complacency we need to shake ourselves up through self-education so that our souls’ reactions correspond to the impressions they receive. People who cannot laugh at anything have as little control over their lives as people who are constantly provoked to uncontrollable laughter. An additional way of training our thinking and feeling is by acquiring a quality we can call “positivity.” ...The erroneous, the bad, and the ugly must not prevent the soul from finding the true, the good, and the beautiful wherever they are present. We must not confuse this positivity with being artificially uncritical or arbitrarily closing our eyes to things that are bad, false, or inferior. It is possible to admire a dead animal's “beautiful teeth” and still see the decaying corpse; the corpse does not prevent us from seeing the beautiful teeth. We cannot consider bad things good and false things true, but we can reach the point where the bad does not prevent us from seeing the good and errors do not keep us from seeing the truth. Our thinking undergoes a certain maturing process in connection with the will when we attempt never to allow anything we have experienced to deprive us of our unbiased receptivity to new experiences. For students of the spirit, the thought, “I’ve never heard of that; I don’t believe it,” should totally lose its meaning. During specific periods of time, we should be intent on using every opportunity to learn something new concerning every thing and every being. If we are ready and willing to take previously unaccustomed points of view, we can learn from every current of air, every leaf, every babbling baby. Admittedly, it is easy to go too far with regard to this ability. At any given stage in life, we should not disregard all our previous experiences. We should indeed judge what we are experiencing in the present on the basis of past experiences. This belongs on one side of the scales; on the other, however, students of the spirit must place Source PDF position 108 · English Read the searchable source transcription their inclination to constantly experience new things and especially their faith in the possibility that new experiences will contradict old ones. We have now listed five soul qualities that students in a genuine spiritual training need to acquire: control of one’s train of thought, control of one’s will impulses, composure in the face of joy and sorrow, positivity in judging the world, and receptivity in one’s attitude toward life. Having spent certain periods of time practicing these qualities consecutively, we will then need to bring them into harmony with each other in our souls. We will need to practice them in pairs, or in combinations of three and one at the same time, and so on, in order to bring about this harmony. —From An Outline of Esoteric Science

Source PDF position 113 · English Open the original source page at full size Read the searchable source transcription Living the Year Spiritually Rhythm and repetition are the heart of spiritual life, as they are of all life. From the tiniest, innermost parts of our bodies through the heavenly bodies of our solar system and galaxy to the very limits of the conceivable universe, we are surrounded everywhere by rhythms. No wonder, then, that for Plato and the ancients the height of wisdom and harmony was to attune the soul to the universal rhythmic nature. Doing so, we order our lives, which is truly the “first step” in inner development. This involves more than order. Since we are cognitive beings, the order and rhythm we come to know become sources of knowledge. By repeating the same meditation, for instance, we learn how it is different every time. The more we keep everything the same, the more the difference appears. And not just difference—for this “difference” teaches us both about the spiritual world (“grace”) and our own contribution in interaction with it. For this reason, Rudolf Steiner gave many exercises and meditations to be done on a daily, weekly, or monthly rhythm. ## Five daily meditations I (morning) In the world’s divinity In the world’s light’s pure rays —February 1912 ## Six-monthly exercise These six basic exercises are recommended as a six-month program. 1. The first requirement is to acquire completely clear thinking. To achieve this goal, you must—if only for a short time everyday, say five minutes, but the more the better—free yourself of the thoughts that flit through your mind like will-o’-the-wisps. You must Source PDF position 118 · English Open the original source page at full size Read the searchable source transcription become the master of your thought world. You are not the master when outer circumstances—job, tradition, social relations, nationality, time of day, certain activities, and so on—determine what you think and how you elaborate it. Therefore, during the time you set aside, of your own free will you must empty your soul of the ordinary daily flow of thoughts and through your own initiative move a single thought to the center of your soul. Do not think that it has to be a particularly striking or interesting thought. It is much better for what you are seeking in esoteric development to begin first with an uninteresting or insignificant thought. You will then more easily arouse the autonomous powers of thinking itself, which is essential. When you start with a “thought” that is already interesting, it carries thinking with it. It is better to do this exercise using a pin as the object of meditation than to try to do it on the life of Napoleon. Starting on your own initiative with such a thought—the pin—associate it with everything that you can find related to it. At the end of your meditation, your thought should be just as colorful and living as it was at the beginning. ... 2. When this exercise has been practiced for about a month, a second may be added. Think of an action that you would certainly not perform in ordinary circumstances; make it your duty to do it every day. It is best to choose an action that will take the longest time to do. Again, it is better to start with an inconsequential action that you must, as it were, compel yourself to perform. For example, buy a plant and water it at the same time each day. After a certain time, another similar activity may be added to the first, and later a third, and so on, as long as they are compatible with carrying out your other responsibilities. This exercise should again last a whole month. As much as possible, during the second month the first exercise should be continued. . .. 3. During the third month, a new exercise should be placed at the center of life; equanimity is developed in relation to life's fluctu- ations of joy and sorrow, pleasure and pain. Inner harmony must consciously replace mood swings from the heights of jubilation to the depths of despair. Be careful not to get carried away by pleasure or knocked down by pain. No experience should lead you to uncontrollable anger or irritation; no expectation should lead to anxiety or fear; no situation should disturb your composure; and so on. Do not be afraid that this exercise will make your life dry or impoverished. Rather, you will quickly notice that the experiences Source PDF position 119 · English Open the original source page at full size Read the searchable source transcription to which this exercise is applied are replaced by purer soul qualities. If you are attentive to subtlety, you will notice one day that inner peace pervades your body.... 4. In the fourth month, as a new exercise, practice “positivity.” This involves always looking for goodness, the excellence, beauty, and so on in every event, being, and thing.... If you turn your mind consciously toward the positive in every experience, you will gradually notice a feeling creeping into you, as if your whole skin were becoming porous. It is as if your soul were opening to all kinds of secret and delicate processes that had escaped your notice. It is most important to overcome lack of attentiveness to these subtle things. Once it has been noticed that this feeling expresses itself in the soul as a kind of bliss, you should try, in thought, to guide this feeling to the heart, and from there let it flow into the eyes, and then into the space all around you. You will notice that you thus acquire an intimate relationship with this space. You grow out and beyond yourself, as it were. You learn to regard this space as part of you.... 5. In the fifth month, try to develop the feeling of meeting every new experience with complete openness. ... At every moment, be ready to encounter and accept completely new experiences. . . . If you pay attention to this attitude, you will notice something coming to life in the space around you. This experience is extremely delicate and subtle. You must make an effort to be attentive to this delicate vibration in the environment, allowing it to flow as it were through all the five senses, especially the eyes, ears, and skin, insofar as the latter contains the sense of warmth.... 6. In the sixth month, repeat all five exercises systematically, alternating them regularly. ## Exercises for the days of the week We usually perform certain soul processes without care or attention. There are eight of these to which we must now begin to give close Source PDF position 120 · English Open the original source page at full size Read the searchable source transcription attention to and care for: Thinking — Judging — Speaking —- Doing —- Organizing —- Caring - Remembering - Examining. Naturally, it is best to begin by undertaking only one process or exercise at a time—for example, the first exercise for one or two weeks, then the second, and so on, until beginning again. The eighth—right meditation—is best done daily. This will help us gradually attain true self-knowledge as well as monitor our progress. After we have gone through the whole sequence of exercises in this way, we may then, beginning with Saturday, practice the sequence for about five minutes on a daily and weekly basis. Saturpay : RIGHT THINKING Be aware of your thoughts. Think only meaningful thoughts. Gradually learn to separate in your thoughts the essential from the nonessential, the eternal from the transitory, and truth from mere opinion. When listening to conversation, try to become inwardly still, renouncing all agreement and, more important, all negative judgments (criticism and rejection). Do this in both thought and feeling. This is “right thinking.” Sunpay : RIGHT JUDGMENT Decide on even the most insignificant issues only after full, well-founded deliberation and reflection. All unthinking behavior and all meaningless actions should be discarded from the soul. Our reasons for everything we do should be fully deliberated. We should abstain from doing anything that has no significant reason. Once we are convinced that a decision is correct, we should adhere to it with inner steadfastness. This is “right judgment,” because it was made independently of attraction or aversion. Mownpay: RiGHT WorpD Only serious, meaningful speech must leave the lips of those who strive for higher development. All talk for the sake of talking—to Source PDF position 121 · English Open the original source page at full size Read the searchable source transcription pass the time, for example—is harmful. Avoid the usual sort of conversation that involves jumbled, simultaneous crosstalk. This does not mean that you should cut yourself off from interacting with others. Especially in such interactions, your speech should gradually become increasingly meaningful. Listen thoughtfully to every statement and answer. Consider every approach. Never speak without a reason. Prefer silence. Try not to talk too much or too little. Listen quietly and process what you hear. This exercise may be called “right word.” Tuespay : RiGHT DEED Our outer actions should not disturb others. When you are moved inwardly (by conscience) to act, carefully weigh how best to employ the occasion for the good of the whole, and the happiness of others and the eternal. When you act from yourself and your own initiative, weigh the consequences of your actions in the most fundamental way. This is called “right deed.” Wepnespay : RIGHT STANDPOINT In ordering your life, live in harmony with nature and spirit. Do not get buried in the external knickknacks of life. Avoid all that brings restlessness and haste to your life. Be neither impetuous nor lazy. Consider life as a means of inner work and development and act accordingly. One may speak, in this context, of “right standpoint.” TuHurspay: RIGHT STRIVING In human striving, take care not to do anything beyond your power. At the same time, however, do not leave anything undone that is within your ability. Look beyond the moment, the ordinary, and pose goals (ideals) for yourself that are connected with the highest of human responsibilities. In relation to these exercises, for example, try to develop yourself so that later—if not immediately—you may be better able to help and advise others. All this may be summed in this way: “Let all the preceding exercises become a habit.” Source PDF position 122 · English Open the original source page at full size Read the searchable source transcription Fripay : RiGHT MEMoRY Strive to learn as much as possible from life. Nothing happens that does not give us the opportunity to gather experiences that are useful for life. If you have done something incorrectly or incompletely, it becomes an opportunity to do it correctly or completely later on. When you see others act, observe them with the same end in mind (but not without love). Do nothing without looking at past experiences that may help in your decisions and actions. If you are attentive, you can learn much from everyone, including small children. This exercise may be called “right memory,” or recalling what you have learned from your experiences. Summary: RiGHT MEDITATION From time to time, turn your gaze inward, even if for only five minutes at the same time each day. You should sink into yourself; take careful counsel with yourself; test and form your principles of life. In your mind, go through your insights—or the opposite. Weigh your duties. Consider the substance and the real goals of your life. Experience serious displeasure at your faults and imperfections. In other words, try to discover what is essential and permanent, and earnestly propose the appropriate goals—for instance, the virtues you should acquire. Do not make the mistake of thinking you have done something well; always strive harder, instead, toward the highest standards. This exercise is called “right mediation.” ## Other sequences I MonTHLy SEQUENCE Source PDF position 123 · English Open the original source page at full size Read the searchable source transcription Month 1: Self-confidence (faith and trust in oneself) Month 2: Self-control (self-rule) Month 3 Perseverance Week 1: How do I attain self-confidence? You are. ### The twelve moods: zodiacal meditations These verses were written in 1915 for the first group of eurythmists, after they had completed their basic training. Each mood expresses an aspect of “the twelvefold quality that exists in the universe as the Zodiac,” as well as “the sevenfoldness that exists as the planetary sequence.” Thus there are twelve verses—for Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces—each of which contains seven lines that express the seven planetary beings: Sun, Venus, Mercury Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and Moon. Introducing the first performance of these moods, Steiner said, “This has nothing to do with imi- tating modern astrologers, whose methods surpass all materialism, simply adding ignorant superstition to materialist ignorance. For example, for the month of April, one would practice devotion from March 21 to May 1. ### The Calendar of the Soul From “Cosmic Hermit” to “Hieroglyph of the Course of the Year” Rudolf Steiner wrote the Calendar of the Soul verses (meditations) in 1912. They allow one to follow the course of the year and in so doing cultivate different soul moods and capacities. Two basic movements are enacted. In the summer half of the year (from Easter to Michaelmas, verse 1 to verse 26), the soul lives into the power of the senses so as to be able to receive the cosmic word. During the winter months (from Michaelmas to Palm Sunday, verse 27 to verse 52), the cosmic word itself appears in the soul through the growing power of active, living thinking. Thereby, by our own insight, we are enabled to rise from the prison of our narrow view to become truly cosmic beings. In nature herself, these two movements are articulated by the Earth's exhalation in the light of summer and her inhalation during winter’s darkness. The structure is simple. One verse in each group corresponds to a verse in the other: 1 to 52;2 to 51...26 to 27. Easter to Michaelmas thus creates a kind of first axis. A second axis, however, is created between St. John’s Tide and Christmas. Thus there are four related groups of thirteen verses each: two complementing two in a square. The year, for Steiner, begins with Easter. He even proposed reframing the way we count the years from the first Easter, 33-34 c.e., rather than from Jesus’ birth. Therefore the Calendar 1912/1913, in which the Calendar of the Soul verses first appeared, was entitled “In the Year 1879 after the Birth of the ‘I.” In his introduction, he explains: The number of a year is established by each part of humanity so that enumeration begins from an event experienced as especially significant for that part of humanity. title: Start Now! — Meditation and Spiritual Exercises
text: Start Now! — Meditation and Spiritual Exercises A chapter-based teaching course through the whole anthology: 38 lessons in 17 book sections, with practices, their purposes and the contexts in which to choose them. How to follow this book Study the chapters in the book’s order, or use the practice directory to find a particular question. Keep one understood main meditation while learning about the others. Reading a later chapter does not require adopting its practice or certify a spiritual attainment. Begin with purpose, a short sitting and clear thinking. Develop the supporting qualities and a rhythm that fits your duties. Choose a daily, weekly, seasonal, symbolic or devotional practice after reading its preparation and source context. title: Body and spirit, human work and cosmic work
text: ← Meditations from the Esoteric School Lesson 23 / 38 · PDF 195–203 Body and spirit, human work and cosmic work Read the larger mantras as structured transformations. What the book teaches and why The bodily-germ and spiritual-germ meditation moves from faculties received in embodied life toward faculties to be cultivated consciously. Other texts place human existence among Earth, plants, animals and future world-becoming. The six processes of imagining, thinking, feeling, willing, dreaming and sleeping require their actual source arrangement. The invocations to cosmic sculptor, thinker and creator, and the materia/spiritus sequence, use a devotional and symbolic account of creation. These are longer works to study as wholes, not a set of disconnected phrases to add automatically to a short morning routine. When this practice or study fits Use for extended spiritual study and consider a whole understood section for practice only after its relationships are clear. title: A book of paths, not a single routine

What the book teaches and why Bamford introduces meditation as an experiential search for truth involving the whole person. His instructions for preparing a phrase, concentrating and releasing it into receptive quiet belong to his introduction; they should not be silently attributed to Steiner. The anthology gathers material from different dates, recipients and spiritual settings. Its chapters can be studied in order while one understood practice remains the main focus. A later chapter is not an automatic promotion to a spiritual rank. Choose one rather than combine every schedule. Keep a brief record of the wording, source and rhythm you choose. A worked example If you want steadier attention, begin with a short understood phrase. A planetary sequence can be studied now without being added to that daily sitting. Check your understanding You want steadier attention and have five quiet minutes. title: The sixteen-petalled lotus and eight soul processes
text: ← Developing the Chakras, or Lotus Flowers Lesson 9 / 38 · PDF 89–94 The sixteen-petalled lotus and eight soul processes Understand the practical conduct behind the spiritual-organ language. What the book teaches and why The chapter describes lotus flowers as supersensible organs and explicitly calls their names analogies. Its exercise for the sixteen-petalled flower concerns ideas, decisions, speech, action, organizing life, effort, learning from experience and inward examination. The practical task is the care of these processes. Accurate words and considered actions matter more than claiming to see a spiritual organ. The bodily locations and petal counts belong to Steiner’s spiritual physiology rather than a conventional anatomical diagram. When this practice or study fits Use as supporting everyday schooling when you can observe your conduct without trying to diagnose a chakra state. Preparation Learn the eight processes and begin with one concrete situation. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Choose meaningful speech as an initial emphasis. Before one important statement, check its accuracy and purpose; listen to the reply. At day’s end examine what you actually did, then gradually include the other processes. A worked example Passing on a rumour because it seems helpful still transmits an unexamined claim. Good intention does not replace checking what you say. Check your understanding Is the task to count or visualize sixteen petals? Read an explanation The supplied directions emphasize disciplined soul processes; the organ description explains their proposed spiritual significance. Use the source and continue Start Now! title: Figures, AUM and transformation
text: ← Meditations from the Esoteric School Lesson 20 / 38 · PDF 175–186 Figures, AUM and transformation Use the actual diagrams rather than invent missing shapes. What the book teaches and why The book joins geometric images with questions about inside and outside, point and circle, material and spiritual relations, and involution and evolution. The figures are part of the exercise: OCR fragments cannot replace their lines and relationships. AUM and the related past/present/future indications place sound and temporal relationship within an esoteric setting. The source does not make every geometrical shape a universal code to apply without study. Original source-page images are included for these drawings. Read the relationship before assigning a meaning Begin with what can be seen. In the lower pair on source page 181, the rays point outward in one drawing and inward in the other; the second also has a circular boundary. Direction and boundary are separate features to notice. Steiner associates these figures with questions about inside and outside, above and below, and material and spiritual relations. The page does not give a complete key that makes every circle or arrow stand for one fixed spiritual meaning. Describe the relation first, then study the particular question. Outward direction Outward direction Six arrows move away from a central area. No enclosing circular boundary is drawn. State the visible relation: from the centre toward the surrounding space. Inward direction with a boundary Inward direction with a boundary Six arrows move toward the central area, within a circular boundary. State both visible features: inward direction and an enclosing circle. Original course schematics for comparing relations; consult the actual source drawing for Steiner’s exercise. These pictures do not demonstrate a physical or spiritual mechanism. Two features to compare Feature First schematic Second schematic Arrow direction Away from the centre Toward the centre Enclosing circle Not drawn Drawn around the arrows If every arrowhead is reversed but the outline stays the same, is the relationship unchanged? Read the explanation No. The boundary is unchanged, but inward and outward movement have exchanged places. Naming only the circle misses that change. The observation does not, by itself, decide what a spiritual interpretation should be. Compare the actual source figure: capture 181, lower pair (Fig. 3). When this practice or study fits Study when you want to understand image-based practice after learning connected thinking and the difference between preparation and meditation. Preparation Look at the source figure and its specific question together. Do not reconstruct it from broken OCR marks. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Describe exactly what lines and relations the figure shows. Reconstruct the relation inwardly, then attend to the associated question. Keep source observation and your interpretation separate; use the actual page again when uncertain. A worked example When a circle is related to a point, consider how a boundary and a centre belong to one form rather than collecting unrelated meanings of circles. Check your understanding Can any newly drawn symbol be called Steiner’s figure? Read an explanation No. Use the supplied image and identify any original diagram or adaptation as your own. title: Five morning and evening meditations
text: ← Living the Year Spiritually Lesson 13 / 38 · PDF 113–117 Five morning and evening meditations Choose a paired daily verse rather than gather every formula into one sitting. What the book teaches and why The five daily meditations move between seeking oneself in the world’s divinity, the flourishing of soul in love, resting and living within spiritual being, steadfastness with bodily references, and light with the warmth of love. Their paired forms change the direction of attention. Morning and evening wordings should be read as related but distinct. Reversing a verse can turn a movement from world toward self into one from self toward world. The source pages provide all five pairs; the example here is the third. When this practice or study fits Choose a pair for a regular daily rhythm when its spiritual language is understood. The chapter does not require all five pairs every day. Preparation Read both versions and identify the sequence before choosing one pair. A text to work with English wording from the supplied anthology; Portuguese is a new study translation. · PDF 115 Morning · III In the world’s divinity In the world’s spirit In the world’s soul I will find myself To rest in it To live in it To be in it Evening I will be I will live I will rest I will find myself In the world’s soul In the world’s spirit In the world’s divinity How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Clarify how seeking, resting, living and being relate in the selected pair. Use the morning wording at the chosen morning time and its corresponding evening wording in the evening. Keep the pair stable long enough to learn its movement; review attention rather than a count of repetitions. A worked example In pair III, the morning moves from the world’s divinity toward resting, living and being; the evening returns through these relations toward the divine. title: The Greater Guardian and the refusal of isolated perfection
text: ← Meeting the Guardians Lesson 35 / 38 · PDF 283–290 The Greater Guardian and the refusal of isolated perfection Understand why the path returns to service. What the book teaches and why The Greater Guardian places the learner’s development within the unfinished development of the world. The temptation is to seek private liberation while abandoning the beings with whom one’s capacities have developed. The chapter’s conclusion makes selfless dedication and collaboration central. Its horizon is liberation of beings together, not a spiritual status that makes ordinary relationships irrelevant. Read the service argument and its historical limits This passage also needs a difficult distinction. Source page 287 places peoples and races into a supposed hierarchy of development before the chapter returns to shared progress and service. That classification is part of the historical text; it is not evidence of any people’s spiritual worth. You can examine the argument that abilities develop through relationships, and that growth should lead to contribution, without accepting the racial hierarchy. Keep these claims separate when explaining what you learned. Service means attending to actual people and their circumstances. Two workshop partners have different language and technical skills. Does their difference establish a spiritual ranking of the peoples they belong to? Read the explanation No. Those particular skills do not establish a collective spiritual hierarchy. Ask what each person can contribute, what support is needed and how the work can be shared. This applies the service question without treating the source’s racial classification as a demonstrated explanation. Reading context: supplied Start Now! captures 287–290. When this practice or study fits Use as a later study of the motive for the whole course and as a review of why you practise. Preparation Recall the earlier principle that knowledge should serve human and world development. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Explain the difference between personal improvement and isolated self-perfecting. Name one way your capacities depend on others. Consider a realistic contribution and examine whether it respects the people concerned. A worked example Learning to attend more carefully becomes socially meaningful when it helps you listen accurately, not when it becomes a reason to regard others as less developed. Check your understanding Why finish the book with a return toward others? Read an explanation The Guardian account makes service integral to the spiritual aim rather than an optional decoration after individual attainment. Use the source and continue Start Now! title: The three-part mantra, sound and butterfly
text: ← Meditations from the Esoteric School Lesson 24 / 38 · PDF 203–208 The three-part mantra, sound and butterfly Keep advanced symbolic sequences intelligible and distinct. What the book teaches and why The three-part mantra joins self-knowledge, the Guardian and spiritual world-becoming, sometimes with the Rosicrucian signature. The JAOUE meditation gives sounds with associated spiritual images. The final butterfly meditation is accompanied by Edith Maryon’s note that butterfly means thought. These works need their contexts. The butterfly’s transformations into bird, depths, fire and ash are symbolic transformations of thought; they are not directions involving an actual animal, fire or consumption of ashes. The chapter’s closing blessing is another text, not an extra line to splice into every mantra. When this practice or study fits Study after the earlier work on clear thinking and meaningful imagery. Choose a sequence only when you can explain its symbolic movement. Preparation Read every line and its source note, including Maryon’s interpretive key. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Map the chosen sequence before meditating: what changes and what remains related? For the butterfly, work with the inward image of thought and its transformations, never a physical enactment. For sound material, preserve the source’s associations without inventing compulsory breath counts or bodily effects. A worked example Thought changing from a captured butterfly to a bird can be explored as a change in mobility and relation; it is not a report that a physical object changed species. Check your understanding Can a striking sensation establish the meaning of a sound sequence? Read an explanation No. Understanding requires the actual source and its context, not the strength of a sensation. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 203–208. title: Heart qualities, deliberate attention and harmony
text: ← Developing the Chakras, or Lotus Flowers Lesson 10 / 38 · PDF 94–99 Heart qualities, deliberate attention and harmony Relate the remaining lotus teachings to the exercises they actually name. What the book teaches and why The twelve-petalled account develops connected thinking, initiative and balanced qualities. The ten-petalled account asks for care over impressions and unconscious associations; the six-petalled account concerns harmony among body, soul and spirit. These descriptions do not provide a quick test of another person’s character or spiritual condition. Their direction is toward greater awareness of one’s own activity and less passive dependence on unexamined impressions. When this practice or study fits Use to deepen supporting practice after understanding the eight processes and the six exercises. Preparation Distinguish a memory association from information you deliberately observed. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Recall an instance in which a passing impression influenced a later thought. Name what you know and what you are inferring. Choose a small adjustment that brings thinking, feeling and action into a more considered relationship. A worked example A headline glimpsed without deliberate reading may later appear as an unexplained thought. Examining its possible origin is clearer than assuming a revelation. Check your understanding Can bodily sensation establish that a spiritual organ has developed? Read an explanation The course does not use sensations as a diagnostic measure. Review the quality of attention and conduct the chapter asks you to cultivate. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 94–99. title: I AM, short themes and the protective image
text: ← Meditations from the Esoteric School Lesson 21 / 38 · PDF 187–191 I AM, short themes and the protective image Distinguish bodily references, spiritual images and ordinary conduct. What the book teaches and why One instruction links I AM, It Thinks, She Feels, He Wills and Divine Life with different fields of attention. It also explicitly warns against self-deception concerning the hands. Other short themes and the light-and-love verse provide different possible contents. The blue aura or protective sheath meditation belongs to the book’s spiritual imagery. It is not evidence that one has become invulnerable or that another person’s thoughts have been detected. The source text must retain its context rather than become a claim about physical protection. When this practice or study fits Study the bodily-reference sequence carefully before choosing it; use a simple understood theme if that is a better present fit. Preparation Read the entire direction rather than isolate a body location or promise. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Identify each wording and its feeling context from the source page. Remain comfortably attentive, without pressing a body point or manufacturing involuntary movements. After a sitting distinguish imagined sheath, sensation and external event. Keep ordinary judgment about situations. A worked example Imagining a boundary can give form to a spiritual theme; it does not establish what another person is secretly thinking. Check your understanding Should the hands be moved to prove that the exercise works? Read an explanation The source itself warns against self-deception; the course does not use movement as a test of spiritual progress. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 187–191. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: The oldest programme of German idealism
text: ← Appendices Lesson 36 / 38 · PDF 291–293 The oldest programme of German idealism Understand the appendix’s historical voice. What the book teaches and why The first appendix presents a philosophical programme linking freedom, imagination, art, reason and a renewed mythology. Bamford places it within the intellectual background of the book. It is not a newly discovered meditation schedule authored by Steiner. The passage asks how ideas can become living and communicable through beauty. Study its ambition while distinguishing a philosophical proposal from an established description of society or spiritual perception. When this practice or study fits Use as contextual study when you want to understand the anthology’s meeting of philosophy and spiritual practice. Preparation Identify the appendix as a different kind of document from an instruction to a student. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Explain one relation it proposes between reason and imagination. Consider how a symbol can express an idea without replacing thought. Compare that relation with the prepared Rose Cross rather than inventing a new compulsory exercise. A worked example A diagram can help a learner perceive relationships, but its beauty alone does not establish the truth of the relationships. Check your understanding Is every appendix a practice to perform daily? Read an explanation No. A historical or conceptual source may explain the background of practice without adding a timetable. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 291–293. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: Imagination, Inspiration and Intuition
text: ← Appendices Lesson 37 / 38 · PDF 293–295 Imagination, Inspiration and Intuition Understand the spiritual horizon without confusing it with ordinary impressions. What the book teaches and why Bamford distinguishes ordinary knowledge from imaginative, inspirational and intuitive knowing. These names have technical meanings in the spiritual account: working with spiritual images, knowing beyond images and participating in the being known. They are not simply creativity, a bright idea and a hunch. The final Steiner passage returns to sustained concentration and transformation of soul experience. The appendix does not give a fixed number of sittings after which a stage can be claimed. Preparation, attention, devotion and discernment remain important. When this practice or study fits Use to understand the purposes claimed for the practices and to review your interpretations of experience. Preparation Separate the activity you intentionally perform from the spiritual status you might be tempted to assign it. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Describe a sitting in terms of content and attention before interpreting it. Compare a deliberately formed image with the technical account of Imagination. Review what remains uncertain, and continue the actual capacities rather than declaring a rank. A worked example Having an unexpected useful thought after meditation can be recorded without concluding that technical Inspiration has occurred. Check your understanding Does a vivid image alone establish spiritual perception? Read an explanation No. The appendix itself emphasizes discernment and the danger of fantasy. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 293–295. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: Study and independence in the Rosicrucian path
text: ← The Rosicrucian Path Lesson 25 / 38 · PDF 209–211 Study and independence in the Rosicrucian path Understand why thinking precedes symbolic practice. What the book teaches and why The chapter presents the teacher as adviser and clear thinking as an inner guide. Its seven stages include study, imaginative knowledge, esoteric script, rhythm, microcosm, macrocosm and beatitude; the text says they need not be completed in a rigid enumerated order. Its account of yoga and Christian paths belongs to Steiner’s historical comparison, not a complete description of all living traditions. The practical emphasis here is to understand what one is doing instead of treating authority as a substitute for thought. When this practice or study fits Use before selecting Rosicrucian symbols or when you need to examine the relationship between guidance and freedom. Preparation Distinguish the chapter’s philosophical study from gathering interesting historical facts. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Work through a clear relation, such as the ideal circle and an imperfect drawing. Explain how understanding differs from receiving a teacher’s assertion. Read the seven stages as a map of this spiritual account, not a personal achievement score. A worked example An adviser can help locate a difficulty, while the student still has to perform the thinking that makes the relation understood. Check your understanding Do the seven stages authorize skipping preparation? Read an explanation No. Their non-rigid order does not abolish the work of developing the capacities they name. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 209–211. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: John’s opening and the seven Christian stages
text: ← The Christian-Gnostic Path Lesson 28 / 38 · PDF 231–236 John’s opening and the seven Christian stages Understand a specifically Christian contemplative path. What the book teaches and why The chapter asks for a lived relation to Christ and treats the opening of John’s Gospel as a meditation, not only a text to reread. Its seven stages use Gospel images including washing the feet, scourging, crowning with thorns, crucifixion, mystical death, burial and resurrection. The practical teaching concerns feelings and spiritual interpretation: humility and gratitude for what supports us, steadiness through difficulty, and transformed self-understanding. The bodily suffering and extraordinary experiences described in the historical account are not exercises to reproduce through injury or forced symptoms. When this practice or study fits Choose devotional practice when the Christ and Gospel framework is meaningful; otherwise study the chapter as an account of this path. Preparation Understand the Gospel episode and its intended quality before choosing a meditation. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Read the opening of John or one whole episode in context. Prepare the quality named by the source; during the sitting remain with the understood content. Carry the quality into a modest relation with another person and review its actual expression. A worked example Washing the feet can prepare gratitude toward those whose often unseen work makes your activity possible. Check your understanding Are the seven stages a seven-day beginner challenge? Read an explanation No. The source describes a long spiritual schooling with guidance and experience; the chapter does not give such a challenge. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 231–236. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: The Lesser Guardian: responsibility made visible
text: ← Meeting the Guardians Lesson 34 / 38 · PDF 277–283 The Lesser Guardian: responsibility made visible Read the threshold account as a demand for self-knowledge. What the book teaches and why The Lesser Guardian confronts the learner with what has been formed through one’s own deeds and development. The account links increased independence with greater responsibility for motives and consequences. This chapter is a description of spiritual experience within Steiner’s system, not an instruction to summon an apparition. Its historical language about collective identities must not be used to assign spiritual worth to people by ancestry, nation or race. When this practice or study fits Study after the ethical and cognitive groundwork; it can clarify why character preparation matters. Preparation Distinguish the literary voice of the Guardian from a direction to generate a frightening image. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Identify what responsibilities the Guardian says the learner must assume. Relate that demand to a real instance of acknowledging a motive or repairing harm. Keep a dream or imagined figure separate from a claim to have met the Guardian. A worked example Admitting an error without blaming circumstances illustrates responsibility; it does not establish a threshold encounter. Check your understanding Should frightening imagery be pursued to prove progress? Read an explanation No. The course teaches the account’s meaning and preparation, not a procedure for producing frightening experiences. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 277–283. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: Living sentences and the higher Self
text: ← Meditations from the Esoteric School Lesson 19 / 38 · PDF 174–179 Living sentences and the higher Self Understand the difference between a spiritual formula and self-assertion. What the book teaches and why The opening exercises ask the learner to contemplate transformations: point and sphere, seed and ear, polarities and hospitality. A “living sentence” is meant to continue generating inquiry rather than end in a quick definition. This section also credits material from earlier traditions, including the higher-Self formula in Annie Besant’s English version and Mabel Collins’s Light on the Path. Their inclusion in Steiner’s teaching does not make him the author of every wording. When this practice or study fits Choose a living sentence for sustained study when you can keep its whole relationship in view. Use the higher-Self formula only with its spiritual meaning understood. Preparation Read the attribution and distinguish the everyday personality from the Self addressed. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Take one relation, such as point and sphere, and describe the transformation in thought. Let the question deepen without immediately filling it with unrelated associations. Return at a later time and record what became clearer, separating an interpretation from a perceived fact. A worked example Hospitality can be contemplated as receiving what is unfamiliar while remaining oneself, before attempting to interpret the section’s midnight-Sun language. Check your understanding Does “I am that Self” mean that every personal wish is divine? Read an explanation No. That would erase the chapter’s distinction between personal desire and spiritual self-knowledge. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 174–179. title: Six months, eight processes and seven weeks
text: ← Living the Year Spiritually Lesson 14 / 38 · PDF 117–124 Six months, eight processes and seven weeks Distinguish the chapter’s different schedules. What the book teaches and why The six-month programme emphasizes thought, initiative, equanimity, positivity, openness and their balance. The weekday exercises name right thinking, judgment, word, deed, standpoint, striving and memory, with inward examination practised daily. The book first recommends learning one process at a time before the weekly rotation. A separate seven-week exercise gives six sentences, each for a week, followed by all six together. These are different programmes, not interchangeable labels for one universal schedule. When this practice or study fits Use a schedule when its actions are understood and its rhythm fits your life. Choose the programme explicitly rather than superimpose all of them. Preparation Learn the ordinary meaning of each quality and identify which source sequence you are following. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. For the six-month programme, begin with thought and add the other emphases gradually. For weekdays, first study and practise individual processes; then use the Saturday-to-Friday rotation with daily examination. If choosing the seven-week sentences, preserve their sequence and distinguish it from the six-month work. A worked example Monday’s right word can mean listening before replying in a conversation; daily examination asks how that intention actually affected the exchange. Check your understanding Are the seven-week sentences the same as the planetary moods? Read an explanation No. The former are a progression over weeks; the latter assign different verses to days in another context. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 117–124. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: The Our Father versions and inward renewal
text: ← The Christian-Gnostic Path Lesson 30 / 38 · PDF 245–254 The Our Father versions and inward renewal Read prayer with its particular theology and purpose. What the book teaches and why The esoteric Our Father places divine nourishment, conduct, mercy and human strength in a relation to the Father within. The Gothic rendering and macrocosmic prayer have different histories and structures; they are not simply substitute translations of one identical devotional formula. The concluding passage concerns the limits encountered in self-knowledge and the experience of renewal in Christ. Its language about disease and denial of God belongs to Steiner’s spiritual interpretation. It should not be used to diagnose illness or judge someone’s health from their beliefs. When this practice or study fits Use an understood prayer as devotional practice when its theological setting is meaningful. Study the variants comparatively before changing between them. Preparation Read the surrounding account and identify who is speaking and what the prayer asks. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Choose a complete prayer rather than assemble lines from different versions. Prepare its movement from address to conduct and relationship. Afterward identify one ordinary expression of mercy or responsible action without treating it as proof of spiritual attainment. A worked example A prayer about mercy can lead you to consider a fair response to an error, including the need to repair harm rather than merely forget it. Check your understanding Does religious doubt establish a medical condition? Read an explanation No. The course attributes the historical interpretation and does not treat belief as a medical test. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 245–254. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: The seven planetary moods
text: ← Living the Year Spiritually Lesson 15 / 38 · PDF 124–133 The seven planetary moods Understand a complete weekday cycle in its original timing. What the book teaches and why The seven moods address an encompassing Spirit and unfold relationships between cosmic being and the human I. The source assigns them to evenings leading into named days, beginning Friday for Saturday. It explains an occult day beginning at 6 p.m. The accompanying letter proposes twenty or thirty minutes for exploring a given verse. That belongs to this particular sequence and is not the minimum required for all meditation. The concluding prayer after each verse is part of the source arrangement. All seven wordings and their common ending are included in the chapter reader. When this practice or study fits Consider when you want sustained devotional study of the sevenfold sequence and can understand the hierarchy and planetary language. Preparation Read the whole cycle, its day labels and its common ending before adopting the schedule. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Locate the verse for the evening-to-day relation specified by the book. Prepare the meaning outside the sitting, then attend to the chosen verse without changing its planetary assignment. Use the shared ending as the source directs; review whether the full rhythm is sustainable. A worked example Friday for Saturday is not a printing error to be replaced by Saturday morning. A learner may adapt the timing, but should name that as an adaptation. Check your understanding Does planetary symbolism tell you what will happen to you that day? Read an explanation The chapter presents meditative relationships, not a daily prediction service. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 124–133. title: Reading to and remembering the dead
text: ← Working with the Dead Lesson 31 / 38 · PDF 255–257 Reading to and remembering the dead Understand the proposed spiritual relationship and its preparation. What the book teaches and why Bamford’s introductory account describes reading as making a spiritual content inwardly alive and offering its meaning, rather than assuming that a deceased person needs a particular spoken language. Remembering asks for accuracy, love and a relation not driven solely by one’s own need. The chapter also describes questions carried into sleep and thoughts noticed on waking. These are presented within the anthology’s spiritual account. A morning thought or a meaningful coincidence is not independently established as a message from someone who has died. When this practice or study fits Consider for voluntary remembrance or devotional practice when the source’s framework is meaningful. You can also study it without undertaking communication practices. Preparation Choose an understood text and distinguish a cherished memory, a present feeling and a claim about another world. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Bring a precise memory of the person to mind with care. Study a spiritual passage until its meaning becomes living thought; offer that meaning inwardly if choosing the source practice. Close deliberately and record the experience without claiming a verified reply. A worked example Reading a meaningful passage and recalling a loved one’s care can be a considered act of remembrance even when no unusual experience occurs. Check your understanding Does an answer in your own voice prove contact? Read an explanation The chapter itself says the waking thought is in one’s own voice. Its origin cannot be settled merely by how significant it feels. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 255–257. title: Reverence, inner peace and listening
text: ← The Way of Reverence and Its Fruits Lesson 7 / 38 · PDF 71–82 Reverence, inner peace and listening Practise receptivity without abandoning discernment. What the book teaches and why Reverence is directed toward truth and knowledge. Steiner connects it with an active inner life: letting an experience resonate rather than rushing to the next impression. In listening, the learner temporarily quiets personal agreement and objection to hear what the other is expressing. Inner peace also allows one to view personal events with more distance. This is not withdrawal from the world; the chapter expects these moments to renew the strength for daily tasks. When this practice or study fits Use in daily encounters and as preparation before a chosen meditation. Preparation Choose a brief, ordinary encounter rather than trying to be inwardly silent all day. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Listen to one person without preparing your rebuttal while they speak. Recall the experience quietly, distinguishing their words from your response. Then exercise judgment and choose an appropriate action. A worked example You can hear a colleague’s reason accurately before explaining why you disagree. Respect and clear judgment can accompany one another. Check your understanding Does reverence require approving every claim? Read an explanation No. Giving something a fair hearing improves the basis for subsequent judgment. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 71–82. Open this chapter’s source and practice texts → Review which practice to choose ← Previous Chapter Next →

title: The evening backward review
text: ← The Backward Review, or Retrospect Lesson 12 / 38 · PDF 109–112 The evening backward review Learn to reconstruct rather than merely replay the day. What the book teaches and why The review begins with a recent event and moves toward earlier events. Steiner recommends small episodes as preparation and describes including oneself as if observing another person. Reversing the order requires active visualization. The chapter relates this to spiritual cognition and to love. An everyday learning outcome is a more accurate view of one’s actions, but that outcome does not by itself establish all of the chapter’s spiritual claims. When this practice or study fits Use in the evening when you want to connect inner practice and learning from conduct. Preparation Choose a manageable episode, especially while learning the method. How to work with it These steps are our teaching arrangement of the source method. Specific historical schedules retain their source context. Picture the latest event first, including your own action. Move to the preceding event while preserving the facts. If reviewing stairs, begin with the top step and reconstruct the earlier steps. Conclude by naming what you learned and a possible repair, then finish rather than endlessly replaying the scene. A worked example Picture putting a cup away, then washing it, then finishing the drink. You reverse the remembered order without inventing a different day. Check your understanding You cooked a meal, answered a message and then put away a cup. In what order would you review these events, and how would you handle a detail you cannot remember? Read an explanation Start with putting away the cup, then answering the message, then cooking. Include your own action as if observing it, while keeping the reverse order distinct from changing the facts. Mark an uncertain detail as uncertain rather than inventing it. Finish with a specific learning or possible repair, then close the review. Use the source and continue Start Now! (2004), supplied PDF positions 109–112.
