title: Fertilizing as enlivening the soil
text: ← Full course Fertilizing as enlivening the soil By the end of this lesson: Explain why the lecture connects fertilization, living soil, animal digestion and the horn. Look beyond the plant’s outline A plant’s visible outline is not the boundary of the conditions it needs. Roots depend on surrounding soil, water, air and the activity of living organisms. Begin there when asking what fertilizing is meant to accomplish. Steiner’s answer goes further than ordinary soil observation: fertilization should enliven the soil so that the plant grows within a living environment and can develop toward fruiting. Why compare soil with a tree? Humus means the relatively stable organic material formed through decomposition in soil. Steiner compares a humus-rich mound with a tree: he treats the mound as approaching a plant covering and tree bark as a further development of that relation. The comparison is intended to make life continuous between plant and soil. His term living ether names the spiritual life-forming activity he places in that environment. Three materials, distinct assigned activities He distinguishes mineral fertilizer, compost and animal manure by the activities he assigns them. Mineral additions are said to affect the watery aspect without enlivening the solid earthy component in the same way. Compost is assigned comparatively stable etheric and astral activity. Here etheric refers to life-forming activity; astral refers to another spiritual dimension associated with animal experience and formative influences. These are the lecture’s categories, not ordinary laboratory measurements. Why the animal and horn matter Animal manure has passed through digestion, so Steiner treats it as carrying activity transformed by the animal. His horn comparison explains why a horn matters later: horns and hoofs are said to return formative streams inward toward digestion, whereas antlers direct streams outward. A stream here means a proposed formative influence, not necessarily a flow of liquid. The horn is therefore an active participant in his theory, not just a convenient container. How to read the smell and microbial claims The lecture also discusses keeping activity within a boundary, using smell and nitrogen as part of its explanation. Steiner treats microorganisms as signs of manure’s condition and rejects inoculation as its fundamental improvement. This is a specific historical position, not a summary of modern soil microbiology. Smell does not establish hygienic safety, and a spiritual description of manure does not replace appropriate treatment and handling. Follow the complete chain The teaching chain is now clear: plant life extends into its environment; fertilization supports that environment; animal manure carries transformed activity; the horn is claimed to concentrate it. This prepares the next lesson’s paired preparations. The lecture’s broader assertions about food forces and the sources of bodily substance remain attributed historical claims in the full reading, rather than dietary advice for the learner. Worked example: a weak plant in a pot Start with questions: what is the root environment like, and what is known about water, air, nutrients and soil condition? A weak plant alone does not answer these questions. Explain the source: Steiner widens fertilization into enlivening that environment and assigns manure a particular spiritual activity. Keep the levels clear: investigating the root environment is an observable task; the etheric and astral explanation is the author’s additional account. Original course teaching example; not a quotation from the book. Two questions — optional What changes when fertilization means enlivening soil? See an explanation The focus extends from adding a substance to supporting the environment in which the plant develops. Steiner gives that environment a further spiritual interpretation through living ether and animal-transformed activity. Why is the horn not incidental packaging in this argument? See an explanation Steiner assigns horns an inward-reflecting formative function associated with digestion. That proposed function is the reason for their place in the next preparation; naming the container alone misses the theory. Fertilizing must consist of enlivening the soil, so that the plant is not growing in dead soil and does not have difficulty reaching the fruiting stage out of its own vitality. Rudolf Steiner; selection from Spiritual Foundations for the Renewal of Agriculture, English translation by Catherine Creeger and Malcolm Gardner, editorial notes by Malcolm Gardner, Bio-Dynamic Farming and Gardening Association © 1993. Line breaks and line-wrap hyphens normalized. SteinerBooks anthology, What Is Biodynamics? A Way to Heal and Revitalize the Earth. Introduction © 2005 Hugh J. Courtney; electronic-edition publication date not stated in the supplied capture. Chapter-specific translation credits are given with each passage. Capture positions and Kindle locations identify the supplied digital source; they are not printed page numbers. Course explanation Understand the idea The opening objects to reconstructing a whole person from a finger and an earlobe: similarly, an isolated substance cannot explain the whole life of a farm or its food. Steiner’s protein example is meant to show the weakness of short-term conclusions. He makes historical claims about amounts, toxicity and later illness, then distinguishes the value of experiments from the limits of the theories drawn from them. At capture 79 he expressly calls experiments useful; his objection concerns interpreting their results within too narrow a framework. His nourishment account is stronger than a general preference for good food. He says most eaten material supplies forces for movement and will, while most substance retained by the body is absorbed through breathing, skin and senses and then condensed. These are his stated spiritual-scientific interpretations, not present-day dietary guidance. They establish the substance/force distinction that he next carries into fertilizing: what matters in his account is how a living activity is supported, rather than only how much material is supplied. The tree and humus mound develop that distinction. Steiner describes a blackboard comparison, but the capture gives its verbal account rather than the drawing. Humus-rich soil contains living ether in his explanation; a mound approaches the plant sheathing that develops further as bark in a tree. Life continues through roots into the surrounding soil, so the plant’s outline is not the boundary of the life on which it depends. He calls plant growth slightly parasitic because it draws on this living soil. The quoted passage makes the consequence explicit: fertilization is to enliven that environment so the plant can develop toward fruiting. The lecture then differentiates watery and earthy activity, and etheric life from astral activity. Steiner says mineral fertilizers stimulate the watery component without enlivening earthiness. Compost has comparatively stable astrality; excessive etheric activity can prevent that astrality from working on nitrogen. His lime example assigns lime a role in taking up etheric activity and oxygen so astrality can act on the earthy component. His odor account also concerns retaining activity within a boundary rather than letting it escape. These linked terms explain his proposal; reducing them to a generic nutrient list would lose its reasoning. Animal manure supplies the next connection. Steiner contrasts horns and hoofs, which turn formative streams inward toward digestion, with antlers, which discharge streams outward into the animal’s surroundings. Manure has passed through an animal’s inner process and therefore carries etheric , astral , nitrogen-bearing and oxygen-bearing activity into soil, in his account. He treats bacteria as indicators of manure’s condition and denies that inoculation can fundamentally improve it. This inward/outer relation provides the explanation for the horn preparation considered next, rather than leaving the horn as an unexplained container. Key concept The lecture’s governing relation is plant–soil life: Steiner explains fertilization through activity extending across the root boundary, with etheric , astral , watery and earthy aspects differentiated. Course example Original reading example: compare two descriptions of the same compost heap. One lists its materials; the other asks which activities Steiner says are held together or allowed to escape. In a notebook, map compost → soil → plant, then add the lecture’s etheric / astral and nitrogen terms. Label those arrows as the author’s explanation; the diagram alone does not demonstrate the proposed forces. Keep this distinction Distinguish a material being present from the living activity Steiner attributes to it. Also distinguish reconstructing his explanation from establishing that explanation by observation. His comments about bodily substance, bacteria and odor need their source attribution; they should not be silently replaced with contemporary scientific definitions. Check your understanding Why does Steiner connect fertilizing with the plant’s surroundings? Because he says life continues from the roots into the soil around them. Because he says plant life is completely enclosed by its visible outline. Because he describes humus as a wholly lifeless container. His criticism concerns the interpretation after the experiment and the wider relationships that he thinks it misses. title: Two preparations, one larger inquiry
text: ← Full course Two preparations, one larger inquiry By the end of this lesson: Compare the two horn preparations by substance, season, direction and intended role. Compare the pair before the numbers Two preparations can share a container and still have different purposes. Steiner pairs a manure-filled horn exposed through winter with a mineral-filled horn exposed through summer. The comparison concerns substance, season, direction and the side of plant life addressed. Learn that relationship before trying to remember preparation numbers or quantities. Horn manure: the soil side The manure preparation uses the horn’s proposed inward-reflecting activity. Steiner describes winter as the period of Earth’s stronger inward etheric and astral activity; the buried horn is said to concentrate this within manure. Its treatment is directed to the soil. Later editorial notes identify this as horn manure, preparation 500. The winter explanation belongs to the lecture’s seasonal picture, not to a universal calendar date for every hemisphere. Horn silica: the plant side The second preparation contains ground quartz, with orthoclase mentioned as an alternative, and spends summer underground. Its treatment is directed to the plant. In the lecture’s image, the manure preparation pushes from below while the mineral preparation pulls from above. Later notes identify horn silica as 501. The two are complementary in that account; one is not simply a stronger dose of the other. Why dilution and stirring enter the theory Dilution and alternating stirring are explained as intimate permeation by an activity, rather than merely spreading a large quantity of nutrient. Steiner also attributes significance to the participant’s movement and feeling. This is his account of dynamic action. The small amount therefore requires an explanation within his theory; it does not by itself demonstrate an effective agricultural dose. What the discussion leaves open The discussion leaves scale, exact measures, horn reuse and several local conditions for investigation. It distinguishes preferred hand stirring from accepted machine spraying and does not impose a general ban on farm machinery. Understanding one preference should not become an invented rule against every machine. Source qualifications belong beside the main explanation because they change what can reasonably be inferred. What the pair is meant to supplement Finally, Steiner says the method enhances ordinary manuring. It is not a replacement for the fertility materials and care a crop requires. He also rejects size or profit alone as the measure of success, asking about nourishment for human life. The course task is to compare the intended roles and the unresolved questions; the historical discussion is not a universal manufacturing or application protocol. Course explanation Understand the idea Steiner connects the winter manure preparation with the horn’s previously described inward-reflecting activity. Surrounded by earth, the horn is said to receive etherizing and astralizing activity that is strongest during the Earth’s inwardly active winter. The manure concentrates this activity; the changed odor reported in the Dornach trial is interpreted through that explanation. Dilution and alternating stirring are described as intimate permeation, not simply as distributing a material nutrient. These are the author’s proposed relations of forces, rather than instructions supplied by this lesson for making a preparation. The second preparation creates a seasonal and directional contrast. Its substance is ground quartz, with orthoclase offered as an alternative, and its horn spends summer underground. The lecture places the manure treatment on the soil side and the mineral treatment on the plant side: one pushes from below, the other pulls from above. The headnote’s root/humus and seed/fruit summary belongs to editor Marcia Merryman means. The numbers 500 and 501 belong to the edition’s explanatory note at capture 95. Steiner’s concluding criterion is the crop’s contribution to whole human life, rather than swollen produce, profit or visible size alone. The discussion does not supply a universally settled formula. Steiner leaves scaling to larger areas for investigation, says weights and measures still need to be worked out, and acknowledges untested horn reuse, sand and rainfall effects. He advises experimentation with cow age, alongside emphatic claims about locality and different hemispheres. Elsewhere he identifies excessive growth and rank patches as a consequence of too much of the manure preparation. Attend to both forms of speech: a stated spiritual explanation and an answer explicitly awaiting experience or a comparison are different parts of the source. Personal participation is also more than a preference for careful work. Steiner says hand movement and feeling enter stirring, and uses the doctor’s enthusiasm and Ritter remedies as an analogy. Later he ascribes effects on plant growth to meditation and a changed relation to nitrogen’s imaginations, and affirms possible parasite control through seasonally appropriate concentration. Keep these as attributed spiritual assertions. They do not imply that every machine is forbidden: he accepts fine machine spraying, and treats the use of farm machinery as practically unavoidable in contemporary social conditions while criticizing continual equipment replacement. The final replies bring insight, trial and communication together. Feeling developed through understanding can guide an initial judgment, but Steiner then asks for results expressed as figures and useful tables, rather than intuition alone. The closing passage gives another limit: horn-manure fertilization enhances ordinary manuring and does not replace it. Taken together, these replies locate the preparations within farming as a whole, with other work still required. A sound reading reconstructs the proposed relation and its qualifications before treating a named preparation as a complete agricultural method. Key concept Winter manure/soil/below and summer mineral/plant/above form the lecture’s complementary polarity. Its discussion also requires investigation, calculable communication and the continuation of ordinary manuring. The first emphasizes the participant’s movement and feeling; the second is accepted because the forces are said to remain bound; the third is discussed in social and practical circumstances. A single label such as “machines prohibited” cannot represent all three replies. Keep this distinction A dynamic or radiant effect in Steiner’s explanation is not simply an account of material quantity. Likewise, the source’s confidence about a spiritual relation does not erase its admissions that particular measures or outcomes need testing. The lecture is a historical explanation to study, not a context-free spraying or medicinal recipe. Check your understanding Which pairing matches the lecture’s two horn preparations? title: Living soil: substances, forces and replenishment
text: ← Full course Living soil: substances, forces and replenishment By the end of this lesson: Distinguish material presence, living-force claims and evidence of a crop response. Presence is not the same as use Presence, availability and use are different questions. A soil may contain a substance without a plant being able to take it up under the existing conditions. This familiar distinction helps introduce Steiner’s concern with receptivity. It does not, by itself, establish his further explanation of living forces, cosmic contributions or transformations of elements. Why replenishment matters Harvest removes material from a farm. Steiner also describes it as removing forces from soil and air that must be replenished. He returns to the picture of soil around roots as a continuation of plant life. In that account, good fertility involves maintaining a relationship among soil, plant and organic material, rather than merely matching an isolated substance with a crop. What a small addition is supposed to do His distinction between material substances and living forces explains why he proposes small additions to manure. The intention is to influence the manure’s capacity to receive, retain and make available what plant life needs. A compost preparation is therefore not presented as a sack of nutrients. The key question in the theory is what activity a substance carries and what relationship it helps organize. Unpack the substance names The lecture discusses carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur in relation to potash and lime. These names identify particular substances and relationships in its argument. Potash concerns potassium compounds; lime concerns calcium compounds. Historical usage can be broader than a single present-day product name. Do not turn every occurrence into an instruction to buy or apply a particular material. What “hidden alchemy” claims Steiner additionally claims that tiny contributions arrive from the cosmos and discusses substances including silicic acid, mercury, arsenic and lead. He invokes Kolisko’s investigations and describes a hidden alchemy, including transformation of potash and lime into nitrogen under hydrogen. That is stronger than ordinary decomposition or nutrient recycling. These are attributed source claims, not instructions to add toxic elements or established chemical transformations. Separate measurement, mechanism and effect The practical learning distinction is between a measurement, an explanation and a predicted effect. A soil analysis can report a measured concentration; it cannot alone verify the lecture’s cosmic mechanism. Likewise, vigorous growth cannot identify which of several possible processes caused it. Explain the proposed relationship first, then say what observations or comparisons would be needed to assess an agricultural outcome. Worked example: a nutrient appears in a soil report Measurement: the report gives a concentration under a stated analytical method. Question: can the crop take up enough under the site’s actual root, water and soil conditions? Presence alone has not answered that. Source interpretation: Steiner adds living and cosmic activities to his account of receptivity. The first distinction helps explain his concern but does not prove those added mechanisms. Original course teaching example; not a quotation from the book. Two questions — optional Why not describe a compost preparation only by the nutrients it contains? See an explanation Its intended role in the lecture is to influence living activity and receptivity within manure and soil. A nutrient inventory alone would miss that proposed role. It also would not establish that the proposed role is effective. Is the hidden-alchemy passage merely another name for recycling nitrogen? See an explanation No. It explicitly asserts transformations into nitrogen from other named materials. A faithful explanation must retain the strength of that claim while distinguishing it from established nutrient cycling. Soil around roots is an extension of plant growth into Earth. The mound/tree-bark comparison carries forward the previous lecture: vitality belongs to relationships among plant, soil and organic products, rather than to an isolated ingredient. Steiner uses flies in a dirty room to challenge microbial inoculation. He treats microorganisms as indicators or consequences of processes in manure and gives priority to the larger process. He also says mineral fertilizers enliven only the watery part, whereas conditioned organic material can enliven solid earth. These are strong historical arguments, not a modern demonstration that microorganisms or mineral nutrients are unimportant. The selected passage distinguishes chemical abundance from a capacity to take up and use what is present. His tiny-dose explanation invokes cosmic contributions, including silicic acid, mercury, arsenic and lead, and credits Kolisko's investigations. Naming those substances explains the lecture's claim; it is not an instruction to add them. Carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulfur are discussed through their interactions with potash and lime. At capture 106 the chemical reasoning becomes explicit: Steiner asserts that hydrogen assists potash and lime in transforming into nitrogen. He also says silicon becomes a substance absent from the contemporary element list. Calling this hidden alchemy preserves what the text claims; translating it merely as ordinary nutrient recycling would change its meaning. His aim is a receptive, self-regulating living process, but the lecture's asserted explanation and independent verification remain different questions. Key concept In the lecture, fertility requires living relationships that supposedly enable reception and use of substances, beyond simply increasing their quantity. Course example The nitrogen discussion needs three distinct boxes. The named starting substances are potash and lime, with hydrogen assigned an assisting role. The proposed process is their transformation into nitrogen. The predicted result is a changed capacity of living soil to supply what plants need. Calling the middle box recycling would imply that existing nitrogen is merely being moved or reused, which is not the claim stated here. Conversely, accurately naming elemental transformation does not establish that it occurred. The reading map preserves a difficult claim so that the proposed mechanism and the evidence for it can be examined separately. Keep this distinction Macrocosmic means the larger cosmic relationships in Steiner's explanation. The flies analogy does not independently establish the causal role of soil microorganisms, and the lecture's alchemy claim is distinct from a chemical measurement. title: Six preparations: differentiated roles and qualified claims
text: ← Full course Six preparations: differentiated roles and qualified claims By the end of this lesson: Compare the six compost preparations by intended role and form, including the source’s qualifications. Learn a family of different roles The six compost preparations are a family with different assigned roles. They are intended as additions to manure or compost, not as six substitutes for it. The later numbers 502–507 are labels supplied in the edition’s notes. Start by asking which relationship each plant is meant to support. The animal enclosures and seasonal exposures are part of the source’s theory, not incidental packaging. Yarrow and chamomile Yarrow, later 502, is related to sulfur and potash and is enclosed in a male red-deer bladder. Chamomile, 503, adds a calcium relationship as well as potash and sulfur, with cattle intestines as its enclosure. Steiner connects those organs and exposures with the activity intended for the manure. He allows possible plant substitutes in parts of the discussion, while preferring the plants he names. Nettle and “intelligent” soil Stinging nettle, 504, is the exception he calls irreplaceable. It has no animal enclosure in his description. He links sulfur, potash, calcium and iron with regulation of decomposition and retention of nitrogen. When he calls manure and soil intelligent, he means a proposed ability to adjust to particular plants’ needs. This is not an assertion that soil thinks conscious human thoughts. Oak, dandelion and valerian Oak bark, 505, is placed in an animal skull and assigned a calcium-related moderation of excessive etheric activity. Dandelion, 506, uses bovine mesentery and is related to receiving silica and potassium influences; mesentery is tissue supporting the intestines. Valerian, 507, is a liquid preparation associated with phosphorus. These different forms matter: the six are not all herbs treated identically. Read the qualifications too Keep the editorial qualifications. Gardner reads the oak calcium percentage as an ash analysis, not a percentage of whole fresh bark, and leaves the exact portion of mesentery uncertain. The lecture’s roles are proposed effects, not independently established disease prevention. Understanding them means knowing both what is claimed and what the source leaves unclear. Growth support has a different aim from weed control Finally, growth promotion is not selective weed control. Steiner acknowledges that supporting growth can benefit plants the grower does not want. He also distinguishes swollen produce from nourishment and retains ordinary manuring. The comparison table below is a study aid to roles and enclosures, not a manufacturing recipe or a field dosage guide. Whether a plant is wanted depends on place and purpose, so a separate question of selective restraint follows. title: Desired growth, unwanted plants and the question of verification
text: ← Full course Desired growth, unwanted plants and the question of verification By the end of this lesson: Explain selective restraint, the historical seed-ash claim and the lecture’s position on verification. Wantedness depends on place and purpose A weed is a plant unwanted in a particular place for a particular purpose. Dandelion can be valued for a preparation and unwanted among young vegetables. Its identity has not changed; its relationship with the grower’s aim has. Steiner explicitly recognizes the plant’s own right to grow. The question becomes selective restraint, not declaring a species worthless everywhere. Growth and a following generation The lecture distinguishes growth within a plant from reproduction into a following generation. In its planetary account, Moon, Mercury and Venus work through earth and lime toward seeds and successive generations; Mars, Jupiter and Saturn work through air, the periphery and silica toward fleshy development. These are the lecture’s proposed relationships. They are not a modern planting calendar, and the account allows influences to persist beyond a single date. What the seed-ash proposal claims His historical weed proposal uses ash from seeds, called pepper because of its appearance. It is meant to reverse reproductive forces rather than promote fertility, with a predicted four-year effect. Understanding the idea requires naming both the target and the proposed reversal. The course explains the historical claim on paper; it does not assign burning or spreading material as a learning activity. Why the lecture’s view of testing needs care The lecture asks for outward verification and invokes the Biological Institute, but also says spiritual-scientific truths are true in themselves and need no experimental confirmation. Steiner presents outward verification as an accommodation to contemporary expectations. Both positions matter: he requests tests while expressing prior certainty about the spiritual account. Do not rewrite him as rejecting every experiment or suspending all judgment until a trial is complete. What an agricultural comparison would need To assess a claimed agricultural effect, conviction and a prediction are not enough. One would need clearly identified plants, comparable treated and untreated areas, records over the claimed period and attention to other differences such as cultivation and weather. This is a course explanation of what a comparison would require, not a report that such a trial has been inspected or that the ash proposal works. Start with the actual interference For a beginner, begin with the concrete problem: where is the plant, what is it doing, and why does it conflict with the crop’s needs? That supports an appropriate management question. Then explain the source’s additional mechanism separately. You can understand a historical proposal accurately while still asking what evidence would support its predicted selective effect. Worked example: dandelion in two places In one designated area, dandelion is being grown for a purpose. Beside a small seedling, the same species may compete for space or resources. Explain the management distinction by location and purpose; the plant has not become a different species. Then state the separate historical claim: seed ash is proposed to counter reproduction over four years. The first observation does not verify the second claim. Original course teaching example; not a quotation from the book. Two questions — optional Why is promoting fertility a different question from selective weed control? See an explanation General growth support can benefit wanted and unwanted plants. Selective restraint asks which plant, where, and for what purpose, then needs its own explanation and evidence. Does asking for tests mean Steiner treats his spiritual account as undecided? See an explanation No. He also declares spiritual truths inherently certain and calls outward verification a concession. Accurate teaching retains his request for tests alongside that prior certainty. title: Pests, plant abnormalities and shared responsibility
text: ← Full course Pests, plant abnormalities and shared responsibility By the end of this lesson: Distinguish organism-specific claims and explain why identification and cooperation matter. Identify the problem before the response A mouse eating stored grain, an insect larva feeding on leaves and a fungal leaf spot are different problems. Identify the organism or process, the damage and the conditions before choosing a response. Steiner also differentiates these cases, though his explanations use spiritual and celestial relationships. Calling everything a pest would hide distinctions needed to understand either the source or the actual farm. Why the mouse argument is different In the mouse discussion, Steiner criticizes poisons, infected bait and compulsory uniform regulation. He proposes a historical skin-ash treatment connected with Venus and Scorpion, arguing that animals carry lunar forces inwardly. This differs from the seed-ash account for unwanted plants. Because mice can return from neighbouring land, his argument also requires cooperation beyond a single property. Read the calendar qualifications The editorial notes distinguish the visible Scorpion constellation from the conventional astrological sign. Gardner tentatively reads behind the Sun as a timing relationship in which Venus sets afterward, rather than an invisible position directly behind it. Keep that editorial interpretation separate from Steiner’s words. The later discussion also leaves species-specific insect timings and larval/adult differences for investigation. Why the plant argument starts elsewhere The plant-abnormality account starts elsewhere. Steiner says plants lack an actual astral body , unlike animals and humans, and therefore do not become ill in the same sense. He describes excessive lunar vitality mediated by water as disrupting the normal path toward seed formation and favouring fungi and parasites. This is the lecture’s anthroposophical explanation, not a diagnosis that can be made from a leaf spot alone. What horsetail is intended to do Horsetail, Equisetum arvense, is proposed to counter that excessive water mediation, with a comparison to kidney activity. The analogy explains the intended role; it does not establish the cause of a particular disease or verify a treatment. The discussion explicitly acknowledges an untested vineyard application and retains proven ordinary methods. Those qualifications prevent the general idea from becoming a promise for every crop and climate. Why responsibility extends beyond the fence Shared responsibility connects the cases. Neighbours may need to coordinate observations and appropriate management because organisms cross boundaries. Steiner prefers persuasion through shared understanding to imposed uniformity and discusses possible misuse of knowledge. For this course, practise identification, records and an explanation of the proposed mechanism. Historical ash procedures, wildlife handling and treatment of an undiagnosed plant problem are not learning assignments. Worked example: a spotted leaf after wet weather Record what is known: crop, visible symptoms, affected area and recent conditions. Wet weather alone does not identify a cause. Explain the lecture’s model separately: excessive water-mediated lunar vitality is said to favour abnormal fungal processes, with horsetail assigned a counteracting role. Seek appropriate identification and management guidance for the real plant. The model, the kidney analogy and the diagnosis are three different things. Original course teaching example; not a quotation from the book. Two questions — optional Why should the same explanation not be applied automatically to weeds, mice and fungal symptoms? See an explanation The source assigns different mechanisms to plant reproduction, animal relationships and excessive water-mediated vitality. Real management also requires identifying the actual organism or process. What does neighbour cooperation establish, and what does it not establish? See an explanation It addresses the fact that organisms and management consequences cross boundaries. It does not, by itself, verify the source’s ash, zodiac or horsetail mechanisms. title: Explaining biodynamics with its sources in view
text: ← Full course Explaining biodynamics with its sources in view By the end of this lesson: Give a clear beginner explanation of biodynamics, its preparation families and the questions still open. Build an explanation from relationships You can now explain biodynamics through a connected sequence rather than a list of unfamiliar names. Begin with a particular place: soil, crops, animals, landscape and human decisions influence one another. Biodynamics treats these relationships as a living individuality within a living cosmos and adds specially prepared materials intended to influence living processes. Give the listener a concrete example Use a real relationship to make that understandable. Crop residues and animal manure can connect one season’s growth with later soil care. Timing changes what work is appropriate. The approach asks about these connections across the whole farm, including what comes in and what leaves. It does not mean a farm has no need for outside resources or that every garden must keep livestock. Include the spiritual premise Then name the additional spiritual explanation. Steiner describes nature beings, formative ethers and celestial relationships as active in life. Courtney selects these lectures to place preparations within that wider view. Understanding that connection is essential: reducing biodynamics to composting would leave out what this anthology is trying to teach, while speaking only of invisible beings would leave out its agricultural argument. Explain preparation families by role Explain preparations by role. Horn manure and horn silica form a soil/plant polarity; the six compost preparations have differentiated intended activities; horsetail belongs to the water-mediated vitality discussion and receives special emphasis from Courtney. Ordinary manuring remains part of the agricultural account. Naming these families communicates more than reciting 500 through 508 without explaining the differences. Say what kind of claim you are making Keep authors and evidence clear. Steiner’s dated lectures, later editorial notes, Courtney’s extensions and the course’s examples do different work. A spiritual mechanism is a proposed explanation; a predicted crop effect is another claim; an inspected agricultural comparison is a further kind of evidence. The discussion includes both requests for tests and strong prior spiritual certainty. A fair explanation retains both. Continue with the wider farm The next step is to follow the questions this selection leaves open. Its three Agriculture chapters are lectures 4–6 of the full eight-lecture course. The companion course adds the surrounding foundations, landscape relationships and animal feeding. Return to a figure or a worked example whenever a term becomes difficult; the goal is to explain the relationships in your own words, not merely recognize book references. Worked example: answer a visitor in three steps “Biodynamics considers the relationships of soil, crops, animals, surroundings and people as a living whole.” “It also understands that whole spiritually, relates work to celestial rhythms and uses preparations assigned distinct roles.” “This course explains those proposals and their sources. Knowing the proposed role is different from having verified an effect on a particular farm.” Original course teaching example; not a quotation from the book. Course explanation Understand the idea The anthology begins by asking how a living farm relates to a living cosmos, then selects lectures that describe an unseen nature world. The 1912 pair concerns soul education, nature spirits, temporal rhythms and planetary purpose. The 1923 pair presents elemental work in plant processes, nourishment, constructive and destructive activity. This gives Courtney a context for interpreting agriculture. The agricultural selections develop a source-specific account of soil vitality, fertilization, horn manure and horn silica; six compost preparations; and the regulation of weeds, animal pests and fungal growth. Steiner’s discussion answers sometimes request practical trials, distinguish enhancement from replacement, and acknowledge untested applications. Editorial notes qualify particular terms and calendar references. These qualifications coexist with Steiner’s assertion, in Agriculture III, that spiritual truths do not depend on experimental confirmation. A faithful explanation must preserve this tension. Explaining a proposed spiritual mechanism, reporting a practice and establishing a reproducible agricultural effect are different tasks. Courtney likewise insists on preparations while admitting uncertainty about calendars and personal interpretation. The course has reviewed the complete supplied anthology, including its headnotes, discussions, notes and bibliography. Its GA 327 selection contains lectures 4–6. The separate Agriculture course now follows all eight lectures and their discussions, adding the whole-farm foundations, landscape and animal-feeding argument. Bibliographic mentions of nutrition or plant science still identify wider work rather than independently evaluated outcomes. Key concept A faithful synthesis explains both the relationships a source proposes and the different status of its claims and qualifications. Course example A short synthesis could begin: Courtney selects spiritual nature lectures to frame his emphasis on preparations. Steiner’s agricultural selections then explain soil vitality, differentiated preparations and proposed control of unwanted growth. Their discussions ask for trials and preserve ordinary farming, while Agriculture III also treats spiritual truths as independently certain. The two statements should remain together: an author can request outward confirmation while regarding the underlying account as already true. A remaining question is what independently examined results would support a specific predicted effect. That question differs from whether the anthology has been accurately summarized. Keep this distinction Finishing this anthology means understanding its selected argument, not completing every agriculture lecture or verifying all the claimed effects. title: 500: horn manure — making and soil application
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 500: horn manure — making and soil application A manure-filled cow horn is matured underground through the local winter. The recovered material is later stirred in water for a soil-directed spray. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Materials and the intended role Fill, bury and recover Store the concentrate, not a diluted spray How and when to apply Worked decision: a dry seedbed Materials and the intended role Classical horn manure uses fresh cow manure and a sound cow horn. It is intended to support the soil/root side of farming within Steiner’s account. The small field dose is an addition to ordinary fertility management, not enough material to replace the crop’s nutrient supply. Fresh, well-formed cow dung with straw, stones and other foreign matter removed. Record the animal source; do not substitute manure species casually. Sound empty cow horns from a traceable preparation-making source; gloves, a dedicated filling tool and a labelled batch container. A marked burial site with suitable soil, a site sketch and a retrieval record. Choose a place outside drainage channels and waterlogged ground. Fill, bury and recover Prepare the horn and manure with the maker’s hygiene procedure. Fill to the tip with manure, using a narrow tool and gentle tapping to reduce empty cavities. Fill consistently without adding soil or compost to the contents. Label the batch and count the horns. Bury in autumn for the local winter; use the seasonal calendar rather than copying European months into the Southern Hemisphere. Choose depth with the local maker according to fertile soil depth, drainage and frost. As a later reference, the Bucher manual describes a pit around 50–60 cm in suitable soil; the supplied translations give differing historical depths. This is not a reason to dig into a saturated or unsuitable subsoil. Surround the horns with soil, backfill and mark the site so every horn can be found. Use the orientation shown by the local making protocol so water does not collect inside open horns. Leave through winter. In spring, uncover carefully, reconcile the count and empty each horn into a clean labelled container. Keep outside soil and sheath fragments out of the preparation. Have the first batch assessed by an experienced maker. Mature material is usually dark, cohesive and earthy; recognizably raw, green or strongly manure-like material needs further assessment. Colour and smell are quality observations, not pathogen tests. Store the concentrate, not a diluted spray Keep the recovered material cool, dark and moist in its own labelled non-food container, protected from drying, freezing and contamination. Do not leave it in a sunlit window with 501. Follow the maker’s lid and storage-box instructions. Write down the retrieval date and inspect regularly. The shared storage page distinguishes moisture from waterlogging. How and when to apply Check that 500 is suitable for the intended food-crop use and observe applicable manure-derived-input restrictions. Keep it off edible plant surfaces. Measure the treated area and use the application guide’s clearly identified metric example or the actual supplier’s directions. Do not translate a spoonful into grams without knowing the material’s density. Add the measured concentrate to clean, mildly warm water in a roomy vessel. Stir with repeated vortex formation and reversal for one full hour. Filter for the nozzle after stirring. Apply promptly to soil in coarse droplets, preferably late afternoon or early evening when soil is moist and conditions allow coverage without drift or runoff. Typical opportunities are soil preparation, sowing, planting and the start or end of the growing season. Use the target and carrier-water volume to calibrate the equipment. The aim is even soil coverage, not washing the plants or irrigating the plot. If heavy rain, frozen ground, drought or saturated soil make the application unsuitable, choose a better window. Worked decision: a dry seedbed If a seedbed is powder-dry, choosing the right calendar symbol does not solve the moisture problem. First address soil and water conditions. Then calculate the dose for the actual area and plan a suitable evening application. Do not double the preparation because the soil is dry or omit ordinary organic-material management. Sources for this method Classical making sequences follow the supplied books. Later numerical protocols are identified explicitly; practitioner directions describe practice and are not independent efficacy trials. Sources checked 24 October 2026. title: 501: horn silica — making and foliar application
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 501: horn silica — making and foliar application Quartz in a cow horn is exposed through the local summer. Its very small application dose is used as a fine mist on established plant growth. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Use the right mineral and control dust Make the summer preparation Apply to established growth, in a suitable morning window Worked decision: the crop is newly transplanted Use the right mineral and control dust The classical material is finely ground quartz, not sand of unknown composition, lime or diatomaceous earth. Steiner also mentions orthoclase, but a mineral substitution changes the recipe and should not be made casually. Horn silica is intended as the plant-side complement to horn manure; its proposed light-related role does not make it a general nutrient spray. For a beginner, obtain mature 501 or professionally prepared quartz paste through an experienced making group. Grinding, transferring and cleaning up dry quartz can create respirable crystalline silica. The traditional method is described below, but this guide does not turn uncontrolled dry grinding into a home exercise. Use dust-controlled equipment and appropriate occupational guidance. Make the summer preparation Use an intact, prepared cow horn reserved for the batch and accurately identified finely ground quartz. Keep the mineral wet during the appropriate controlled preparation process. Mix the quartz with clean water into the thin paste described in the book. Fill the horn consistently. Let the maker assess settling, excess water and how the opening is secured; these details vary between making methods. Bury for the local summer at the group’s marked, well-drained site. This reverses 500’s winter exposure. Keep a separate record so 500 and 501 horns are not confused. Retrieve in autumn. Recover the mineral without adding outside soil or fragments of horn. Label it 501 with making and retrieval dates. Store the finished mineral dry according to the maker’s instructions, generally in a glass vessel in a light position. Retain dust precautions whenever handling dry material; dry storage is not a licence to disperse powder. Apply to established growth, in a suitable morning window Confirm the product and crop-specific instructions. Use after the soil-side 500 application in the practitioner sequence and when roots and leaf growth are established; a newly transplanted or stressed plant is not an automatic candidate. Use a sufficiently precise balance for the metric example in the application guide. This is a very small quantity. Do not estimate by a household teaspoon when following a mass-based protocol. Add the measured preparation to clean water and stir with alternating vortex and reversal for one hour. Filter without allowing the measured mineral to be lost as a large settled residue; follow the supplier’s mixing and filtering directions. Spray promptly as a fine, evenly distributed mist over foliage in the early morning, using equipment calibrated for that mist. Avoid dripping saturation, drift and inhaling the spray. Choose a calm window appropriate to the crop, with no impending frost or rain and no severe heat or water stress. Number of repeats depends on crop and protocol; do not turn “several applications” into a daily treatment rule. Worked decision: the crop is newly transplanted The morning may be calm, but crop stage is a separate condition. Give the plant time to establish and check the maker’s directions before choosing 501. Do not copy a neighbouring mature orchard’s spray programme onto nursery trees or young transplants. Early morning describes a window, not permission to ignore plant age or weather. title: 502: yarrow in a stag bladder
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 502: yarrow in a stag bladder Yarrow flowers pass through a summer exposure and then winter burial. The matured contents become a solid compost preparation. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Identify the plant and sheath Follow both phases How and when to use the finished preparation Common mistake: stopping after summer Identify the plant and sheath Yarrow flower heads, Achillea millefolium, positively identified and collected from a suitable uncontaminated site. Dry thinly in shade if they cannot be used at once. A legally sourced stag bladder, prepared for this use by a knowledgeable maker; thread, filling tool, label and a protective hanging basket that admits light and air. A marked winter burial site, batch log and separate storage jar for the final contents. Follow both phases Prepare the flowers and bladder with the making group. If the sheath is dried, soften it using the group’s procedure. Moisten dried flowers only as that procedure specifies; do not turn the contents into a soaking slurry. Fill the bladder with flower heads, close the opening and label it. Keep enough structure to contain the flowers without tearing the sheath. Hang in a protected, light and airy position through the local summer, guarding against pests, loss and destructive weather. Summer exposure is part of this method; it is not yet the final compost product. In autumn, bury the filled bladder in the marked soil site through winter. Record its position and date so it can be recovered without cutting through it. Lift in spring and separate the matured contents from soil and surviving sheath. Have the first batch assessed before storing and portioning it. Do not treat the fresh hanging flowers as finished 502. How and when to use the finished preparation The source links this preparation with sulfur and potassium relationships. That intended role explains its place in the set; the method is more specific than putting a yarrow plant beside a heap. Use the finished material as one member of the complete 502–507 set in newly assembled manure or compost, following the shared compost-placement guide. Keep the five solids separate until each is placed in its own position. The quantity is a measured small addition, not a layer of raw flowers or bark. Do not give this solid an hour of stirring or spray it directly over vegetables. Store a reserve separately, cool, dark and moist under the maker’s directions. Record the batch, retrieval date and pile receiving it. The month of manufacture is different from the time of compost application: a finished stored preparation can be used when a suitable new pile is assembled. Common mistake: stopping after summer A dry, flower-filled bladder after summer has completed only the first phase. Label the next task as winter burial, not compost application. The two-season sequence is the distinguishing making process. Sources for this method Classical making sequences follow the supplied books. Later numerical protocols are identified explicitly; practitioner directions describe practice and are not independent efficacy trials. Sources checked 24 October 2026. title: 503: chamomile in cattle intestine
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 503: chamomile in cattle intestine Identified chamomile flowers are enclosed in prepared cattle intestine and matured through winter burial. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Use flowers and the correct casing Make and bury the flower-filled casing How and when to use the finished preparation Common mistake: confusing the flower with the preparation Use flowers and the correct casing German chamomile, Matricaria chamomilla, also known as M. recutita, with the flower heads collected and gently dried if required. Do not choose a lookalike by common name alone. Prepared cattle intestine from a traceable, permitted source, together with tying thread and a suitable filling tool. Obtain the casing already prepared for this purpose; handling an unprocessed organ is not needed for a first application lesson. A labelled, protected burial location and a separate storage vessel. Make and bury the flower-filled casing Check the plant identity and remove foreign material. Follow the group’s procedure for moistening dried flower heads so they can be packed without becoming a wet slurry. Prepare a manageable length of casing, tie one end and fill with the flowers. Distribute the contents evenly; avoid both loose air pockets and overfilling that splits the tissue. Close the other end, attach a durable identification record and place in the protected burial site in autumn. Cover with suitable soil and leave through winter. The site should permit transformation without flooding, disturbance by animals or roots growing through the contents. Recover in spring, keeping each batch separate. Remove outside soil and remaining sheath, assess the matured contents and place in the 503 storage jar. Record any batch that is incomplete rather than silently mixing it with sound material. How and when to use the finished preparation Steiner assigns chamomile a relationship with calcium, sulfur, potassium and retention of nitrogen in manure. The preparation is not the same as chamomile tea poured over soil. Use the finished material as one member of the complete 502–507 set in newly assembled manure or compost, following the shared compost-placement guide. Keep the five solids separate until each is placed in its own position. The quantity is a measured small addition, not a layer of raw flowers or bark. Do not give this solid an hour of stirring or spray it directly over vegetables. Store a reserve separately, cool, dark and moist under the maker’s directions. Record the batch, retrieval date and pile receiving it. The month of manufacture is different from the time of compost application: a finished stored preparation can be used when a suitable new pile is assembled. Common mistake: confusing the flower with the preparation A bag of dried chamomile is a making ingredient. A packet of mature 503 contains material that has passed through the enclosing and burial process. Read the label before calculating a compost addition. title: 504: nettle — the full-year preparation
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 504: nettle — the full-year preparation Nettle is the classical compost preparation without an animal sheath. Its distinguishing maturation period is a full year underground. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Harvest the suitable above-ground material Allow the complete year How and when to use the finished preparation Common mistake: substituting liquid nettle feed Harvest the suitable above-ground material Identified stinging nettle, classically Urtica dioica, harvested around the beginning of flowering. Use above-ground material, removing roots and coarse unwanted matter. Regional nettle substitutions require a knowledgeable local maker. Protective gloves and clean cutting tools. Dry material, if used, needs the making group’s specified moistening procedure. A retrievable soil-contact arrangement that keeps the nettles identifiable and separates them from surrounding soil; the book describes a peat surround. A labelled marker and separate storage jar complete the record. Allow the complete year Harvest and sort the plant, using gloves to avoid stings. Chop or arrange the material so it packs evenly and can later be recovered. Prepare the marked site and the group’s retrievable container or separation layer. Pack nettle material consistently. No bladder, intestine, skull or mesentery is added. Bury and record the exact date, location and quantity. Keep surrounding insulation or soil out of the plant material as far as the chosen method allows. Leave for a whole year, through both summer and winter. Make the next annual batch before relying on the current one being ready; this prevents a gap in supply. Recover after the annual cycle and assess. The remaining amount may be much smaller than the original plant bulk. Remove outside material and store the dark matured contents as 504; some stems may remain identifiable. How and when to use the finished preparation The source assigns nettle a regulating role in decomposition and nitrogen retention. “Intelligent soil” describes the proposed responsiveness to different plants, not human consciousness in the heap. Use the finished material as one member of the complete 502–507 set in newly assembled manure or compost, following the shared compost-placement guide. Keep the five solids separate until each is placed in its own position. The quantity is a measured small addition, not a layer of raw flowers or bark. Do not give this solid an hour of stirring or spray it directly over vegetables. Store a reserve separately, cool, dark and moist under the maker’s directions. Record the batch, retrieval date and pile receiving it. The month of manufacture is different from the time of compost application: a finished stored preparation can be used when a suitable new pile is assembled. Common mistake: substituting liquid nettle feed Nettle soaked in a barrel to make a liquid plant feed is a different product. It has not passed through 504’s year underground. Do not use the same name, dose or storage record for the two. Sources for this method Classical making sequences follow the supplied books. title: 505: oak bark in a prepared animal skull
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 505: oak bark in a prepared animal skull The classical method encloses crushed oak bark in a skull and exposes it to a wet, organic environment through winter. This requires a controlled making site. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Choose traceable material and a contained site Fill, expose and recover through the group’s protocol How and when to use the finished preparation First-season choice Choose traceable material and a contained site The book names Quercus robur bark and a domestic-animal skull. Obtain identified bark from a suitable supplier or trained collector without damaging a living tree by ring-barking it. The bark is reduced to small particles; it is not an oak-leaf infusion. Use a lawfully sourced skull professionally prepared for this work. Historical accounts discuss the brain cavity and its lining, while later preparation and animal-by-product procedures differ. Do not use a found carcass or remove brain tissue yourself. A local preparation group should supply and handle the appropriate sheath and disposal procedure. The winter environment is deliberately wet and rich in decomposing plant matter. Choose a contained, protected preparation-making arrangement that prevents contamination of wells, streams and irrigation water. The historical reference to a swamp-like place is not permission to put animal materials into a public watercourse. Fill, expose and recover through the group’s protocol Identify the oak bark, prepare the particles and document the skull source. Prepare the container or wet pit before opening or filling the sheath. Under the trained maker’s procedure, pack the bark into the prepared cranial cavity and secure the openings so contents remain identifiable and recoverable. Place in the controlled wet organic environment in autumn. Maintain the intended moisture relationship through winter without allowing uncontrolled escape of animal residues or contaminated water. Retrieve in spring using dedicated tools and gloves. Recover the transformed bark separately from skull fragments and outside material. Let the experienced maker assess the batch and any required conditioning before storage. Keep the batch identity and arrange lawful disposal or permitted reuse of the remaining sheath. Strong odour is not a test of either efficacy or food safety. How and when to use the finished preparation Steiner assigns oak bark a calcium-related moderation of excessive etheric activity. This is the intended role in the set, not a diagnosis or a demonstrated cure for every plant disease. Use the finished material as one member of the complete 502–507 set in newly assembled manure or compost, following the shared compost-placement guide. Keep the five solids separate until each is placed in its own position. The quantity is a measured small addition, not a layer of raw flowers or bark. Do not give this solid an hour of stirring or spray it directly over vegetables. Store a reserve separately, cool, dark and moist under the maker’s directions. Record the batch, retrieval date and pile receiving it. The month of manufacture is different from the time of compost application: a finished stored preparation can be used when a suitable new pile is assembled. First-season choice If you do not have a suitable making group and contained site, obtain mature 505 and learn compost placement first. This still teaches its actual application. Improvising with an unidentified skull beside a stream does not make the classical method more faithful. Sources for this method Classical making sequences follow the supplied books. title: 506: dandelion in bovine mesentery
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 506: dandelion in bovine mesentery Dandelion flowers are wrapped in the specified bovine membrane and matured through winter burial. The membrane is not the stomach lining called tripe. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Identify flower and membrane separately Form the flower parcel How and when to use the finished preparation Common mistake: substituting tripe Identify flower and membrane separately Dandelion flowers, classically Taraxacum officinale, accurately identified and harvested at an appropriate flowering stage. Use clean, sound flowers and dry them gently if needed. Prepared bovine mesentery or the membrane specified by the chosen making tradition, from a permitted traceable source. The supplied edition notes uncertainty over the exact portion: record what the maker actually uses. Thread, a label, dedicated tools, a protected winter burial location and a separate storage jar. Form the flower parcel Prepare flowers and membrane by the group’s established procedure. If dried flowers are moistened before filling, use only the amount needed for that method rather than making a watery mass. Lay out the prepared membrane, place the flowers inside and fold it into a contained parcel. Secure with thread so the contents remain together during burial. Label and bury in autumn in the marked fertile-soil location. Protect it from animal disturbance, flooding and invasive roots. Leave through the local winter and retrieve in spring. Locate the parcel from the site record rather than probing blindly through it. Separate the matured flower material from outside soil and surviving membrane. Assess and store as 506. Keep an incomplete or questionable batch separate for review rather than adding it to the established supply. How and when to use the finished preparation The source relates this preparation to silica and potassium reception. Its membrane and seasonal process distinguish it from raw dandelion leaves, root tea or an ordinary compost ingredient. Use the finished material as one member of the complete 502–507 set in newly assembled manure or compost, following the shared compost-placement guide. Keep the five solids separate until each is placed in its own position. The quantity is a measured small addition, not a layer of raw flowers or bark. Do not give this solid an hour of stirring or spray it directly over vegetables. Store a reserve separately, cool, dark and moist under the maker’s directions. Record the batch, retrieval date and pile receiving it. The month of manufacture is different from the time of compost application: a finished stored preparation can be used when a suitable new pile is assembled. Common mistake: substituting tripe Tripe and mesentery are anatomically different. Ask the maker to identify the sheath and write it into the batch record. A local variation should be named as a variation, not silently presented as the book’s exact specification. Sources for this method Classical making sequences follow the supplied books. title: 507: valerian flower liquid
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 507: valerian flower liquid Valerian is the liquid member of the compost set. It is made from flowers, not valerian-root medicine, and it is not buried in an animal organ. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Begin with the flower method A classical pressed-flower route Use as the liquid part of the compost set Common mistake: confusing concentrate and spray Begin with the flower method Use correctly identified Valeriana officinalis flowers and clean, dedicated crushing, pressing, straining and bottling equipment. Root tinctures sold for human use are not interchangeable with 507. The supplied introduction describes flower juice allowed to ferment for a few weeks; later makers use several extraction methods. Record whether a batch is pressed juice or a specified water extraction, because the resulting concentrations may differ. A classical pressed-flower route Collect sound flowers from an identified clean source and remove stems or foreign material according to the maker’s method. Work promptly so a heap of flowers does not heat and spoil. Crush the flowers with dedicated clean equipment and press out the juice. Strain into a labelled non-food vessel, recording flower source, date and yield. Use the maker’s controlled fermentation procedure. Keep the vessel protected and cool, and permit fermentation gas to escape safely. Do not seal an actively fermenting batch in a rigid airtight bottle. The book’s few weeks is a broad indication, not a universal finished-on-day-21 specification. Temperature, extraction and batch condition matter. Have a first batch assessed before use. Once the process is complete and gas production has ceased, transfer to the maker’s specified labelled storage bottle, generally brown glass in a cool dark place. Follow directions about headspace and closure. Recheck for renewed pressure and contamination. Use as the liquid part of the compost set The intended role in Steiner’s account relates to phosphorus. In compost application, a measured amount of finished 507 is diluted and stirred for the short time in the chosen compost protocol, then introduced to the pile. It is not automatically stirred for an hour like the field sprays. The shared compost page gives one complete-set method and identifies its source. Use the supplier’s dose for the actual liquid, because juice and water-extract methods are not necessarily equivalent. Keep concentrate and diluted application mixture in distinctly labelled containers. Do not drink or use the liquid as a human remedy. Later frost-related uses and mixtures with 500 are separate practitioner protocols. This course’s core compost instruction does not establish frost protection and does not replace frost cloth, irrigation designed for frost management or crop-specific weather planning. Do not add 507 to every field spray merely because a different supplier combines it in one product. Common mistake: confusing concentrate and spray A small bottle of 507 concentrate and several litres of diluted compost mixture are different stages. Label the first with its extraction method and batch; label the second with dilution and time of mixing. This prevents using a diluted mixture later as though it were the original concentrate. title: 508: horsetail — fresh and fermented decoctions
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course 508: horsetail — fresh and fermented decoctions Learn two distinct horsetail methods. “Fresh tea” means freshly made decoction; it does not necessarily mean the starting herb was freshly harvested. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Identify the herb before making a batch JPI fresh-decoction protocol JPI fermented-decoction protocol Choose a window and keep the recipes separate Worked dilution: one plus nine is ten parts Identify the herb before making a batch The named plant is Equisetum arvense. Obtain positively identified material from a reliable grower or supplier; other horsetail species are not interchangeable and some are toxic. Do not identify it from this course’s symbolic comet drawing. Use a dedicated cooking vessel, clean water, strainer, labelled containers, timer and appropriate sprayer. Horsetail is proposed in the source for excessive water-mediated vitality and fungal problems. A wet period is a reason to inspect a crop, not enough to diagnose every leaf mark. Check crop identity, symptoms, weather, drainage and appropriate plant-health advice before relying on a spray. JPI fresh-decoction protocol Use 1.5 oz dried herb (about 42.5 g) in 1 US quart water (about 0.95 L). Simmer 1 hour; cool and strain. Add 2 US gallons water (about 7.6 L); stir 20 minutes. Apply as a fine foliar spray. The stated batch covers up to 1 acre (about 4,047 m²). JPI fermented-decoction protocol Simmer the same herb amount in 1 US gallon water (about 3.8 L) for 1 hour; cool. Ferment under a loose lid in a cool place for 10–14 days; filter. Dilute 1 part concentrate with 9 parts water; stir 20 minutes. Direct this version to soil. Choose a window and keep the recipes separate These are JPI’s later practitioner recipes, not numerical directions quoted from Steiner. US units and approximate metric conversions are shown together so the two methods cannot be accidentally combined. Evaporation changes the recovered volume; do not promise an exact final volume from the starting water alone. Prepare the fresh version for prompt use after cooling. For the fermented version, label the concentrate with its making date and dilution; use the maker’s storage and expiry directions. Fermentation gases require a safe venting arrangement. Keep all material out of food and animal feed. Choose conditions that permit the intended target to be covered without runoff, wind drift or immediate wash-off. A repeated-treatment schedule belongs to a crop-specific protocol; do not assume a daily spray is needed throughout the season. Do not add the fermented concentrate to a foliar batch merely because both containers say 508. Worked dilution: one plus nine is ten parts For the fermented method, 100 mL of concentrate plus 900 mL of water makes 1 L of application mixture. It does not mean 100 mL topped up with 1 L of water. A ratio describes dilution; area coverage still depends on the chosen protocol and calibrated sprayer. Sources for this method Classical making sequences follow the supplied books. Later numerical protocols are identified explicitly; practitioner directions describe practice and are not independent efficacy trials. Sources checked 24 October 2026.
