title: Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Distinguish preparation dose, carrier-water volume and treated area. Then match equipment, plant stage and weather to the preparation. All preparations Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Three quantities that must not be confused Work the area calculation before mixing Calibrate with clean water first The one-hour stirring sequence for 500 and 501 When the conditions fit Why another supplier may give another amount Record what was actually done Three quantities that must not be confused Dose means the amount of mature preparation for an area. Carrier water is the liquid used to distribute that dose. Area is the ground surface being treated. Increasing carrier water does not automatically mean increasing preparation. Neither 500 nor 501 is irrigation or a bulk nutrient application. For the worked metric example here, use 500 at 100 g/ha and 501 at 4 g/ha, each in 50 L/ha of carrier water. These are later manual rates, not universal values dictated in the 1924 lecture. The Bucher manual allows 25–50 L/ha; this calculator consistently uses its 50 L end. Brazilian ABD guidance also gives 4 g/ha in 50 L for 501. Work the area calculation before mixing One hectare is 10,000 m². Multiply the per-hectare quantity by your area divided by 10,000. A rectangular bed 5 m by 20 m is 100 m², or 0.01 ha. Keep units written beside the numbers so grams are not mistaken for millilitres. The table and calculator below are arithmetic teaching aids for this one metric protocol. They are not a recommendation to measure a nearly invisible quantity with a kitchen spoon. For tiny silica doses, obtain an accurately measured portion, use a suitable precision balance, or work with a group treating a larger measured area. Keep the full stirring time even when the area is smaller. Worked examples for this metric protocol Area (m²) 500 (g) 501 (g) Water for either spray (L) 100 1 0.04 0.5 1,000 10 0.4 5 10,000 100 4 50 Calculate this example for your area This scales one cited example. Check the actual product protocol before using the result. Preparation 500 — horn manure 501 — horn silica Measured area in square metres (m²) Measure the area first. An acre is not a hectare. Retain the full one-hour stirring time. Preparation amount: 10 g Carrier water: 5 L The calculator requires JavaScript. Use the worked table and formula above without it. Calibrate with clean water first Mark a known area and fill the sprayer with a measured volume of clean water. Use the actual nozzle, pressure, walking speed and target pattern you intend to use. Spray the test area evenly and measure the water consumed. Scale this to the whole treated area. A pressure setting alone does not establish a volume per hectare. For 500, arrange a coarse soil-directed pattern; for 501, a fine mist directed at established foliage. Keep people, animals, nearby crops and water supplies out of drift. Check that the planned carrier volume can actually cover the site with your equipment. If it cannot, adjust equipment or use the supplier’s suitable carrier-volume guidance; do not silently change preparation dose. Clean the sprayer and filter, check for leaks and reserve enough time to apply the batch promptly after stirring. Equipment used for pesticides or other incompatible products requires appropriate decontamination; dedicated clean equipment avoids that problem. The one-hour stirring sequence for 500 and 501 Prepare clean water in a roomy stable vessel with enough space for vigorous movement without splashing out the measured dose. Use mildly warm rather than hot water, as the chosen maker directs. Add the separately measured preparation. Start the timer when the actual stirring sequence begins. Stir in one direction until a deep rotating funnel forms. Reverse decisively, breaking that pattern, then build a funnel in the opposite direction. Continue alternating formation and reversal. Continue for one full hour. Smaller areas change dose and carrier volume, not the duration. Mixing two preparations together is a separate protocol; do not infer permission from the fact both are stirred. Filter as required by the nozzle, maintaining the intended mixture. Apply promptly; do not plan to leave a stirred batch overnight or treat it as stored concentrate. Compost-valerian and horsetail methods have their own shorter stirring instructions. “All preparations need an hour” is incorrect. When the conditions fit 500: moist workable soil, commonly late afternoon or early evening around soil preparation, sowing, planting or seasonal transition. Do not spray edible surfaces or create runoff. 501: established roots and appropriate foliage, commonly a calm early morning. Check crop restrictions; avoid frost risk, impending rain and severe heat or water stress. For both: distinguish a typical practice window from a guarantee. A forecast, soil observation and crop stage are more useful than following a calendar date while ignoring unsuitable conditions. Follow the actual product’s directions on repeat frequency and permitted use. Disease symptoms, nutrient shortage or water stress need their own diagnosis and management. Why another supplier may give another amount JPI describes 500 in a quarter-cup unit per acre and 501 in a teaspoon unit, each with a US-gallon carrier recipe. Those are product-specific volumetric directions. This guide’s metric example uses mass per hectare. A teaspoon is not automatically 4 g and a cup of moist manure does not have a universal mass. Follow one coherent protocol for the supplied product. Prepared 500, 500P, barrel compound and proprietary starters may contain other materials. Their doses are not automatically those of plain horn manure. Likewise, a supplied packet of compost preparations is not defined by the mass of an arbitrary pinch. Record what was actually done Date, location, measured area, crop and growth stage; preparation identity, maker and batch. Protocol, measured dose, carrier-water volume, water source, stirring start/end and spraying start/end. Weather, wind, soil moisture, sprayer/nozzle and coverage; other management done at the same time. Later observations, including no visible difference, adverse effects and a comparable untreated area where feasible. Keep interpretation separate from the observation. title: A seasonal calendar for making and applying
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course A seasonal calendar for making and applying Plan by the local season and crop cycle. The season for making a preparation is not automatically the season for applying it. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 Storage, batch quality and working records Four dates for one preparation A first-year route that does not require waiting for every batch Moon and zodiac calendars: identify the system Worked decision: summer in January Four dates for one preparation Record ingredient harvest, enclosure or burial, recovery and field or compost application as separate dates. For example, 500 is made through winter but applied when an appropriate soil-management window occurs. A stored compost preparation can be inserted whenever a suitable new pile is made. Do not confuse six months of preparation-making with the maturation time of that pile. The table below describes temperate seasonal correspondences. Northern autumn is approximately September–November; Southern autumn is approximately March–May. Actual frost, soil moisture, rainfall pattern and growing season can shift the work. At high altitude or near the equator, obtain a regional making calendar instead of merely swapping month names. Approximate seasons in temperate climates Season Northern Hemisphere Southern Hemisphere Autumn September–November March–May Winter December–February June–August Spring March–May September–November Summer June–August December–February Making and use sequence — seasonal reference Preparation Sequence Exposure or duration Use when ready 500 Autumn burial → spring recovery Winter Apply when soil-management conditions fit 501 Spring burial → autumn recovery Summer Apply to suitable established growth 502 Flowers and summer hanging → autumn burial → spring recovery Summer plus winter Insert mature material into a new suitable pile 503 / 505 / 506 Autumn placement → spring recovery Winter; 505 has its own wet environment Insert mature material into a new suitable pile 504 Bury → recover about one year later Full annual cycle Plan supply a year ahead 507 Harvest flowers → extraction and controlled fermentation No winter animal-sheath burial Dilute the finished liquid by the chosen compost protocol 508 Identified herb → fresh decoction or specified fermentation No horn burial Match version, crop question and target A first-year route that does not require waiting for every batch Before the growing season: obtain correctly stored mature preparations, learn the measuring and application method, and plan ordinary soil and compost work. At the chosen soil-preparation window: use the selected 500 protocol when soil and crop conditions fit. Record it; do not set a compulsory interval to 501 without the crop-specific protocol. Once plants are established and a suitable morning arrives: consider 501 under the maker’s crop guidance. Keep a record of stage and conditions. When building a suitable pile: insert the complete compost set by its own protocol. Continue compost management and allow maturity before use. Through the year: collect correctly identified ingredients in their harvesting seasons and join a making group for the summer and winter preparations. Plan 504 a full year ahead. When wet conditions or symptoms raise a plant-health question: inspect and diagnose first. If choosing a horsetail protocol, identify fresh versus fermented use and its target rather than following a fixed weekly calendar. Moon and zodiac calendars: identify the system Some biodynamic schools add Moon phases, ascending/descending Moon or constellation categories to their timing. These systems are not interchangeable, and the supplied introduction itself records disagreement and incomplete reproducibility. If you use one, record the calendar, edition, time zone and category. Explain that it is an additional practitioner framework. This guide does not invent universal “root-day” or full-Moon instructions for every preparation. A frozen or flooded bed, strong wind, an unestablished crop or a food-safety restriction is not corrected by an auspicious calendar symbol. Choose a usable agronomic window and follow the specific preparation protocol. Worked decision: summer in January In a temperate Southern Hemisphere location, January is normally part of summer. Treating it as winter because a European example uses January would reverse the intended making exposure. Start with the local season, then check soil and climate; tropical wet/dry cycles require a local adaptation rather than an automatic six-month shift. title: Applying the complete compost set: 502–507
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 Place the five finished solids and the valerian liquid into a suitable manure or compost pile. The preparation set does not replace making and managing the pile properly. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Check the pile and the set A weighed alternative for mature homemade preparations One labelled protocol: the JPI complete set Why the positions and closing matter Care after application Worked decision: a very small garden heap Check the pile and the set Confirm that you have finished 502, 503, 504, 505 and 506 plus finished liquid 507. Raw yarrow, chamomile and nettle are not a substitute for the mature set. Check the supplier’s declared pile capacity; sets from different makers need not contain the same amount. Assess moisture and aeration before insertion. A bone-dry pile or saturated, airless mass needs management first. Suitable composting also requires an appropriate material balance, pile design and decomposition process. Adding preparations does not correct every structural problem or sanitize animal manure. Use dedicated tools and labelled portions. If the material is intended for a food crop, comply with the applicable compost-process and manure-derived-input rules. A dark colour, earthworms or a pleasant smell alone cannot establish a validated pathogen-reduction process. A weighed alternative for mature homemade preparations Bucher’s later manual gives this separate example: 2 g of each solid 502–506 and 5 mL of finished 507 for a heap about 1.5–2 m wide, 1.5 m high and 5–10 m long. Stir the valerian in 3–5 L water for 10–15 minutes; use part inside and the remainder over the surface. See manual pages 65–66. Distribute the five weighed solids separately inside the pile and close the positions as described in the classical method. Use this as a complete named example with a maker who has assessed your material. Sloping heap sides and bulk density mean its outside dimensions are not a universal grams-per-cubic-metre rule. Do not substitute these amounts for the contents of the JPI set below. One labelled protocol: the JPI complete set Make six distributed holes to about mid-depth. Place the five solids separately, one per hole. Stir the supplied 507 dose in 1 US gallon (about 3.8 L) of water for 10 minutes. Pour half into the sixth hole; close every hole with mature compost or soil. Mist the other half over the pile. JPI uses its whole set on smaller piles too, up to a stated 15 tons. Confirm the ton unit with the supplier; do not use the field calculator. Six distributed positions in a compost pile Schematic top view: five separate positions for solids 502 to 506 and a sixth for part of the diluted valerian. Not to scale. 502 503 504 505 506 507 Original course schematic: distribute positions through the actual pile; the drawing prescribes neither compass orientation nor a fixed spacing. The remaining valerian goes over the surface in the selected protocol. Why the positions and closing matter The source describes preparations surrounded by manure, distributed rather than all dropped into one exposed hollow. The practical result is a retrievable application record: each named material has a place, and the hole is closed so it is not left as a drying channel. This diagram is an original course schematic, not a reconstruction of Steiner’s blackboard. The selected JPI example is one method, not a universal rule for every product. Other makers specify a set by cubic metres, a weighed portion or a different valerian distribution. Do not convert tons into cubic metres without the pile’s bulk density, and do not combine half of one protocol with half of another. Care after application Mark the pile with date and preparation batch. Maintain moisture, aeration and the composting process appropriate to the material and intended use. Monitor temperature and condition using the composting plan. If a pile needs turning for sound process management, do not abandon that need because preparations were added. Whether to reapply after rebuilding belongs to the chosen maker’s protocol. Allow the pile to mature for its intended use. A preparation application date is not a compost-ready date and is not the start of a universally valid harvest interval. For slurry or liquid manure, use a specific protocol for that system. The six-hole heap method cannot simply be poured into any tank without regard to mixing, volume or handling hazards. Worked decision: a very small garden heap If you bought a maker’s garden-sized set, follow its stated pile range. If you bought the JPI set described above, do not invent an area-based fraction because the heap occupies only a few square metres. A pile dose and a field-spray dose answer different questions. Measure the pile in the unit required by the supplier. Sources for this method Classical making sequences follow the supplied books. Later numerical protocols are identified explicitly; practitioner directions describe practice and are not independent efficacy trials. Sources checked 24 October 2026. title: Practical guide: preparations 500–508
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course Practical guide: preparations 500–508 Learn what to make, when to make it, how to store it, and where and when to apply it. Begin with the three preparation families, then follow the dedicated method for each material. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Start with the task, not the number A practical learning sequence Set up the work area What these instructions establish Choose a preparation 500: horn manure — making and soil application A manure-filled cow horn is matured underground through the local winter. The recovered material is later stirred in water for a soil-directed spray. 501: horn silica — making and foliar application Quartz in a cow horn is exposed through the local summer. Its very small application dose is used as a fine mist on established plant growth. 502: yarrow in a stag bladder Yarrow flowers pass through a summer exposure and then winter burial. The matured contents become a solid compost preparation. 503: chamomile in cattle intestine Identified chamomile flowers are enclosed in prepared cattle intestine and matured through winter burial. 504: nettle — the full-year preparation Nettle is the classical compost preparation without an animal sheath. Its distinguishing maturation period is a full year underground. 505: oak bark in a prepared animal skull The classical method encloses crushed oak bark in a skull and exposes it to a wet, organic environment through winter. This requires a controlled making site. 506: dandelion in bovine mesentery Dandelion flowers are wrapped in the specified bovine membrane and matured through winter burial. The membrane is not the stomach lining called tripe. 507: valerian flower liquid Valerian is the liquid member of the compost set. It is made from flowers, not valerian-root medicine, and it is not buried in an animal organ. 508: horsetail — fresh and fermented decoctions Learn two distinct horsetail methods. “Fresh tea” means freshly made decoction; it does not necessarily mean the starting herb was freshly harvested. The shared practical guides Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Storage, batch quality and working records Start with the task, not the number Making a preparation and making a spray are different operations. A winter-matured horn-manure preparation may spend months underground; its spray is mixed in water on the day of application. Dried chamomile flowers are an ingredient for 503, not the finished preparation. This guide keeps ingredients, mature preparations and application mixtures distinct. The field preparations are horn manure 500 for soil and horn silica 501 for aerial plant parts. Preparations 502–507 form the compost family: five matured solids and one valerian liquid. Horsetail 508 is a separate herbal decoction, with fresh and fermented versions. Do not give all nine the same stirring time, target surface or storage treatment. A practical learning sequence Read application and quantities first. Learn area, dose, carrier water, stirring and sprayer calibration before mixing a batch. Read the page for the preparation you intend to use. Make a materials list and identify the season, maturation period and application target. Read the shared storage page before obtaining finished material. A prepared substance can be spoiled by the wrong storage even when it was made well. For a first season, obtaining mature preparations from a reliable maker lets you learn application immediately. Making them in a regional group teaches identification, animal-sheath handling and assessment of maturity. Keep a dated record and a comparison area where practicable. Record ordinary soil care too. A crop response alone does not identify a spiritual or material cause. Set up the work area Use dedicated labelled containers, clean stirring tools, a timer, a measuring jug, a suitable balance, a strainer and a sprayer whose output you have measured with clean water. Use gloves for manure, animal tissues and nettles; cover cuts, wash hands, and keep tools out of food preparation. Obtain animal materials through a lawful, traceable source and protect buried material from wildlife. Use clean water and prevent runoff to wells, streams and irrigation supplies. A manure-derived preparation is not automatically hygienically safe because it looks earthy or has little smell. Check the applicable produce-safety and certification requirements before use on food crops. Fine quartz dust can harm lungs. Obtain ready-made 501 or use a trained preparation-making group with appropriate dust controls. Do not dry-grind quartz in a kitchen blender, make airborne dust, or rely on an ordinary cloth face covering. Check plant identity before harvest. Horsetail species are not interchangeable; the drawing in the course is an explanation, not an identification key. What these instructions establish These pages teach the classical methods described in the supplied books and identify later practitioner protocols where numerical examples are used. A detailed recipe explains a practice; it does not by itself establish that the claimed spiritual mechanism or a disease-control effect is true. Ordinary fertility, water management, plant diagnosis and food hygiene remain part of the work. The guide is not a certification standard. Product concentrations, local seasons, permitted animal materials and crop restrictions can differ. Follow the protocol and label for the preparation actually in your hand. Where the books give broad indications rather than a fixed specification, the guide says so instead of inventing a universal value. title: Storage, batch quality and working records
text: ← What Is Biodynamics? course Storage, batch quality and working records Keep mature preparations distinct from raw ingredients and diluted mixtures. Storage requirements differ across the preparation families. All preparations Field application: quantities, stirring and spraying Applying the complete compost set: 502–507 A seasonal calendar for making and applying Label three different stages Different materials need different conditions Inspect condition without claiming a safety test A making record that can be checked later Printable application record Label three different stages An ingredient jar, a finished-preparation jar and a diluted spray container should never carry an ambiguous label such as “nettle” or “500 mix”. Include identity, stage, source, batch, date and, for diluted material, the dilution and time mixed. A plant infusion or a proprietary combined product should be named as such. Keep a small inventory so the amount on hand matches planned work. Obtain only what you can store correctly, and follow the actual maker’s expiry and handling directions. Classical storage traditions vary; the practical aim is to preserve identity and condition without contamination, desiccation, excess water or dangerous pressure. Different materials need different conditions 500 and the five mature solids 502–506: separate labelled jars, cool and dark, retaining their intended moisture without sitting in water. Follow the maker’s breathable-lid and insulated-box arrangement; keep insulation outside the preparation. 501: store the mature mineral dry in its specified glass container in a light location. Do not place it in the moist dark storage used for 500. Avoid releasing dry quartz dust. 507: mature valerian liquid belongs in its own cool, light-protected bottle. Vent active fermentation safely; close as directed once stable. Reassess renewed gas production or a changed batch rather than storing pressure in an airtight container. 508 ingredient: dry identified herb is separate from brewed or fermented liquid. Keep the herb dry, labelled and protected from contamination. Brew fresh material for the planned work; follow the specific maker’s storage directions for any fermented concentrate. Diluted 500 and 501: mix for the application session and use promptly. A bottle left overnight is not a reserve of the original mature preparation. Inspect condition without claiming a safety test Inspect the label, moisture, appearance, pests, container damage and unexpected change before taking a portion. Use clean dedicated tools and do not return a contaminated scoop to the reserve. Keep an uncertain batch separate and ask the maker to assess it. Do not restore an unknown spoiled material merely by adding water or another preparation. Traditional maturity signs such as earthy texture are useful descriptive observations. They do not prove absence of pathogens or establish a food-crop harvest interval. Animal-derived materials and compost must meet the applicable hygiene requirements for their intended use. Keep them away from kitchen utensils, food, drinking water and animal feed. A making record that can be checked later Preparation number and name; plant identification, harvest date and material supplier. Animal-sheath source, preparation method, ingredient amounts and any named departure from the classical recipe. Site plan, depth or container arrangement, burial/exposure date, expected retrieval season and number of units. Recovery date, quantity recovered, observations, assessor and any rejected or incomplete portion. Storage location, condition checks, batches supplied to which field or compost pile, and remaining inventory. Printable application record The form below is a reusable working template. Print it or save the page as a PDF using your browser. It does not transmit entries or save them in this browser. Write the protocol and actual measurements, not only “sprayed biodynamics”. Reusable application record Field Record Date / time ________________________________________________ Place / measured area ________________________________________________ Crop / growth stage ________________________________________________ Preparation / maker / batch ________________________________________________ Protocol / dose / carrier water ________________________________________________ Stirring start / end ________________________________________________ Application start / end ________________________________________________ Weather / wind / soil moisture ________________________________________________ Sprayer / nozzle / calibration ________________________________________________ Other management / comparison area ________________________________________________ Later observations / next action ________________________________________________ Print this page You can also print through the browser menu.
